    SC1 --> Return
    SC3 --> Return
    SCm1 --> Return

Figure 2 — Per-isophote fit loop. Stop codes carry semantics: 0 ok, 1–2 caution, 3 and −1 failure. See Section 8 for the full table.

Convergence with a noise floor

When sigma_bg is provided, effective_rms = max(rms, sigma_bg / √N) with N the number of surviving samples after masking and sigma clipping. This stops the solver from chasing noise-induced asymmetries in LSB regions where rms can dip below the photon-noise limit.

Convergence scale factor

scale in the convergence test is an SMA-dependent factor set by convergence_scaling. The default 'sector_area' uses scale = max(1, sma · Δsma · Δθ) with Δsma the SMA step and Δθ = 2π/N the angular sample spacing, so the threshold scales roughly with the area of one sample sector; 'sqrt_sma' uses max(1, √sma) and 'none' uses 1.

Lazy gradient

By default the radial gradient is evaluated once on iteration 0 and reused. If the geometry stops improving for three consecutive iterations the gradient is re-evaluated. The gradient costs one extra sampling pass (a one-sided difference reusing the current sample), so iterations that reuse the cached gradient cost one sampling pass instead of two.

Gradient-SNR damping

If the local gradient is noisy (SNR < 3), geometry_damping is dynamically reduced so the iteration cannot overfit the noise floor.

Step clipping

Hard caps clip_max_shift, clip_max_pa, clip_max_eps bound the per-iteration update. This prevents runaway divergence when a single iteration crosses an image defect or extreme noise patch.

docs.title: 3. Geometry update mapping
docs.text:
Step 7 of the fit loop picks one geometry parameter to correct per iteration (in the default geometry_update_mode='largest'): the parameter whose harmonic amplitude is largest. This is the same coordinate-descent strategy used by photutils.isophote and IRAF Ellipse (Jedrzejewski 1987). The 'simultaneous' mode instead updates all four parameters every iteration and pairs naturally with a smaller geometry_damping.

argmax index Harmonic term Basis Updated parameter 0 A₁ sin(θ) Center, minor-axis component 1 B₁ cos(θ) Center, major-axis component 2 A₂ sin(2θ) Position angle (PA) 3 B₂ cos(2θ) Ellipticity, with bounds & wrap handling

Constraint flags (fix_center, fix_pa, fix_eps) zero the corresponding harmonic terms in the dominance selection so that constrained axes simply do not enter the argmax.

docs.title: 4. Sampling — φ vs eccentric anomaly
docs.text:
The ellipse is sampled by scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates through compute_ellipse_coords at n_samples = max(64, int(2·π·sma)) points. There are two angular conventions for the basis of the harmonic fit:

flowchart LR
    subgraph phi["use_eccentric_anomaly = False  (default)"]
      P1[Sample uniform in φ<br/>position angle] --> P2[Harmonic basis: φ]
      P2 --> P3[Geometry update in φ]
    end
    subgraph ea["use_eccentric_anomaly = True"]
      E1[Sample uniform in ψ<br/>eccentric anomaly] --> E2[Harmonic basis: ψ]
      E2 --> E3[Geometry update<br/>still in φ-space]
    end

Figure 3 — The two angular conventions for harmonic sampling. Stepping ψ uniformly distributes samples more evenly around a highly elliptical isophote than stepping φ — though not exactly uniformly in arc length — which is one of the two motivations for Ciambur 2015. The other, and the stronger one, is that the geometry corrections are themselves derived in ψ.

When to switch on EA mode

Recommended for ellipticity above ~0.3 and required for edge-on disks and X-shaped / peanut bulges where uniform-in-φ sampling under-samples along the major axis. Geometry updates are still computed in φ-space so that x0, y0, eps, pa retain their usual geometric meaning.

docs.title: 5. Solver — OLS vs WLS
docs.text:
ISOSTER uses a single design-matrix solver internally. The only difference between the two paths is the inner-product matrix.

flowchart TD
    VMChk{"variance_map<br/>provided?"}
    VMChk -- no --> OLS["OLS: min ‖y − Ax‖²<br/>cov = (AᵀA)⁻¹ · σ²_res<br/>(σ²_res from fit residuals)"]
    VMChk -- yes --> WLS["WLS: min ‖W^{½}(y − Ax)‖²<br/>W = diag(1 / σ²ᵢ)<br/>cov = (AᵀWA)⁻¹  (exact)"]
    OLS --> Same["Identical fitting loop, identical convergence rule.<br/>No variance map ⇒ plain OLS solve everywhere."]
    WLS --> Same

Figure 4 — OLS / WLS branch. The WLS covariance is exact: no residual-variance rescaling is needed.

Quantity OLS WLS Normal equations AᵀA x = Aᵀy AᵀWA x = AᵀWy Parameter covariance (AᵀA)⁻¹ · σ²_res (AᵀWA)⁻¹ Intensity error rms / √N √[(AᵀWA)⁻¹]₀₀ (fit covariance; forced photometry uses the exact 1/√Σ σᵢ⁻²) Gradient error scatter-based √(Var(mean_c) + Var(mean_g)) / Δr with Var(mean) = 1/Σ σᵢ⁻²

What WLS buys you

Errors come directly from the per-pixel variance map rather than from fit residuals; cosmic rays and hot pixels are automatically down-weighted; gradient error is separated from galaxy-structure scatter (arms, dust, bars). WLS composes with all constraint and harmonic modes.

docs.title: 6. Harmonics — post-hoc vs ISOFIT
docs.text:
All higher-order harmonics (a₃, b₃, a₄, b₄, … for orders in harmonic_orders, default [3, 4]) are available, but how they are computed differs along two axes: when they are fitted, and which design matrix is used during iteration. The two paths converge on the same output schema.

flowchart TD
    SH{"simultaneous_harmonics?"}
    SH -- "false (default)" --> Post["Inside loop: 5-param fit<br/>(I₀, A₁, B₁, A₂, B₂ only)"]
    Post --> PostFit["After convergence:<br/>fit harmonic_orders post-hoc<br/>on converged geometry"]
    SH -- true --> ModeChk{"isofit_mode"}
    ModeChk -- "'in_loop'" --> InLoop["Joint design matrix every iteration:<br/>[1, sin θ, cos θ, sin 2θ, cos 2θ,<br/>sin n₁θ, cos n₁θ, …]<br/>Cross-correlations between<br/>geometry & higher harmonics"]
    ModeChk -- "'original'" --> Orig["5-param fit inside loop;<br/>one extended joint fit<br/>after convergence<br/>(Ciambur 2015 original)"]
    InLoop --> FBChk{"n_points <<br/>2 · L + 5?<br/>(L = len(harmonic_orders))"}
    Orig --> FBChk
    FBChk -- yes --> Fallback["Fall back to 5-param fit<br/>(RuntimeWarning on first hit)"]
    FBChk -- no --> Done
    Fallback --> Done([a_n, b_n, errors in dict])
    PostFit --> Done

Figure 5 — Harmonic-fit modes. 'in_loop' is the most aggressive variant and produces the cleanest RMS estimate at ~25–35% extra cost over the default post-hoc path.

docs.title: 7. LSB outskirt strategies
docs.text:
Two independent features address geometry drift in the low-surface-brightness outskirts. They are designed to compose: outer-region regularization is a soft Tikhonov damping that runs in every outward iteration once the SMA crosses an onset radius; the automatic LSB lock is a hard one-way switch that, when triggered, freezes geometry for the remainder of outward growth.

flowchart TD
    Outward([Outward growth iteration]) --> OR{"use_outer_center<br/>_regularization?"}
    OR -- yes --> Ref["Inner reference (built once):<br/>flux-weighted mean of inward<br/>isophote (x₀, y₀, eps, pa)<br/>up to sma0·outer_reg_ref_sma_factor"]
    Ref --> Ramp["Per-iteration:<br/>λ(sma) = strength / (1 + exp(−(sma − onset)/width))<br/>damps Δx₀, Δy₀, Δeps, Δpa toward reference<br/>(damping mode) or pulls geometry (solver mode)"]
    Ramp --> AL
    OR -- no --> AL
    AL{"lsb_auto_lock?"}
    AL -- yes --> Detect["Each new outward iso:<br/>trigger if grad_r_error > lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr<br/>OR grad ≥ 0 OR stop_code = −1"]
    Detect --> Streak{"debounce streak<br/>≥ lsb_auto_lock_debounce?"}
    Streak -- "no (clean iso resets)" --> Free[Continue free fit]
    Streak -- yes --> Commit["Commit lock to isophote<br/>immediately BEFORE the streak<br/>(known clean anchor)"]
    Commit --> Locked["Locked clone:<br/>fix_center = fix_pa = fix_eps = True<br/>integrator = lsb_auto_lock_integrator (median)<br/>continue outward growth"]
    AL -- no --> Free
    Free --> Next([next sma step])
    Locked --> Next

Figure 6 — LSB outskirt strategies. The two mechanisms are independent and compose cleanly: soft damping pre-lock, hard freeze post-lock.

docs.title: Soft regularization details
docs.text:
• The inner reference is built from inward isophotes with acceptable stop codes and sma ≤ sma0 · outer_reg_ref_sma_factor. If none qualify, the reference falls back to the anchor.
  • outer_reg_mode='damping' (default) shrinks harmonic geometry steps in the outer region; 'solver' additionally pulls the geometry toward the reference. Both are applied in the geometry-update equations (after the harmonic solve), not inside the linear system.
  • A complementary selector penalty (compute_outer_center_regularization_penalty) contributes to effective_amp so the best-iteration tracker also prefers regularized geometries.
  • Per-axis weights outer_reg_weights={"center", "eps", "pa"} let you damp some axes and leave others free.

docs.title: Hard auto-lock details
docs.text:
• The detector reads grad, grad_error, and grad_r_error from each outward isophote, so debug=True is required and is silently turned on with a UserWarning if the caller left it off.
  • lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr defaults to 0.3, strictly more sensitive than maxgerr=0.5, so the lock commits before a gradient failure would have.
  • The lock anchor is the isophote immediately before the trigger streak, not the trigger isophote itself, whose geometry may already have drifted.
  • The transition is one-way per fit. Inward growth and the central pixel are unaffected.
  • Auto-lock conflicts with fix_center, fix_pa, or fix_eps at validation time. With template mode, the feature is silently inactive and a warning is emitted.

Default behaviour

Both features are disabled by default. Existing fits are byte-identical unless the user explicitly opts in. The soft feature is still under validation on a broader range of surveys; it is recommended for deep imaging with expected contamination.

docs.title: 8. Stop codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning Trigger Action 0 Success Converged: |max_amp| < conver · scale · effective_rms with i ≥ minit Keep 1 Too many flagged samples actual_points < total_points · (1 − fflag) Inspect mask / clipping; treat with caution 2 Max-iter fallback Reached maxit without convergence; best-so-far geometry returned Keep with caution 3 Too few points Fewer than 6 valid samples for the harmonic fit Discard this radius −1 Gradient failure Outward-only two-strike rule: gradient checks fail twice, or grad = 0 Treat as boundary / failure

In regular-mode growth, codes 0, 1, and 2 are considered acceptable for continued propagation (constant ACCEPTABLE_STOP_CODES). Codes 3 and −1 are unacceptable: the failed isophote's geometry is not propagated to the next SMA step (in the default strict mode), but growth continues to the configured radius limit (max(minsma, 0.5) inward, maxsma outward) — a stop code never terminates a growth loop early.

docs.title: 9. References
docs.text:
• Jedrzejewski, R. I. 1987, MNRAS, 226, 747 — original Fourier-harmonic ellipse-fit algorithm; the basis of all later Ellipse-family implementations.
  • Ciambur, B. C. 2015, ApJ, 810, 120 — IRAF Isofit / Cmodel; introduces the eccentric-anomaly sampling that ISOSTER's use_eccentric_anomaly mode reproduces. arXiv:1507.02691.
  • Stone, C. J., Arora, N., Courteau, S., & Cuillandre, J.-C. 2021, MNRAS, 508, 1870 — AutoProf; modern Python pipeline with ML-style fit stabilization, the most directly comparable tool to ISOSTER. arXiv:2106.13809.

Source files referenced in this walkthrough: isoster/driver.py, isoster/fitting.py, isoster/sampling.py, isoster/config.py. See the algorithmic foundation in the technical chapter for the prose discussion this page summarizes visually.

docs.title: Configuration decision tree
docs.text:
"What should I set?" — pick the config branch that matches your data, your galaxy, and your science goal. Each leaf names the specific flags involved and links into the technical chapter for the underlying mechanism.

ISOSTER ships with sensible defaults: IsosterConfig() with no arguments will fit a "typical" galaxy reasonably well. The questions below isolate the situations where the defaults are not appropriate, and tell you which flags to flip.

docs.title: 1. High-level decision flow
docs.text:
The five branches below are independent: turning on eccentric-anomaly sampling does not preclude WLS, and the LSB lock composes cleanly with all sampling modes. The high-level tree is therefore a stack of yes/no questions, not a tree with mutually exclusive leaves.

flowchart TD
    Start([Start configuration]) --> Q1{"A. variance / invvar<br/>map available?"}
    Q1 -- yes --> WLS["Pass variance_map=…<br/>→ WLS path, exact errors"]
    Q1 -- no --> OLS["OLS path,<br/>residual-scaled errors"]
    WLS --> Q2
    OLS --> Q2
    Q2{"B. high ellipticity,<br/>edge-on, X-bulge?"}
    Q2 -- yes --> EA["use_eccentric_anomaly = True<br/>(+ simultaneous_harmonics for X-bulge)"]
    Q2 -- no --> Phi["use_eccentric_anomaly = False<br/>(default)"]
    EA --> Q3
    Phi --> Q3
    Q3{"C. deep imaging,<br/>LSB outskirts?"}
    Q3 -- yes --> LSB["integrator = 'adaptive'<br/>+ lsb_auto_lock<br/>(+ outer-region regularization<br/>if contamination expected)"]
    Q3 -- no --> NoLSB["integrator = 'mean'<br/>(defaults)"]
    LSB --> Q4
    NoLSB --> Q4
    Q4{"D. forced photometry<br/>across bands /<br/>fixed geometry?"}
    Q4 -- yes --> Tpl["template = <results dict<br/>or list or FITS path>"]
    Q4 -- no --> Free["Regular free fit"]
    Tpl --> Q5
    Free --> Q5
    Q5{"E. batch / unattended<br/>processing?"}
    Q5 -- yes --> Robust["max_retry_first_isophote = 5<br/>permissive_geometry = True"]
    Q5 -- no --> Done([Use the config])
    Robust --> Done

Figure 1 — High-level decision tree. Each branch is independent; the final config layers the answers together.

docs.title: 2. Branch A — what data do I have?
docs.text:
The single biggest config decision is whether you can supply per-pixel variances. If your survey pipeline gives you an inverse variance map (HSC, DECaLS, SDSS, …), use it.

flowchart LR
    Img[2-D image only] --> OLS["fit_image(image, mask=…, config=…)"]
    OLS --> OLSOut["OLS:<br/>cov = (AᵀA)⁻¹·σ²_res<br/>errors from fit residuals"]
    ImgV["image + inverse-variance<br/>map (FITS)"] --> Conv["variance = np.where(invvar > 0,<br/>1.0 / invvar, np.nan)"]
    Conv --> WLS["fit_image(image, mask=…,<br/>config=…, variance_map=variance)"]
    WLS --> WLSOut["WLS:<br/>cov = (AᵀWA)⁻¹  (exact)<br/>errors from variance map<br/>cosmic rays auto-down-weighted"]

If you have a variance map

variance_map = np.where(invvar > 0, 1.0 / invvar, np.nan)
results = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config, variance_map=variance_map)

Leave invvar == 0 pixels as NaN rather than substituting a large finite value like 1e30: ISOSTER marks non-finite entries invalid and drops them from the fit, whereas a finite 1e30 is valid and stays in the ring, inflating the reported gradient error by orders of magnitude instead of removing the pixel.

WLS error bars are not systematically larger or smaller than OLS: under independent samples with a common, correctly specified variance the two have the same expected covariance, and they diverge only where those assumptions fail. What WLS buys is error bars traceable to a stated noise model rather than to residual scatter that mixes photon noise with unfitted structure. The OLS path is byte-identical when variance_map=None, so there is no downside to passing one when it exists. See variance-aware fitting in the technical chapter.

docs.title: 3. Branch B — what kind of galaxy?
docs.text:
Sampling and harmonic-fit modes depend on isophote shape. The default (uniform-in-φ sampling with post-hoc higher harmonics) is good for round-ish ellipticals; everything else has a recommended upgrade.

flowchart TD
    G([What does the galaxy look like?]) --> Round{"Mostly round,<br/>eps < 0.3?"}
    Round -- yes --> Default["Defaults are fine.<br/>compute_deviations = True<br/>for a3, b3, a4, b4 post-hoc."]
    Round -- no --> HighEps["use_eccentric_anomaly = True<br/>(more even sampling in ψ)"]
    HighEps --> Shape{"Strong non-elliptical<br/>structure?"}
    Shape -- "edge-on disk" --> Edge["+ harmonic_orders = [3, 4]<br/>(default is enough)<br/>+ relax maxgerr ≈ 1.0–1.2"]
    Shape -- "X-shaped / peanut bulge" --> XB["+ simultaneous_harmonics = True<br/>+ isofit_mode = 'in_loop'<br/>+ harmonic_orders = [3, 4, 6]"]
    Shape -- "bar with strong<br/>m=4 / m=6 component" --> Bar["+ simultaneous_harmonics = True<br/>+ harmonic_orders = [3, 4, 6]"]
    Shape -- "no strong structure" --> Edge

Default — round-ish elliptical or low-eps spiral

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0, maxsma=120.0,
    compute_deviations=True,    # a3, b3, a4, b4 post-hoc
)

Post-hoc higher harmonics are cheap and correct on low-to-moderate ellipticity.

High ellipticity (eps > 0.3) and edge-on disks

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0, maxsma=200.0,
    use_eccentric_anomaly=True, # step ψ uniformly, not the position angle
    compute_deviations=True,
    maxgerr=1.0,                # relax for high-eps gradient noise
)

Uniform-in-φ sampling under-samples the major axis on highly elliptical isophotes. Stepping ψ instead distributes samples more evenly, though not exactly uniformly in arc length. The harmonics are then fitted in ψ and the geometry update consumes those coefficients directly — there is no conversion back to φ — which is correct rather than approximate. The output schema is unchanged. See eccentric anomaly + ISOFIT in the technical chapter.

X-shaped / peanut bulges (and barred galaxies with strong m=4/m=6)

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0, maxsma=200.0,
    use_eccentric_anomaly=True,
    simultaneous_harmonics=True,
    isofit_mode="in_loop",
    harmonic_orders=[3, 4, 6],
)

Higher-order harmonics genuinely interact with geometry on these galaxies. Fitting them jointly inside the iteration loop (true ISOFIT, Ciambur 2015) absorbs the cross-correlations and produces cleaner RMS estimates than the post-hoc path, at ~25–35% extra cost. isofit_mode='original' reproduces Ciambur's original variant (post-hoc joint solve) and is useful as a consistency check.

docs.title: 4. Branch C — what S/N regime am I pushing into?
docs.text:
In the high-S/N interior of a galaxy the defaults are robust. The outskirts are where geometry drift, gradient failures, and contamination become real problems. ISOSTER offers a layered set of responses ranging from "do nothing different" to "freeze geometry past a detected LSB transition."

flowchart TD
    R([How far into the LSB do you push?]) --> HSB{"High-S/N only,<br/>sma ≲ R_e?"}
    HSB -- yes --> Hsb["Defaults.<br/>integrator = 'mean'"]
    HSB -- no --> Far{"Pushing to<br/>μ ≳ 27 mag arcsec⁻²?"}
    Far -- yes --> Clean{"Field clean?"}
    Far -- no --> Mid["integrator = 'adaptive'<br/>lsb_sma_threshold = 50–100 px"]
    Clean -- yes --> SoftLock["lsb_auto_lock = True<br/>lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr = 0.3<br/>lsb_auto_lock_debounce = 2<br/>lsb_auto_lock_integrator = 'median'<br/>debug = True"]
    Clean -- "no, contamination<br/>(companions, scattered<br/>light, nearby bright<br/>sources)" --> Combo["lsb_auto_lock = True<br/>+ use_outer_center_regularization = True<br/>outer_reg_sma_onset ≈ 0.5–0.7 · maxsma<br/>outer_reg_sma_width ≈ 0.1 · maxsma<br/>outer_reg_strength = 1.0–3.0<br/>outer_reg_weights = center/eps/pa: 1.0"]

Figure 3 — LSB outskirt strategy. Soft regularization runs every outward iteration; the auto-lock is a one-way hard switch. They compose: soft pre-lock, hard post-lock.

Mid-S/N (μ ≲ 27 mag arcsec⁻²)

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0, maxsma=200.0,
    integrator="adaptive",
    lsb_sma_threshold=80.0,     # switch to median past this SMA
)

Median is more robust against the asymmetric tails of the intensity distribution in the LSB regime, but loses some information in the interior. Adaptive mode keeps the harmonic-fit mean inside and the robust median outside the threshold.

Deep, clean field — hard auto-lock

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0, maxsma=300.0,
    integrator="adaptive",
    lsb_sma_threshold=100.0,
    lsb_auto_lock=True,
    lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr=0.3,
    lsb_auto_lock_debounce=2,
    lsb_auto_lock_integrator="median",
    debug=True,                 # required for detector diagnostics
)
result = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config, variance_map=variance)
print("lock committed at sma =", result["lsb_auto_lock_sma"])

The detector freezes x0, y0, eps, pa at the last clean isophote before the gradient diagnostics break down, so the LSB tail cannot drift. The lock is one-way per fit and only affects outward growth. See LSB outskirt strategy in the technical chapter.

Deep, contaminated field — soft regularization + hard lock

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0, maxsma=300.0,
    integrator="adaptive",
    lsb_sma_threshold=100.0,
    # Hard lock (kicks in late)
    lsb_auto_lock=True,
    debug=True,
    # Soft pre-lock regularization
    use_outer_center_regularization=True,
    outer_reg_sma_onset=150.0,    # ~0.5 maxsma
    outer_reg_sma_width=20.0,
    outer_reg_strength=2.0,
    outer_reg_weights={"center": 1.0, "eps": 1.0, "pa": 1.0},
)

The soft Tikhonov damping starts gently pulling the outward fit toward a flux-weighted inner reference well before the hard lock would commit. This bounds drift caused by faint companions, scattered light, or nearby bright sources, without freezing geometry prematurely. The two features are independent — either can be used alone.

Conflict with explicit fixes

lsb_auto_lock=True raises a ValidationError if combined with fix_center=True, fix_pa=True, or fix_eps=True — those switches make the lock trivially equivalent to ordinary fixed-geometry fitting.

docs.title: 5. Branch D — free fit, template, or multi-band?
docs.text:
Three workflow patterns dominate, and ISOSTER routes them through exactly two code paths. Multi-band is the one decision that takes you out of isoster.fit_image entirely.

flowchart TD
    W([Workflow]) --> Single{"Single-band<br/>discovery fit?"}
    Single -- yes --> SF["fit_image(image, mask=…, config=…)<br/>→ free geometry from scratch"]
    Single -- "no, apply a fixed<br/>geometry to other data" --> Tpl{"Have a template?"}
    Tpl -- "results dict / FITS<br/>(reuse another band's fit)" --> Forced1["fit_image(image2, …,<br/>template=results_g)<br/>→ template-based forced photometry"]
    Tpl -- "list of dicts<br/>(custom SMA grid)" --> Forced2["template = [<br/>  {'sma': s, 'x0': …, 'y0': …,<br/>   'eps': …, 'pa': …}<br/>  for s in [5, 10, 20, …]<br/>]<br/>→ forced extraction at chosen SMAs"]
    Single -- "no, multiple bands<br/>at once" --> MB["isoster.multiband.<br/>fit_image_multiband(images, …,<br/>variance_maps=…)<br/>→ joint free fit;<br/>see multi-band chapter"]
Workflow API entry point Features that apply Single-band free fit fit_image(image, …) Everything — full feature surface. Template-based forced fit_image(image, …, template=…) Sampling mode, harmonic mode, WLS apply. Auto-lock and outer-region regularization are silently inactive (warnings emitted). Multi-band joint free isoster.multiband.fit_image_multiband(…) Detailed in the multi-band chapter.

Forced-photometry caveats

The LSB auto-lock and outer-region regularization are wired only into the regular-mode driver. With template=… they emit a UserWarning and silently do nothing. Build the template geometry under a clean free fit; let the forced pass just extract.

docs.title: 6. Branch E — batch / robustness knobs
docs.text:
For unattended batch processing (a survey or mock catalogue), two flags make the failure modes much more graceful.

Recommended batch defaults

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0, maxsma=200.0,
    max_retry_first_isophote=5,  # retry with perturbed sma0/eps/pa
    permissive_geometry=True,    # do not poison geometry on one bad iso
    first_isophote_fail_count=3, # emit FIRST_FEW_ISOPHOTE_FAILURE after 3
)

max_retry_first_isophote retries the anchor isophote with perturbed starting geometry (different sma0, eps, pa) when the first fit returns an unacceptable stop code. Without it, a single bad anchor causes the whole fit to silently fall back to just the central pixel. permissive_geometry=True propagates the latest fit's geometry even on failure, so one bad isophote does not poison every subsequent SMA in the growth loop.

docs.title: 7. Suggested starting presets
docs.text: Three preset combinations cover the majority of real fits. Each one is a single IsosterConfig(...) call you can paste and tweak.

docs.title: Preset 1 — "Round elliptical, single band, defaults"
docs.text:
from isoster import fit_image
from isoster.config import IsosterConfig

config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0,
    maxsma=120.0,
    compute_deviations=True,    # a3, b3, a4, b4 post-hoc
    full_photometry=True,
    compute_cog=True,
)
results = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config)

docs.title: Preset 2 — "High-ellipticity / edge-on, WLS"
docs.text:
config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0,
    maxsma=200.0,
    use_eccentric_anomaly=True,
    maxgerr=1.0,
    integrator="adaptive",
    lsb_sma_threshold=80.0,
    compute_deviations=True,
    full_photometry=True,
)
results = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config,
                    variance_map=variance)

docs.title: Preset 3 — "Deep LSB, contaminated field, WLS"
docs.text:
config = IsosterConfig(
    sma0=10.0,
    maxsma=300.0,
    use_eccentric_anomaly=True,
    integrator="adaptive",
    lsb_sma_threshold=100.0,
    # Hard auto-lock
    lsb_auto_lock=True,
    lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr=0.3,
    lsb_auto_lock_debounce=2,
    lsb_auto_lock_integrator="median",
    debug=True,
    # Soft pre-lock damping
    use_outer_center_regularization=True,
    outer_reg_sma_onset=150.0,
    outer_reg_sma_width=20.0,
    outer_reg_strength=2.0,
    outer_reg_weights={"center": 1.0, "eps": 1.0, "pa": 1.0},
    # Batch robustness
    max_retry_first_isophote=5,
    permissive_geometry=True,
)
results = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config,
                    variance_map=variance)

This page is an opinionated entry point, not a full parameter reference. For the full schema (62 parameters across 14 functional groups), see Configuration reference. For the internal logic each flag triggers, see the Algorithm walkthrough.

docs.title: §1. ISOSTER: design, performance, and features
docs.text:
We introduce ISOSTER (ISOphote on STERoid), an open-source Python library for elliptical-isophote analysis of resolved galaxy images. ISOSTER is a faithful descendant of the Jedrzejewski (1987) Fourier-harmonic algorithm family that has driven non-parametric surface-photometry pipelines for nearly four decades, but it is written from scratch around three goals that previous Python implementations did not jointly achieve: (i) speed, through end-to-end vectorization of the per-isophote sampling and harmonic fit, with optional Numba JIT acceleration on the inner kernels; (ii) flexibility, through a configuration surface that exposes the algorithm's many quality and stability knobs (variance-aware fitting, eccentric-anomaly sampling, simultaneous higher-order harmonics, low-surface-brightness regularization, joint multi-band free fitting) as flags on validated Pydantic configuration objects — one for single-band fits and a deliberately separate sibling for the multi-band path; and (iii) scientific power, through new features designed for the deep, wide-field surveys (HSC-SSP, LSST, Euclid, Roman) that will dominate the next decade of resolved-galaxy work.

The remainder of this section is structured as follows. §1.1 reviews the algorithmic foundation just deeply enough that later subsections can refer back to it without re-deriving anything. §1.2 sketches the implementation: the module organization, the single user entry point, and the output schema. §1.3 explains why ISOSTER is fast — the four algorithmic choices that the Python predecessors do not jointly make — at the level of operation counts and code-path structure; concrete benchmark numbers, cross-tool tables, and aggregate metrics live in the separate benchmark chapters that draw from the Huang2013, S4G, and SGA2020 campaigns. §1.4 surveys the new features — eccentric-anomaly sampling, ISOFIT-style joint harmonics, variance-aware fitting, the LSB outskirt strategy, batch-robustness primitives, the joint multi-band free fit, and the diagnostics infrastructure — and accompanies each with one cherry-picked demonstration case that shows the feature in isolation. §1.5 compares ISOSTER conceptually with photutils.isophote, AutoProf (Stone+ 2021), and the IRAF Isofit / Cmodel tasks (Ciambur 2015) on a feature-by-feature basis. §1.6 lists the current limitations and the roadmap.

We emphasize that this section is an explain-and-demonstrate chapter, not a benchmark chapter. The demonstration cases are cherry-picked: each is chosen to make one specific feature visible in isolation, not to certify aggregate performance. The aggregate question — how does ISOSTER perform on a representative sample of galaxies, across multiple tools and configuration combinations — is answered in the dedicated benchmark chapters.

Status: all sections §1.0 through §1.6 are drafted. Outline at docs/publication/outline-technical-section.md.

docs.title: §1.1 Algorithmic foundation
docs.text:
The Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm treats elliptical-isophote analysis as a 1-D harmonic-fitting problem on resampled radial profiles. The image is not modeled globally; instead, the algorithm moves outward through a sequence of semi-major axis lengths \(a_k = a_{k-1} \cdot (1 + s)\) for some geometric step \(s\) (or \(a_k = a_{k-1} + s\) for linear stepping), and at each \(a_k\) samples the image intensity along the current trial ellipse. Let \(\theta\) denote the angular coordinate along the ellipse and let \(I(\theta)\) be the sampled intensity at \(N\) points uniformly spaced in \(\theta\), with \(N = \max(64, \lfloor 2\pi a_k \rfloor)\) chosen so the angular sampling rate matches the pixel scale on the ellipse perimeter. ISOSTER samples through scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates with bilinear interpolation (first-order spline) for the intensity and variance values and nearest-neighbor (order zero) for the mask, producing the intensity vector \(\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^N\) in one C-level call per isophote.

For a fixed geometry the sampled profile \(I(\theta)\) is constant up to noise and intrinsic isophote-shape deviations. The classical construction expresses both effects through a Fourier expansion,

\[ I(\theta) = I_0 + \sum_{n \ge 1} \left[ A_n \sin(n\theta) + B_n \cos(n\theta) \right], \]

truncated at some maximum harmonic order. The first- and second-order coefficients \((A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2)\) encode the geometric mismatch between the trial ellipse and the true isophote: \(A_1\) and \(B_1\) measure the centroid offset along the minor and major axes respectively, \(A_2\) measures position-angle mismatch, and \(B_2\) measures ellipticity mismatch. The higher-order coefficients \((A_n, B_n)\) for \(n \ge 3\) measure intrinsic isophote shape: \(B_4 > 0\) corresponds to a disky isophote, \(B_4 < 0\) to a boxy one, \(A_3 / B_3\) capture asymmetric distortions, and so on. This clean separation between geometry-mismatch terms (orders 1–2) and shape terms (orders \(n \ge 3\)) is what makes the harmonic basis the right one for non-parametric isophote analysis.

The fitting loop is a coordinate-descent solver. At iteration \(i\) with trial geometry \(\mathbf{g}_i = (x_0, y_0, \varepsilon, \mathrm{PA})_i\), the algorithm

  1. samples \(\mathbf{I}_i = I_i(\theta)\),
  2. fits the first- and second-order harmonics by ordinary least squares on a five-column design matrix \(\mathbf{A} = [\mathbf{1}, \sin\theta, \cos\theta, \sin 2\theta, \cos 2\theta]\), yielding \((I_0, A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2)\) and a residual RMS \(\sigma\),
  3. selects the dominant amplitude \(a_\max = \max(|A_1|, |B_1|, |A_2|, |B_2|)\),
  4. converts \(a_\max\) into a single-parameter geometry update via the local radial gradient \(dI/da\) (estimated from one-sided offset-SMA sampling), and
  5. checks convergence: if \(\lvert a_\max\rvert < c \cdot S(a) \cdot \sigma\) for a threshold \(c\) and an SMA-dependent scale factor \(S(a)\), and \(i\) has exceeded a minimum iteration count, the isophote is declared converged.

This is the classical Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm. ISOSTER implements it with three refinements that we describe in detail in §1.3 and §1.4, but that are worth naming up front because they appear in the algorithm sketch above:

  • Lazy gradient evaluation. The radial gradient \(dI/da\) is expensive (it requires an extra sampling pass at an offset SMA, on top of the pass at the current SMA) and changes slowly across iterations once the geometry has approximately settled. ISOSTER computes the gradient on iteration \(i = 0\) and reuses the cached value until one of three things forces a re-evaluation: the dominant amplitude fails to improve for three consecutive iterations; the cached value carries no usable uncertainty; or a gradient-quality strike is currently active. The last condition is the one that is easy to omit and costly to omit. The outward sweep applies a two-strike rule to gradient quality (§1.4.6), and a cached gradient computed before the first strike is precisely the value whose reliability is in question — reusing it lets the fit decide, from a stale number, whether to record a gradient failure. Reuse is therefore suppressed while a strike is outstanding.
  • Convergence with a noise floor and an SMA-dependent scale. The convergence criterion is \(\lvert a_\max\rvert < c \cdot S(a) \cdot \sigma_\mathrm{eff}\), where \(\sigma_\mathrm{eff} = \max(\sigma, \sigma_\mathrm{bg}/\sqrt{N})\) and \(S(a)\) is a convergence-scale factor (config field convergence_scaling). The default 'sector_area' choice sets \(S(a) = \max(1,\ a \cdot \Delta a \cdot \Delta\theta)\), with \(\Delta a\) the SMA step and \(\Delta\theta = 2\pi / N\) the angular sample spacing, so the threshold scales roughly with the area of one sample sector; 'sqrt_sma' (\(\max(1, \sqrt{a})\)) and 'none' (\(S = 1\)) are also offered. In the low-surface-brightness regime the residual RMS \(\sigma\) can drop below the photon-noise floor; without the floor, the solver would chase noise-induced asymmetries indefinitely.
  • Best-iteration tracking. Rather than returning the geometry at the last iteration, ISOSTER tracks the iteration that minimizes an "effective amplitude" \(a_\mathrm{eff} = |a_\max| + \lambda\, \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{g})\) — the dominant harmonic amplitude plus an optional regularization penalty \(\mathcal{R}\) — and returns that. The penalty is zero by default and only contributes when the LSB outer-region regularization of §1.4.3 is enabled.

The image-level pipeline wraps the per-isophote loop in five stages: (1) a central-pixel measurement at \(a = 0\); (2) a free-geometry anchor isophote at the user-specified \(a_0\); (3) an inward loop from \(a_0\) down to \(\max(a_\mathrm{min}, 0.5\,\mathrm{px})\); (4) an outward loop from \(a_0\) up to \(a_\mathrm{max}\); (5) an optional curve-of-growth attachment. The inward loop is executed unconditionally before the outward loop — this is a precondition for the LSB outer-region regularization (it needs an inner reference centroid) but is always on so that the output isophote list remains a deterministic function of the input.

A single mode switch sits above this pipeline: if the user supplies a template (a results dictionary, a list of isophote dicts, or a FITS path), the regular fitting loop is bypassed and ISOSTER runs a template-based forced extraction that reuses each template geometry at its own SMA. Forced extraction is the standard multi-band photometry workflow for older surveys; ISOSTER also provides a joint multi-band free fit for same-grid imaging (§1.4.5). The two are alternatives rather than a replacement and its predecessor: they report intensities on differently chosen aperture sequences and therefore estimate different quantities, as §1.4.5.1 sets out.

Two angular conventions for the harmonic basis are supported. The default uses the position angle \(\phi\) measured in the image plane, which is the convention of IRAF Ellipse and photutils.isophote. The alternative, controlled by use_eccentric_anomaly=True, uses the eccentric anomaly \(\psi\), which distributes samples far more evenly along the perimeter than uniform-in-\(\phi\) sampling does (though not exactly uniformly in arc length — that would require an elliptic-integral parametrization neither convention uses). The latter is the right basis for highly elliptical isophotes — edge-on disks, X-shaped / peanut bulges, strongly barred galaxies — where uniform-in-\(\phi\) sampling under-resolves the major axis.

In both modes the harmonic coefficients are fitted in the active angular coordinate and fed directly to the same geometry-update formulas. That is exact in \(\psi\)-mode and approximate in \(\phi\)-mode, because the update formulas above are themselves derived from an eccentric-anomaly parametrization of the trial ellipse — the \((1-\varepsilon)\) and \(2(1-\varepsilon)/a\) factors are its signature. The geometry parameters retain their standard geometric meanings in either mode, but the two modes neither follow the same trajectory nor necessarily converge to the same geometry on a flattened isophote carrying real higher-order structure. §1.4.1 gives the derivation and quantifies the discrepancy.

The output is a Python dictionary with two mandatory keys — isophotes (a list of per-SMA dicts sorted by ascending \(a\)) and config (the resolved IsosterConfig object that produced the fit) — plus optional metadata keys for the higher-level features (LSB auto-lock anchor, outer-region reference, multi-band schema version). The per-isophote dicts carry the geometry \((x_0, y_0, \varepsilon, \mathrm{PA})\), the intensity statistics \((I_0, \sigma, \sigma_{I_0})\), parameter uncertainties, optional higher-order harmonic coefficients, stored normalized as \(a_n = A_n^\mathrm{raw} / (a\,\lvert dI/da\rvert)\) (§1.4.6), optional aperture-photometry diagnostics, and a stop code in \(\{0, 1, 2, 3, -1\}\) that summarizes the per-isophote outcome (full table in §1.4.6).

docs.title: Module organization
docs.text:
The package is organized into a small core and a multi-band parallel tree. The core comprises six Python modules that map cleanly to the algorithm description in §1.1:

Module Role isoster/driver.py Image-level orchestration. Implements the central-pixel → anchor → inward → outward → CoG pipeline, the mode-selection switch, and the propagation of inherited geometry between SMAs. isoster/fitting.py Per-isophote fitting loop. Runs the iteration sketched in §1.1, applies geometry updates with damping and step clipping, attaches optional post-hoc blocks (higher-order harmonics, parameter errors, aperture metrics). isoster/sampling.py Vectorized ellipse sampling through scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates. Computes the ellipse coordinates, performs mask-aware sampling, and returns IsophoteData objects carrying \((\theta, \phi, I, r, \sigma^2)\). isoster/config.py IsosterConfig Pydantic schema. Sixty-two parameters in sixteen functional groups; cross-parameter validators (e.g. \(\mathtt{minit} \le \mathtt{maxit}\), lsb_sma_threshold required when integrator='adaptive'). isoster/model.py 2-D model reconstruction by radial interpolation between converged isophotes. Auto-detects whether eccentric-anomaly sampling was used and selects the correct harmonic-evaluation basis. isoster/numba_kernels.py Optional Numba-JIT inner kernels (harmonic design-matrix builder, ellipse-coordinate construction, harmonic-model evaluation, eccentric-anomaly conversion). Falls back to byte-equivalent NumPy implementations when Numba is absent.

Auxiliary modules round out the core: isoster/cog.py (curve-of-growth assembly with crossing detection), isoster/utils.py and isoster/_shared.py (serialization helpers, FITS / ASDF writers and readers, plus the estimator helpers that single-band and multi-band must agree on), isoster/plotting.py (QA figures, including cross-tool comparison panels for photutils.isophote and AutoProf alongside ISOSTER), and isoster/optimize.py, a thin façade that re-exports the per-isophote primitives (fit_isophote, compute_gradient, compute_deviations, extract_isophote_data, …) at a stable import path. That façade matters for the input-validation discussion of §1.4.2.3: those functions are public, so they may legitimately be handed a raw, unvalidated variance map, which is why the sanitization guarantees fit_image provides internally cannot simply be assumed downstream.

The multi-band parallel tree (isoster/multiband/) is a sibling package: it imports a handful of low-level helpers from the core modules but provides its own driver, fitting loop, sampling stack, configuration schema, and Numba kernels, and exposes a separate CLI entry point (isoster-mb). This separation is by design — the joint-multi-band path is algorithmically different enough from single-band that sharing the per-SMA loop would have produced an unmaintainable mass of conditionals, and the multi-band path carries operational failure modes (per-band mask asymmetry, a variance map missing in one band, misalignment) that have no single-band counterpart. We describe the joint multi-band algorithm in §1.4.5.

docs.title: Canonical user-facing call
docs.text:
The entire public API for the single-band case is one function and one Pydantic configuration object. A typical free-fit looks like:

from isoster import fit_image, isophote_results_to_fits
from isoster.config import IsosterConfig

config = IsosterConfig(sma0=10.0, maxsma=200.0, full_photometry=True)
results = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config, variance_map=var)
isophote_results_to_fits(results, "galaxy_isophotes.fits")

Every algorithmic feature described in §1.4 — eccentric anomaly, ISOFIT, WLS, LSB auto-lock, outer-region regularization, batch retry policies — is enabled by flipping a flag on IsosterConfig. There is no separate "expert API" with a different signature; the beginner's call and the survey-pipeline call differ only in how many config flags are set.

docs.title: Mode selection
docs.text:
The single user-level mode switch is template vs regular:

Trigger Mode Internal driver template argument provided Template-based forced photometry _fit_image_template_forced Otherwise Regular iterative free fit inline in fit_image

template accepts three forms: a results dictionary (the typical "reuse band-A geometry on band B" call), a list of isophote dicts (custom-SMA forced extraction), or a path to a previously saved FITS file (cross-pipeline portability). The deprecated alias template_isophotes is still accepted for backwards compatibility.

docs.title: Output schema and serialization
docs.text:
fit_image returns a dictionary. The two mandatory keys are isophotes (a list of per-SMA dicts, sorted by ascending semi-major axis) and config (the resolved IsosterConfig object). Each isophote dict carries a fixed set of always-present geometry, intensity, and stop-code fields plus a set of optional blocks controlled by configuration flags (higher-order harmonics, aperture metrics, curve-of-growth, debug diagnostics, LSB lock markers). The full per-field reference lives in the user guide; the present section emphasizes the invariants that downstream tools can rely on:

  • The list is sorted by ascending semi-major axis.
  • The central pixel (when \(a_\mathrm{min} \le 0\)) is always prepended as a single dict with \(\mathtt{sma} = 0\).
  • Stop codes are drawn from \(\{0, 1, 2, 3, -1\}\) with documented triggers (§1.4.6); the constants \(\mathtt{ACCEPTABLE\_STOP\_CODES} = \{0, 1, 2\}\) define which codes propagate geometry into the next SMA step.
  • Higher-order harmonic amplitudes, when present, are reported in the Bender-normalized form \(a_n = A_n^\mathrm{raw} / (a\,\lvert dI/da\rvert)\). The raw \(A_n^\mathrm{raw}\) are scale-dependent and not directly comparable across SMAs; we follow the convention used throughout the isophote-analysis literature.

Three serialization paths are provided, of which two are archival and one is a convenience: isophote_results_to_fits writes a four-HDU FITS file with PrimaryHDU, a BinTableHDU named ISOPHOTES, a BinTableHDU named CONFIG carrying the full configuration as JSON-serialized (PARAM, VALUE) rows, and a BinTableHDU named META carrying the remaining top-level result keys in the same JSON row format, so that information which is neither per-isophote nor a configuration field (lock state, first-isophote retry outcomes, outer-region references) survives the round trip rather than being silently dropped; isophote_results_to_asdf writes the same information in ASDF format, preserving native Python types (particularly useful for nested dicts and numpy arrays in the multi-band schema); and isophote_results_to_astropy_tables returns the isophote list as an astropy.table.Table for downstream analysis without going through disk — the table carries the isophote columns only, and deliberately drops the configuration and the run metadata, so it is an analysis convenience rather than an archival format. The two on-disk writers share a common helper layer in isoster/_shared.py to guarantee that the same configuration object yields the same serialized configuration content in either format. This matters for the reproducibility argument of §1.3.4: the saved CONFIG block records the resolved configuration — every field, including those left at their defaults — so re-running the fit does not depend on the defaults of whichever ISOSTER release happens to be installed. It is worth being exact about the scope of that claim. The file records the configuration, not the experiment: the input image, mask and variance map, the ISOSTER version, and the numerical environment (BLAS/LAPACK build, Numba availability) all sit outside it. Reproducing a fit means supplying those separately and pairing them with the saved configuration.

docs.title: Configurability surface
docs.text:
IsosterConfig carries 62 parameters across 16 functional groups (geometry initialization, SMA control, fitting control, geometry update control, quality control, constraints, outputs and features, integration mode, eccentric-anomaly sampling, higher-order harmonics / ISOFIT, geometry update strategy, central region regularization, outer-region center regularization, permissive geometry mode, first-isophote robustness, automatic LSB geometry lock). Cross-parameter validators reject inconsistent combinations at construction time — for example, integrator='adaptive' raises ValidationError without an accompanying lsb_sma_threshold, and lsb_auto_lock=True rejects combination with any of fix_center, fix_pa, fix_eps. The guiding principle is that an IsosterConfig that successfully constructs cannot produce a behavior that is intrinsically self-contradictory. This pushes a meaningful fraction of the "misconfigured run" failure mode out of the runtime path and into the configuration path, where the error message points the user at the exact field involved.

IsosterConfig is an ordinary mutable Pydantic model — assigning to a field on an existing instance works — so the guarantee ISOSTER offers is about behaviour, not about the type: fit_image never mutates the config it receives. Where the driver needs different settings mid-fit (for example, the LSB auto-lock needs fix_center=fix_pa=fix_eps=True once the lock commits) it derives a clone via config.model_copy(update={...}) and uses that, leaving the caller's object untouched. The original therefore remains usable for a subsequent fit on a different image without surprises. What is not guaranteed is that a config cannot change under the user, and the gap is wider than it looks. IsosterConfig does not enable Pydantic's validate_assignment, so post-construction assignment runs no validation at all: neither the cross-field rules nor even the per-field constraints. config.sma0 = -5.0 is accepted on an existing instance although IsosterConfig(sma0=-5.0) raises ValidationError, and config.integrator = 'adaptive' is accepted without the lsb_sma_threshold the constructor would demand. The validation guarantee of the previous paragraph is therefore a guarantee about construction. Building a fresh IsosterConfig is the supported way to change settings, and a pipeline that mutates a config in place forfeits the protection this section is about.

This is the entire user-visible interface. §1.3 turns to what happens inside that interface and how it compares with the direct Python predecessor.

docs.title: §1.3 Why ISOSTER is fast
docs.text: ISOSTER and its Python predecessors implement the same underlying Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm. Most of the runtime difference between them is therefore not a difference in what is being computed but in how that computation is organized across Python, C, and JIT-compiled code — with one exception, the lazy gradient below, which does change the numbers and is treated as such — and in how much of it the implementation is willing to amortize across iterations and across the callers (regular fitting and forced extraction) that need elliptical sampling. This section explains the four algorithmic choices that together account for the speed gap. Concrete numerical comparisons across image size, sampling density, and configuration combination live in the separate benchmark chapters that draw from the Huang2013, S4G, and SGA2020 campaigns; here we focus on the reasons.

docs.title: §1.3.1 Where Python predecessors spend their time
docs.text:
Three patterns dominate the runtime of the existing Python elliptical-isophote stack. We name them at the abstraction level of "loops vs vectors" rather than by specific function name, since implementations evolve and a citation to a function name in a release notes section would age out within a release cycle.

Per-point Python-level sampling. The classical formulation samples intensity at \(N\) points around each trial ellipse. A direct implementation evaluates each point through a Python-callable integrator that pulls a small neighborhood of pixels out of the image and returns either the bilinear-interpolated central value or a small area integral. With \(N\) on the order of \(2\pi a\), an isophote at \(a = 100\,\mathrm{px}\) requires more than six hundred such calls per iteration, and there are typically ten to thirty iterations per isophote and tens to hundreds of isophotes per image. Each call is fast in absolute terms but carries Python interpreter overhead, and the cumulative cost is what dominates wall time at the image level.

Redundant gradient evaluation. The geometry-update step needs the local radial intensity gradient \(dI / da\), estimated by a one-sided difference: the image is sampled at one SMA offset above the current one, and the sample at the current SMA is reused. In the classical algorithm this gradient is re-evaluated on every iteration, even though the geometry typically changes by a few percent per iteration once it has approximately settled. Each gradient evaluation costs one additional sampling pass — an extra ellipse sampled at \(N\) points — so the gradient alone roughly doubles the sampling cost per iteration in the classical formulation.

Duplicated sampling code paths. Regular fitting and forced photometry extraction both need to sample the image along elliptical paths, but for historical reasons each is implemented with its own sampling helpers. The same operation — "compute the pixel coordinates of \(N\) points along an ellipse with parameters \((x_0, y_0, a, \varepsilon, \mathrm{PA})\) and look up the image intensities at those points" — is written and tested more than once. The duplication is not just a code-maintenance liability; it also means that an optimization applied to one caller does not automatically benefit the other, and that the call sites can drift in their conventions (half-pixel offsets, boundary handling, mask treatment) until they disagree on what "the same isophote" means.

These three patterns compound. A fit at moderate image size and SMA density is bottlenecked by tens of thousands of Python-level sampling calls, each of which is redundantly invoked through one of several parallel code paths. None of them is individually fatal, but together they set the wall-clock floor.

docs.title: §1.3.2 What ISOSTER does differently
docs.text: ISOSTER replaces these patterns with four choices. Three are independently speedups — vectorized sampling, the Numba kernels, and the lazy gradient. The fourth, the shared sampling stack, is primarily a maintenance-and-correctness design whose performance effect is indirect: it lets an optimization written once benefit both sampling callers. Together they form the core of the performance argument.

docs.title: Vectorized path-based sampling
docs.text:
The first and most fundamental change is to replace the per-point sampling loop with a single vectorized call into scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates. Given an image array and an array of \(N\) fractional pixel coordinates \((x_j, y_j)\), map_coordinates evaluates a \(k\)-th order spline interpolation at all \(N\) points in a single C-level pass, returning the intensity vector \(\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^N\) as a NumPy array. ISOSTER uses bilinear interpolation (first-order spline) for the intensity and variance samples and nearest-neighbor for the mask, which matches the accuracy needs of the isophote fit while collapsing the Python loop into one external call. The coordinate array itself is computed analytically from the ellipse parameters in a few NumPy operations. In the default mode the angle \(\theta_j = \phi_j\) is the image position angle, stepped uniformly, and the radius follows the polar equation of the ellipse:

\[ r_j = \frac{a(1-\varepsilon)} {\sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)^2\cos^2\phi_j + \sin^2\phi_j}}, \] \[ x_j = x_0 + r_j \cos\phi_j \cos\mathrm{PA} - r_j \sin\phi_j \sin\mathrm{PA}, $$ $$ y_j = y_0 + r_j \cos\phi_j \sin\mathrm{PA} + r_j \sin\phi_j \cos\mathrm{PA}, \]

In eccentric-anomaly mode (§1.4.1) the eccentric anomaly \(\psi\) is stepped uniformly instead, with \((x'_j, y'_j) = (a\cos\psi_j,\ a(1-\varepsilon)\sin\psi_j)\) on the principal axes before the same rotation by PA.

so the entire sampling pipeline — coordinates, interpolation, and mask application — is a small constant number of NumPy / SciPy calls per isophote regardless of \(N\). The Python interpreter is involved only in launching the call, not in iterating over the \(N\) points.

This single change accounts for the largest share of the speed gap between ISOSTER and the direct Python predecessor. It is also the choice that fixes the loop overhead exactly — there is no "Python loop with \(N\) iterations" left in the sampling layer at all. The remaining Python loops in the fit are over iterations of the per-SMA solver, which numbers in the tens, not over sample points, which number in the hundreds.

docs.title: Numba-accelerated inner kernels
docs.text:
A small number of operations sit between sampling and convergence checking that are awkward to vectorize cleanly in NumPy but are trivially expressible as JIT-compiled loops. The chief examples are the harmonic design-matrix builder \(\mathbf{A} = [\mathbf{1}, \sin\theta, \cos\theta, \sin 2\theta, \cos 2\theta]\) for the five-parameter geometry fit, the ellipse-coordinate construction behind the sampling call above, the harmonic-model evaluation used to reconstruct the fitted model on a ring (for residuals and convergence), and the eccentric-anomaly to position-angle conversion of §1.4.1. ISOSTER implements these with Numba @njit decorators in isoster/numba_kernels.py so that each one compiles to a tight loop in machine code at first call, then runs at speeds comparable to a hand-written C implementation. (The joint multi-band design-matrix builder of §1.4.5 gets the same treatment in isoster/multiband/numba_kernels_mb.py; the dominant-coefficient selection \(\max(|A_1|, |B_1|, |A_2|, |B_2|)\) is a one-line np.argmax in isoster/fitting.py and is not JIT-compiled.)

Two implementation properties are worth flagging. First, every Numba kernel has a byte-equivalent NumPy fallback in the same file: if the Numba import fails or the user explicitly disables it, the fallback is dispatched transparently and produces identical numerical output. This matters for reproducibility on systems where LLVM is unavailable and for the configuration where ISOSTER is run on a small number of galaxies. The cold-process penalty is real, and §1.6.5 breaks it into the three costs it is usually conflated from: importing the stack (\(0.84\,\mathrm{s}\) (IQR \(0.83\)–\(0.86\)) on the reference machine), reading the compiled kernels back from Numba's on-disk cache on first dispatch (\(0.101\,\mathrm{s}\) (IQR \(0.099\)–\(0.103\))), and genuinely compiling them when that cache is empty (a further \(0.36\,\mathrm{s}\) (IQR \(0.36\)–\(0.37\))). Only the last is compilation, and it is paid once per compatible cache rather than once per installation: a Numba or ISOSTER upgrade invalidates the cached objects, and an environment that cannot write the cache directory pays it every time. This is why an earlier version of this section, which observed the \(0.1\,\mathrm{s}\) cache load on a machine that had already run ISOSTER and called it "JIT compilation", understated the cost by about a factor of four. Second, the kernels are deliberately small. The Numba-compiled region is the design-matrix construction and the coordinate and angle arithmetic; the linear solve itself is delegated to NumPy, which already wraps LAPACK — numpy.linalg.lstsq on the unweighted design matrix in the OLS path, and numpy.linalg.solve on the explicitly formed weighted normal equations in the WLS path of §1.4.2. We do not attempt to JIT-compile the solver, because doing so would require duplicating LAPACK behaviour inside Numba for no measurable gain.

docs.title: Lazy gradient evaluation
docs.text:
The radial gradient \(dI / da\) is the single most expensive quantity in the per-iteration cost budget, because evaluating it requires one additional sampling pass at an SMA offset from the current isophote. The classical formulation re-evaluates it every iteration. ISOSTER instead computes the gradient on iteration \(i = 0\), caches the value, and reuses it on every subsequent iteration of the same isophote unless one of three conditions forces a re-evaluation: the dominant harmonic amplitude \(|a_\max|\) fails to improve for three consecutive iterations; the cached value carries no usable uncertainty; or a gradient-quality strike is currently outstanding (§1.4.6). The last condition matters more than its size suggests — a cached gradient computed before the first strike is exactly the value whose reliability the strike is questioning, so reusing it would let a stale number decide whether to record a gradient failure.

The justification for caching at all is that the gradient is a local property of the image at the current geometry. Once the iteration is reasonably close to the converged isophote, the geometry moves by a few percent per iteration and the gradient changes by less, because the gradient is itself a slowly varying function of \(a\) wherever the fit is well conditioned. The stall detector is an inexpensive safeguard for the case where the cached value is meaningfully wrong — for instance when the iteration has wandered into a region of low gradient SNR — and restores the classical behaviour there at the cost of a few extra sampling passes on the affected isophote.

What it saves. On a representative fit — an \(n = 2\) Sérsic model, \(R_e = 30\,\mathrm{px}\), \(\varepsilon = 0.4\), \(S/N = 50\), 59 isophotes from \(a_0 = 10\) to \(a_\max = 120\,\mathrm{px}\) — the lazy path performs 60 gradient evaluations against 414 for the classical path — a factor of \(6.9\), and the one figure here that is exactly reproducible, since it is a count rather than a time. The wall-clock saving that follows has a median of \(24\%\) across eighteen sessions, with an interquartile range of \(23.0\%\) to \(24.1\%\).

We quote the median and the interquartile range, and deliberately not the extremes, because the extremes are not a stable statistic here. In the archived set the individual sessions fall between \(22.2\%\) and \(24.4\%\). That looks tight, and within a single archive it is; but an earlier eighteen-session archive on the same machine contained a session that returned a negative saving, with the cached path running slower. We did not diagnose it. The result is consistent with external load on the machine during that session, which is the usual cause, but we did not instrument the run and cannot say so; it stands as an unexplained timing outlier. That is the point: the width of the extremes is itself a property of the particular run, and quoting it would present as a measured bound something that changed by a factor of several between two archives taken on one machine. The median and the quartiles reproduce across independent sets to within a percentage point; the minimum and maximum do not reproduce at all. Earlier drafts of this section quoted min-to-max intervals from three sessions and had to revise them three times, which is what that instability looks like from the inside. The evaluation count remains the robust part of the result — what it converts into depends on how much of a given fit is sampling, which varies with the galaxy and the configuration (reproduced by benchmarks/draft_timings/run_draft_timings.py --sessions 18; measurement protocol in §1.6.5). Note that the iteration count is essentially unchanged (414 against 414 here). The saving is in sampling passes per iteration, not in shorter iteration sequences, and describing it as "fewer iterations" would misattribute where the time goes.

What it costs. This is the only change in §1.3.2 that is not a pure software-engineering optimization: it modifies the algorithm. Because a cached gradient differs slightly from the freshly evaluated one, each geometry update differs slightly, and the differences accumulate along the iteration trajectory. The converged output is therefore not identical to the classical path, and it is worth being precise about the size of the difference rather than asserting equivalence. Comparing use_lazy_gradient=True against False on the fit above, and on the same model at two other noise levels:

\(S/N\) median \(\lvert\Delta\rvert / \sigma\) max \(\lvert\Delta\rvert / \sigma\) max \(\lvert\Delta x_0\rvert\) (px) max \(\lvert\Delta\mathrm{PA}\rvert\) (rad) 200 \(3 \times 10^{-4}\) 0.22 0.0036 0.0031 50 \(1 \times 10^{-3}\) 1.6 0.64 0.013 10 \(4 \times 10^{-3}\) 2.6 3.0 0.072

(\(\Delta\) is the difference in a geometry parameter between the two modes; \(\sigma\) is that parameter's own reported uncertainty on the same isophote. The first two columns aggregate over \(x_0\), \(y_0\), \(\varepsilon\) and PA. Every entry is a median across eighteen noise realisations of the same model — one per session, since the difference between two converged fits is fixed once the image is fixed, so a single realisation would report a spread of zero rather than no spread at all. Run-to-run variation in the tail is appreciable: across those realisations the \(S/N = 50\) maximum has an interquartile range of \(1.2\)–\(1.9\) and individual realisations range from \(0.81\) to \(2.6\). The column to read is therefore the order of magnitude, not the digits.)

The pattern is the honest summary of the trade. For the overwhelming majority of isophotes the two modes agree to a small fraction of the fitted uncertainty — the median disagreement stays below one percent of \(\sigma\) at every noise level tested. But the tail grows sharply as the data get noisier: at \(S/N = 200\) the worst isophote in the sequence moves by about a fifth of its own uncertainty, while at \(S/N = 10\) it moves by more than \(2\sigma\) and its centre by a few pixels. This is the expected behaviour rather than a defect: the low-gradient, low-SNR regime is exactly where a cached gradient is least representative and where the geometry update is most sensitive to it. It does mean that the lazy gradient should be understood as a fast approximation rather than an exact reformulation, and that a user pursuing per-isophote geometry in the LSB outskirts — the regime of §1.4.3 — has a defensible reason to set use_lazy_gradient=False and pay the roughly 31% surcharge.

docs.title: Shared sampling stack
docs.text:
The fourth change addresses the duplicated-sampling-path pattern of the classical Python implementations. ISOSTER has one sampling module (isoster/sampling.py) that exposes one entry point (extract_isophote_data) and one return type (IsophoteData). Both sampling callers route through it:

  • Regular fitting (isoster/fitting.py) calls it on each iteration of each isophote.
  • Forced photometry extraction (extract_forced_photometry in the same module) calls it once per template isophote with the template geometry held fixed.

2-D model reconstruction (isoster/model.py) is the exception, and naming it matters because the earlier version of this section claimed it as a third caller. It does not sample along elliptical paths at all: it solves the opposite problem. Sampling asks "what is the image intensity at these \(N\) points on this ellipse"; model reconstruction asks "what intensity does the fitted model assign to every pixel in this grid", which it answers by determining each pixel's semi-major-axis coordinate under the locally interpolated geometry and evaluating a radial interpolant of the fitted intensities there. That is a different operation with a different kernel (scipy.interpolate.interp1d over the isophote list, not map_coordinates over the image), so it neither shares the sampling stack's mask and boundary conventions nor inherits its optimizations.

A bug fix to mask treatment, a change to the boundary-handling convention, or an optimization to the coordinate-construction arithmetic therefore lands once and benefits both sampling callers. The half-pixel offset convention is enforced in one place for them. The sampling output schema — what IsophoteData carries — is the same wherever sampling happens.

This is a software-engineering argument, not directly an algorithmic-speed argument. Its one concrete performance consequence is that optimizations to the shared sampling stack amortize across both sampling callers; in particular, the vectorized-map_coordinates choice automatically benefits forced photometry in addition to regular fitting, which is significant because forced photometry is the dominant workflow in multi-band survey pipelines. Separately, the multi-band extension (§1.4.5) was buildable as a parallel module precisely because the single-band sampling stack was self-contained: the multi-band path imports the low-level coordinate helpers without having to also inherit the sampling callers' historical peculiarities.

docs.title: §1.3.3 Algorithmic complexity and where it goes
docs.text:
The four choices in §1.3.2 do not change the asymptotic complexity of the algorithm — they reduce the constant factors. It is worth naming the asymptotic structure explicitly so that the speed argument can be quantified later without ambiguity.

Per-isophote cost is dominated by two terms. The sampling step performs \(N = \max(64, \lfloor 2\pi a \rfloor)\) interpolations through one map_coordinates call, costing \(\mathrm{O}(N)\) in image-area terms and \(\mathrm{O}(1)\) in the Python interpreter. The linear-system solve is \(\mathrm{O}(p^2 N)\) where \(p\) is the number of fit parameters (five for the geometry-only fit, \(5 + 2L\) for an extended ISOFIT fit with \(L\) higher orders, and \(B + 4 + 2L\) for a multi-band joint fit with \(B\) bands; see §1.4.1 and §1.4.5). Both terms are linear in \(N\), so per-isophote cost is asymptotically linear in the semi-major axis \(a\) and effectively independent of image area beyond what enters through map_coordinates' interpolation kernel.

Image-level cost is the per-isophote cost summed over the inward and outward growth loops. Let \(K\) be the number of isophotes (typically of order 50 in a geometric-stepping fit from \(a_0 = 10\,\mathrm{px}\) to \(a_\max = 200\,\mathrm{px}\) with astep = 0.1), and let \(\overline{m}\) be the average per-isophote iteration count. Worst-case total cost is \(\mathrm{O}(K \cdot \overline{m} \cdot N_\max)\) where \(N_\max\) is the sample count at the largest SMA. In practice \(\overline{m}\) is well below the configured maxit because most isophotes converge in under twenty iterations, and the lazy-gradient optimization makes \(\overline{m}\) matter less because each additional iteration costs just one sampling pass rather than two.

The two consequences worth pointing out:

  • Image area enters only through map_coordinates interpolation cost. The interpolation kernel reads a small neighborhood (\(k+1\) pixels per dimension for a \(k\)-th order spline) around each of the \(N\) sample points. The total pixel reads per isophote is therefore \(\mathrm{O}(N \cdot k^2)\) — sublinear in the image area for any modern image size. This is why the fit time scales with the number of isophotes and the typical semi-major axis, not with the image dimensions, in the regime where the galaxy occupies a small-to-moderate fraction of the image.

  • Sampling density and ISOFIT cost. The user-facing knobs that most strongly affect runtime are astep (geometric SMA step, which sets \(K\)) and the harmonic-fit configuration (which sets \(p\), and therefore the LAPACK solve cost). The ISOFIT path with harmonic_orders=[3, 4] carries \(p = 9\) rather than \(p = 5\), raising the solve cost by a constant factor that the benchmark chapters quantify in absolute terms.

The point of this complexity sketch is not to predict wall time but to clarify which knobs in IsosterConfig are the runtime-relevant ones. The benchmark chapters then quantify the constants.

docs.title: §1.3.4 Correctness guarantees alongside speed
docs.text:
The performance argument is only useful if the faster code computes the same thing as the slower code where the algorithm overlaps. ISOSTER provides three guarantees that together establish this:

  1. Plain OLS path when variance_map = None. The weighted-least-squares (WLS) machinery introduced in §1.4.2 is only engaged when the user supplies a variance map; in its absence, the linear-system solve is the ordinary unweighted least-squares solve used by every classical implementation (NumPy's SVD-based least-squares driver on the design matrix itself, rather than the explicitly formed normal equations the weighted path uses), so given identical sampled data the fitted coefficients agree to within the floating-point determinism of LAPACK on the host platform. The configuration flag is therefore binary at the algorithm-correctness level: variance_map is either supplied (WLS) or it is not (OLS), and the two paths share no shared mutable state.

  2. Round-trip serialization preserves the fit and its configuration. Saving a fit through isophote_results_to_fits and reading it back through isophote_results_from_fits recovers the per-isophote values and reconstructs an IsosterConfig whose fields match the original; the same holds for the ASDF writer–reader pair, and the META HDU carries the top-level result keys that are neither per-isophote nor configuration fields so that they survive too. Because the CONFIG HDU records the resolved configuration — every field, including those the user left at their default — the settings need never be supplied out of band, and a default that changes between releases cannot silently alter the meaning of an existing file. What we claim is reproducibility of the configuration, not of the fit from the file alone: the file contains neither the image, the mask nor the variance map, and reproducing the numbers additionally depends on the ISOSTER version, the host LAPACK, and whether the Numba kernels were available.

  3. Regression-test coverage of the fast paths. The test suite pins the Numba kernels against their NumPy fallbacks element-by-element — design-matrix construction, ellipse coordinates, harmonic-model evaluation, and the eccentric-anomaly conversion — including the degenerate and high-ellipticity cases where the two implementations would be most likely to diverge. Serialization round-trips, the stop-code contract, and the per-feature behaviour of each configuration flag are covered at the per-SMA dictionary level on synthetic galaxies generated deterministically from seeded factories rather than from stored reference files. The suite runs on every commit.

Two things §1.3.4 deliberately does not claim. It does not claim a specific numerical-agreement number with photutils.isophote, Isofit, or AutoProf; those are quantitative empirical questions that the benchmark chapters answer on representative samples. And it does not claim that every fast path is output-identical to its slow counterpart. Three of the four choices in §1.3.2 are: vectorized sampling, the Numba kernels, and the shared sampling stack all compute the same numbers as the implementations they replace. The lazy gradient does not, by construction, and §1.3.2 quantifies the difference rather than asserting it away.

docs.title: §1.4.1 Eccentric-anomaly sampling and ISOFIT-style joint harmonics
docs.text: The classical Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm samples the trial ellipse uniformly in the image position angle \(\phi\) and decomposes the resulting intensity profile in the same \(\phi\)-basis. This is a natural choice for low-ellipticity isophotes, where uniform-in-\(\phi\) sampling is approximately uniform-in-arclength and the harmonic basis is approximately orthogonal with respect to the path on the ellipse. It fails — sometimes severely — when the isophotes themselves are highly elliptical, as they are in edge-on disks, X-shaped / peanut-bulge galaxies, and strongly barred systems where the bar component dominates a range of SMAs. ISOSTER provides two related features that together extend the classical algorithm into this regime: eccentric-anomaly sampling (Ciambur 2015), which replaces \(\phi\) with the eccentric anomaly \(\psi\) as the angular basis; and ISOFIT-style joint harmonics, which fits higher-order deviation coefficients jointly with the geometry harmonics inside the iteration loop rather than as a post-hoc add-on. Both can be used independently; together they recover the Ciambur (2015) formulation faithfully within the ISOSTER framework.

docs.title: §1.4.1.1 Why uniform-in-\(\phi\) sampling fails at high ellipticity
docs.text:
Consider an elliptical isophote with semi-major axis \(a\), ellipticity \(\varepsilon\), and semi-minor axis \(b = a(1 - \varepsilon)\). Parametrize the ellipse by the image position angle \(\phi\) measured from the major axis. The radial distance from the ellipse center to the boundary at angle \(\phi\) is

\[ r(\phi) = \frac{b}{\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon(2 - \varepsilon)\cos^2\phi}}, \]

and the arc-length increment per unit \(\phi\) is

\[ \frac{ds}{d\phi} = \sqrt{r^2(\phi) + \left(\frac{dr}{d\phi}\right)^2}. \]

For \(\varepsilon \to 0\) (a circle), this is constant and uniform \(\phi\)-sampling is uniform in arc length. For \(\varepsilon\) approaching unity, \(ds / d\phi\) varies by orders of magnitude over the ellipse perimeter: it is large near \(\phi = 0\) (along the major axis, where the path moves quickly outward in image coordinates per unit \(\phi\)) and small near \(\phi = \pi / 2\) (along the minor axis, where the path doubles back tightly). The consequence is that uniform-in-\(\phi\) sampling under-samples the major-axis region — exactly the region where edge-on disks and peanut bulges have their most distinctive isophotal structure — and over-samples the minor-axis region, where the path is shortest and the structural information per sample is least.

It is worth being precise about what this does and does not cause, because the intuitive version of the argument is wrong. Non-uniform sampling density does not manufacture harmonic content out of nothing: a geometrically perfect ellipse has constant intensity along its boundary, and a constant is a constant in any angular coordinate. Fitting \(I(\phi) = \mathrm{const}\) in the \(\phi\)-basis returns \(I_0\) exactly and all harmonic coefficients zero, at any ellipticity. There is no "sampling-density artefact" that a perfect ellipse acquires and that a change of basis removes.

The two real problems are different, and both are consequences of the same fact: \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are related by a nonlinear reparametrization, \(\tan\phi = (1 - \varepsilon)\tan\psi\), and a nonlinear reparametrization does not preserve which Fourier orders are present.

First, the geometry-update algebra is derived in \(\psi\). This is the load-bearing point and it is easy to miss. Consider a trial ellipse displaced from the true isophote by a small offset \(\delta\) along its major axis, and parametrize position on the trial ellipse by the eccentric anomaly: \((a\cos\psi,\ b\sin\psi)\) in the ellipse frame. The semi-major axis of the isophote passing through that sample point is \(a' \approx a - \delta\cos\psi\), so the sampled intensity is \(I \approx I_0 - (dI/da)\,\delta\cos\psi\) — a pure \(\cos\psi\) term. Repeating the exercise for a minor-axis offset gives a pure \(\sin\psi\) term with an extra factor \((1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\); for an ellipticity error, a pure \(\cos 2\psi\) term with coefficient \((dI/da)\,a\,\delta\varepsilon / [2(1-\varepsilon)]\); for a position-angle error, a pure \(\sin 2\psi\) term. Inverting those four relations gives exactly the four update formulas ISOSTER applies — including the \((1-\varepsilon)\), \(2(1-\varepsilon)/a\) and \([(1-\varepsilon)^2 - 1]\) factors that would otherwise look arbitrary. In other words, the classical geometry corrections are already an eccentric-anomaly result. Feeding them coefficients measured in \(\psi\) is exact; feeding them coefficients measured in \(\phi\) is an approximation whose error grows with ellipticity and vanishes as \(\varepsilon \to 0\), where \(\phi \to \psi\).

Second, orders mix under the reparametrization, and the mixing runs downhill into the geometry terms. Because the map between the two angles is nonlinear, a residual that is a pure order-\(n\) harmonic in one basis is not a pure order-\(n\) harmonic in the other. The direction that matters is the one that contaminates the geometry update: genuine higher-order isophotal structure, expressed in \(\phi\), acquires first- and second-order components, and those components are indistinguishable from a geometry mismatch. The effect is easy to quantify. Take a residual that is exactly \(\cos 3\psi\) — pure third-order shape, no geometry error whatsoever — on an isophote of axis ratio \(b/a = 0.3\). Fitting the five-parameter geometry model in \(\psi\) returns all four geometry coefficients as zero, correctly. Fitting the same data in \(\phi\) returns a first-order cosine coefficient of \(-0.180\): an \(18\%\) spurious geometry signal conjured entirely out of real third-order structure by the choice of angular coordinate. The iteration then "corrects" a geometry error that does not exist.
