Both problems are therefore about interpretation of the coefficients rather than about the sampling being visibly sparse somewhere, and both are absent for round isophotes and severe for flattened ones — which is precisely the regime where edge-on disks and peanut bulges live.

docs.title: §1.4.1.2 The eccentric-anomaly parametrization
docs.text:
The eccentric anomaly \(\psi\) is the angular parameter that runs uniformly along the ellipse when the latter is mapped to an auxiliary unit circle. In the ellipse's principal coordinate system (major axis along \(x'\), minor along \(y'\)), the ellipse is the image of the unit circle under the affine map \((x', y') = (a\cos\psi, b\sin\psi)\). The arc-length increment per unit \(\psi\) is

\[ \frac{ds}{d\psi} = \sqrt{a^2 \sin^2\psi + b^2 \cos^2\psi}, \]

which varies between \(b\) and \(a\) over a full cycle, so its maximum-to-minimum ratio is exactly \(a / b\); it never vanishes, and it is more uniform than \(ds / d\phi\) at any fixed ellipticity. At \(b/a = 0.3\), for instance, \(ds/d\psi\) spans a factor of \(3.33\) against \(4.87\) for \(ds/d\phi\). The improvement is real but modest, and it is not a clean power law: the \(\phi\)-density ratio has no simple closed form and is not \((a/b)^2\), as an earlier version of this section asserted. The sampling-uniformity argument is worth making qualitatively and not worth over-quantifying, because — as §1.4.1.1 sets out — it is the weaker of the two reasons to prefer \(\psi\) anyway.

The relationship between \(\psi\) and the polar angle \(\theta\) measured from the ellipse center (the true anomaly, not the image position angle \(\phi\) used elsewhere in this section) is

\[ \tan\theta = \frac{b}{a}\tan\psi = (1 - \varepsilon)\tan\psi. \]

ISOSTER computes ellipse-boundary coordinates by stepping uniformly through \(\psi \in [0, 2\pi)\), evaluating \((x', y')\) on the principal axes via the closed-form mapping, then rotating into image coordinates by the position angle PA. The sampling step in isoster/sampling.py is the same vectorized scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates call described in §1.3.2; only the coordinate construction differs. The harmonic fit is then performed in the \(\psi\)-basis: the design matrix becomes

\[ \mathbf{A}_\psi = [\mathbf{1}, \sin\psi, \cos\psi, \sin 2\psi, \cos 2\psi, \sin n_1\psi, \cos n_1\psi, \ldots], \]

and the coefficients \(A_n^\psi\), \(B_n^\psi\) are the ones the geometry-correction algebra of §1.4.1.1 was written for. For a perfect ellipse the higher-order coefficients vanish in either basis, as §1.4.1.1 established — that property is not what the change of basis buys, and claiming it would contradict the argument made there. What the \(\psi\)-basis buys is that a non-zero shape deviation is expressed in the coordinate the correction formulas assume, so it stays in the harmonic order it belongs to instead of leaking down into orders 1 and 2.

One subtlety bears emphasizing, because it is easy to describe incorrectly. The eccentric anomaly is defined relative to the current trial geometry — its definition depends on the trial \(\varepsilon\) and PA — so as the iteration updates the geometry, the mapping \(\psi \to (x_\mathrm{image}, y_\mathrm{image})\) updates with it. The natural worry is that feeding \(\psi\)-basis coefficients into a geometry-update rule derived in the \(\phi\)-basis is a category error, and that one should convert the coefficients back to \(\phi\)-space first.

ISOSTER does not perform that conversion, and neither does ISOFIT. The coefficients \((A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2)\) fitted in \(\psi\) are fed directly to the classical update formulas of §1.1, which map the dominant amplitude onto \((x_0, y_0, \varepsilon, \mathrm{PA})\) through the local radial gradient. The polar angle \(\phi\) is carried alongside \(\psi\) through sampling and sigma-clipping, but only so that the angular bookkeeping stays aligned for diagnostics and error propagation; it does not enter the update.

No conversion is needed, because — as §1.4.1.1 sets out — the correction formulas were derived in \(\psi\) in the first place. The \(\psi\)-basis coefficients are exactly the quantities those formulas expect, so consuming them directly is the correct operation, not a tolerated approximation. It is the default \(\phi\)-mode that feeds the formulas coefficients from the wrong basis, and does so for compatibility with IRAF Ellipse and photutils.isophote rather than because it is more accurate.

It is worth resisting a tempting but invalid defence of the \(\phi\)-mode here, since it is the kind of argument that sounds right. One might argue that the iteration is driven to a fixed point where the residual first- and second-order content vanishes, so the two bases must agree on where the mismatch is zero even if they disagree about its size mid-iteration. They need not. A nonlinear reparametrization does not preserve which orders vanish: the \(\cos 3\psi\) example of §1.4.1.1 has exactly zero first- and second-order content in \(\psi\) and a first-order coefficient of \(-0.180\) in \(\phi\), so the two bases place the fixed point in different locations. The fixed points coincide only in the limit \(\varepsilon \to 0\).

The practical consequences for a user are therefore narrower than "the flag only changes the basis". The geometry parameters do retain their classical geometric meaning, and the converged \((x_0, y_0, \varepsilon, \mathrm{PA})\) remain directly comparable between modes in the sense that they denote the same things. But the two modes do not follow the same path, and on a flattened isophote with real higher-order structure they need not converge to the same place either. Which one to believe is not a matter of taste: the \(\psi\)-mode geometry is the one whose corrections were derived for the coefficients being fed to them.

docs.title: §1.4.1.3 ISOFIT-style joint harmonics
docs.text:
The default ISOSTER fit (and the classical Jedrzejewski / photutils fit) restricts the inside-loop harmonic basis to orders 1 and 2:

\[ \mathbf{A}_5 = [\mathbf{1}, \sin\theta, \cos\theta, \sin 2\theta, \cos 2\theta], \]

where \(\theta\) is the angular basis (\(\phi\) or \(\psi\) depending on the sampling mode). Higher-order coefficients \((A_n, B_n)\) for \(n \ge 3\) are fitted post-hoc on the converged geometry: each order \(n\) is fit separately with a three-column design matrix \([\mathbf{1}, \sin n\theta, \cos n\theta]\) on the sampled profile (the compute_deviations path). This post-hoc approach has two advantages: the inside-loop solve is cheap (the design matrix has only five columns); and the convergence criterion is decoupled from how many higher orders the user wants to measure.

It has one disadvantage. The higher-order coefficients describe isophotal shape that is potentially correlated with the geometry update: a slight error in the converged geometry can leak into the higher-order coefficients through the cross-correlation of the basis functions on the sampled intensity profile. For weak deviations from ellipticity the leakage is negligible, and the post-hoc approach is the right trade-off. For strong deviations — X-shaped bulges, peanut bulges, strongly disky / boxy isophotes — the leakage can be a significant fraction of the higher-order amplitude itself, and the converged geometry can be biased away from the geometry that would minimize the full harmonic residual including the higher orders.

ISOFIT (Ciambur 2015) addresses this by performing the joint inside-loop fit on an extended design matrix that includes the higher-order columns:

\[ \mathbf{A}_\mathrm{ISOFIT} = [\mathbf{1}, \sin\theta, \cos\theta, \sin 2\theta, \cos 2\theta, \sin n_1\theta, \cos n_1\theta, \ldots, \sin n_L\theta, \cos n_L\theta], \]

where \(\{n_1, \ldots, n_L\}\) are the orders specified in harmonic_orders (default \(\{3, 4\}\), with \(L = 2\)). The linear-system solve is now \(p = 5 + 2L\) parameters wide rather than \(5\), and the cross-correlations between geometry harmonics and higher-order harmonics are absorbed into the joint covariance matrix rather than leaked into the geometry update.

ISOSTER provides two ISOFIT variants, both gated by simultaneous_harmonics = True:

  • isofit_mode = 'in_loop' runs the joint solve on every iteration of every isophote. This is the most aggressive variant: the geometry update at each iteration is computed from the joint solve, so the geometry trajectory through iteration space differs from the post-hoc fit. The cross-correlations are absorbed throughout the iteration, not just at the end.

  • isofit_mode = 'original' runs the classical 5-parameter fit inside the loop and, after convergence, fits all requested higher orders jointly in a single post-hoc solve on the converged geometry. The post-hoc design matrix is \([\mathbf{1}, \sin n_1\theta, \cos n_1\theta, \ldots]\) — it carries the higher-order columns without the geometry columns, so the orders share one solve and their cross-correlations are absorbed into the joint covariance, but the geometry harmonics are not re-fit. This matches the original Ciambur (2015) procedure's intent: the inside-loop trajectory is identical to the default, and only the reported higher-order coefficients (and their uncertainties) differ from the per-order post-hoc path. (The multi-band 'simultaneous_original' mode of §1.4.5 goes one step further and re-solves the full system — geometry columns included — once post-hoc; the two paths deliberately differ in that respect.)

In both variants, the extended linear system is solved through the same NumPy / LAPACK pipeline used in the 5-parameter fit, and the dominant-coefficient selector for the geometry update continues to operate on indices 1–4 of the coefficient vector (corresponding to \(A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2\)). Coefficient storage in the output dictionary follows the convention \([I_0, A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2, A_{n_1}, B_{n_1}, A_{n_2}, B_{n_2}, \ldots]\), with the \(k\)-th higher order occupying indices \(5 + 2k\) and \(5 + 2k + 1\).

docs.title: §1.4.1.4 Caveats and fallbacks
docs.text:
Three caveats apply to the ISOFIT path and are worth flagging explicitly:

Sample-count fallback. The extended design matrix requires at least \(2L + 5\) sample points to be well-posed. At small SMAs where \(N\) is at the floor of \(\max(64, \lfloor 2\pi a \rfloor) = 64\), the condition holds easily for \(L = 2\) (\(2L + 5 = 9\)) but begins to strain for \(L = 4\) or larger when combined with severe masking (say, more than 80% of the ellipse masked out by a defect or a nearby source). When the available sample count falls below the threshold, ISOSTER falls back to the 5-parameter fit for that isophote and emits a RuntimeWarning on the first occurrence, so the fallback is announced rather than silent. The fallback is byte-equivalent to running with simultaneous_harmonics = False for that isophote alone; the rest of the fit proceeds with the joint solve.

Compute overhead. The two features cost very different amounts, and quoting one figure for the pair obscures which one to worry about. Measured on a whole-galaxy fit (\(n = 2\) Sérsic, \(R_e = 30\,\mathrm{px}\), \(\varepsilon = 0.4\), 59 isophotes, harmonic_orders=[3, 4]) against the same fit in the default configuration:

configuration wall time ratio to default default (\(\phi\), post-hoc) 48.9 ms 1.00 eccentric anomaly only 51.0 ms 1.04 ISOFIT in_loop only 62.2 ms 1.27 eccentric anomaly + ISOFIT 63.8 ms 1.30

(Absolute times are from one session and are machine- and session-dependent; the ratios are the less machine-dependent part, though not portable either — hardware, BLAS and library versions shift ratios too. Across eighteen sessions the combined ratio has a median of \(1.34\) and an interquartile range of \(1.32\)–\(1.36\). Reproduced by benchmarks/draft_timings/run_draft_timings.py; measurement protocol in §1.6.5.)

The eccentric anomaly is nearly free — it changes how the sample coordinates are computed, not how much work is done. Essentially all of the cost is ISOFIT's wider linear system, at about \(30\%\) for \(L = 2\) orders, and it will grow with the number of orders and vary with the platform's LAPACK. For most science use cases the overhead is dwarfed by the cost of the image-level outward loop, but it is real and should be budgeted when running ISOSTER on large samples.

Geometry-update path unchanged. Both the 'in_loop' and the 'original' variant update the geometry through the same coordinate-descent rule used by the default fit: the largest of \(|A_1|, |B_1|, |A_2|, |B_2|\) is identified, and the corresponding geometry parameter is updated by an amount proportional to the amplitude scaled by the local radial gradient. The ISOFIT path does not introduce a multi-parameter update step; the geometry trajectory through iteration space differs from the default only because the harmonic coefficients themselves differ (their values absorb cross-correlations with the higher orders). This is intentional and matches Ciambur (2015) §4: the joint solve clarifies the values, not the update rule.

A practical point worth mentioning: the combination use_eccentric_anomaly = True and simultaneous_harmonics = True with isofit_mode = 'in_loop' is the closest faithful reimplementation of the Ciambur (2015) IRAF Isofit task within the ISOSTER framework. It is the recommended configuration for edge-on disks, peanut bulges, and strongly barred galaxies where the higher-order harmonic structure carries the science of interest, and where the user wants both the sampling-basis correction and the cross-correlation absorption.

docs.title: §1.4.1.5 Demonstration: synthetic edge-on disk
docs.text:
To make the difference visible we use a synthetic edge-on disk generated through the MockGal renderer in isophote_test (an external companion repository, not part of the ISOSTER source tree). The recipe is a single-component Sersic profile with \(n_\mathrm{Sersic} = 1.0\) (exponential), effective semi-major axis \(R_e = 60\,\mathrm{px}\), ellipticity \(\varepsilon = 0.70\) (near-edge-on aspect ratio \(a / b \approx 3.3\)), position angle \(\mathrm{PA} = 45^\circ\), and total flux scaled so the central surface brightness is well above the sky noise. The image is \(512 \times 512\,\mathrm{px}\) with Gaussian sky noise corresponding to \(\mu_\mathrm{sky} = 26\,\mathrm{mag\,arcsec^{-2}}\) in a fiducial band, and the rendered image is convolved with a Gaussian PSF of FWHM \(= 2\,\mathrm{px}\) before noise addition.

A note on what this demonstration must not be. An earlier version of this subsection proposed a pure elliptical mock and predicted that the \(\phi\)-mode fit would show a spurious rise in \(A_4^\mathrm{norm}\) that the \(\psi\)-mode fit would not. That prediction is wrong, for the reason given in §1.4.1.1: a perfect ellipse has constant intensity along its boundary, and a constant has zero harmonic content in either angular coordinate. Both modes would return \(A_4^\mathrm{norm} \approx 0\) and the figure would show nothing. A demonstration built on a pure ellipse cannot exhibit the effect, because there is no effect to exhibit.

The mock therefore carries a genuine fourth-order deviation. We add a disky perturbation to the exponential disk above, of normalized amplitude \(B_4^\mathrm{norm} = 0.03\) applied uniformly across the SMA range, on top of the \(\varepsilon = 0.70\) base ellipse. The truth is then non-trivial and known: the correct recovered profile is a flat line at \(0.03\), and the correct geometry is the planted \((\varepsilon, \mathrm{PA})\) at every radius.

Which geometry parameter should be affected, and which should not. The perturbation is aligned with the ellipse axes, so it enters as a \(\cos 4\psi\) term. Re-expressed in \(\phi\) at \(b/a = 0.3\), that term projects onto the five-parameter geometry model with \(B_2 = -0.538\) per unit amplitude and \(A_2 = 0.000\) — it contaminates the coefficient that drives ellipticity and, by symmetry, leaves the position-angle coefficient untouched. (The misaligned partner \(\sin 4\psi\) does the reverse, projecting onto \(A_2\) with the same magnitude.) An earlier version of this subsection predicted a bias in both \(\varepsilon\) and PA from an aligned perturbation; that was wrong, and the symmetry makes the prediction sharp rather than vague: for this mock the \(\phi\)-mode ellipticity should be biased and the \(\phi\)-mode PA should not. A figure showing a PA bias here would indicate a bug, not the effect.

The comparison must vary one thing at a time. Contrasting a default \(\phi\)-mode post-hoc fit against an EA+ISOFIT joint fit changes the angular basis and the harmonic-fit strategy at once, so any difference is unattributable. The demonstration is therefore a \(2 \times 2\): \(\{\phi, \psi\} \times \{\)post-hoc, ISOFIT in-loop\(\}\), four fits on the same image, mask, starting geometry, astep and maxsma. The basis effect is then the difference along one axis at fixed strategy, and the ISOFIT effect the difference along the other.

[FIG X.4.1 — to be generated. Four fits as above. Panel A: the mock image with the \(\psi\)+ISOFIT isophotes overlaid. Panel B: the recovered \(B_4^\mathrm{norm}(a)\) for all four configurations against the planted truth (black dashed at \(0.03\)). Panel C: the recovered \(\varepsilon(a)\) and \(\mathrm{PA}(a)\) against the planted constants. The questions the panels are to answer: does the \(\phi\)-basis ellipticity depart from truth at fixed harmonic strategy, and by how much; is the PA left unbiased as the symmetry argument requires; and does the ISOFIT axis change the answer independently of the basis axis. Data source: to be generated by the recipe below. Nothing in this figure has been produced or measured; the ellipticity/PA expectations above are consequences of the projection arithmetic, not results.]

Panel C is the load-bearing panel, and it is the one the earlier draft omitted: the argument for the eccentric anomaly is about the geometry being contaminated by real higher-order structure, not about a phantom higher-order signal appearing on a featureless ellipse.

The recipe for the \(2 \times 2\) is:

from itertools import product
from isoster import fit_image
from isoster.config import IsosterConfig

common = dict(sma0=10.0, maxsma=180.0, harmonic_orders=[3, 4],
              x0=256.0, y0=256.0, eps=0.5, pa=0.0)

results = {}
for basis, strategy in product(("phi", "psi"), ("posthoc", "isofit")):
    cfg = IsosterConfig(
        **common,
        use_eccentric_anomaly=(basis == "psi"),
        simultaneous_harmonics=(strategy == "isofit"),
        isofit_mode="in_loop" if strategy == "isofit" else "original",
        compute_deviations=True,
    )
    results[(basis, strategy)] = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=cfg)

All four use the same starting geometry (\(x_0 = y_0 = 256\,\mathrm{px}\), \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(\mathrm{PA} = 0\)), so the two axes of the comparison are cleanly separated. The output dictionaries can be passed to isoster.plotting.plot_comparison_qa_figure to build the panels. These runs have not been performed; the block above is the intended recipe, not a record of an executed experiment.

A final note on when not to enable this combination. On round-ish isophotes (\(\varepsilon \lesssim 0.2\)) both effects of §1.4.1.1 are small — \(\phi \to \psi\), so the correction formulas are being fed nearly the right coefficients and the order-mixing is weak — and the post-hoc higher-harmonic fit is consistent with the joint solve. Switching to EA+ISOFIT in that regime adds the ~30% compute overhead measured above without producing scientifically distinguishable results. The \(\varepsilon \lesssim 0.2\) boundary is a rule of thumb from the scaling of §1.4.1.1 — both effects fall away as \(\phi \to \psi\) — and not a measured threshold; where exactly it sits depends on how much genuine higher-order structure the galaxy carries, since that is what leaks into the geometry terms. The combination is therefore reserved for the regime where the user has identified strong elliptical or non-elliptical isophote structure as a science target; on a survey pipeline the simplest policy is to apply EA+ISOFIT only to galaxies with morphological classifications or photometric proxies indicating high-ellipticity or peanut-bulge morphology.

docs.title: §1.4.2 Variance-aware fitting
docs.text:
The Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm and the Python predecessors that implement it fit harmonics by ordinary least squares with uniform weights. Modern wide-field surveys — HSC-SSP, DECaLS / BASS / MzLS, DES, eventually LSST — deliver a per-pixel inverse-variance map alongside the science image, but the classical algorithm has no mechanism for consuming it. The information is therefore thrown away, with two consequences: outlier pixels (cosmic rays, hot pixels, masked-bad pixels that survived the bad-pixel map) carry the same weight in the harmonic fit as good pixels; and parameter uncertainties are estimated from the scatter on the ellipse — which conflates per-pixel photon noise with the intrinsic azimuthal scatter from galaxy structure (spiral arms, dust lanes, bars, faint companions) — rather than from the photon noise the variance map already encodes.

ISOSTER closes this gap by accepting a variance_map argument to fit_image and routing all harmonic fits through a weighted least-squares (WLS) path when one is supplied. The path is algorithmically separate from the OLS path: every WLS branch is gated on a variance map having actually been supplied, so when variance_map = None not one weighted operation executes and the output is bit-for-bit what the same code produced before the WLS path existed. When a variance map is supplied, every harmonic fit on every isophote — geometry fit, ISOFIT extended fit, post-hoc higher-order fit, forced-extraction fit, multi-band joint fit — switches to WLS uniformly. There is no half-WLS configuration in which some harmonic fits use weights and others do not.

docs.title: §1.4.2.1 OLS vs WLS at the algorithm level
docs.text:
The OLS normal equations for the design matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and the sampled intensities \(\mathbf{y}\) are

\[ \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}, \]

with parameter covariance

\[ \mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{x}})_\mathrm{OLS} = (\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A})^{-1}\,\hat\sigma_\mathrm{res}^2, \]

where \(\hat\sigma_\mathrm{res}^2\) is the residual variance estimated empirically from the fit residuals,

\[ \hat\sigma_\mathrm{res}^2 = \frac{1}{N - P}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(y_i - [\mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}]_i\right)^2, \]

with \(P\) the number of parameters the fit actually carried. The residual-variance rescaling is necessary precisely because OLS has no external scale for the noise — the matrix \((\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A})^{-1}\) alone has the wrong units, and the only available scale is what the residuals themselves provide.

Two details of that rescaling matter enough to state. First, it is computed once per isophote, from the exact fitted model — the five-parameter model, or the wider ISOFIT model when higher orders were fit inside the loop — evaluated at the angular coordinate the coefficients were fitted in. That single value scales both the geometry block and the higher-order harmonic errors, so one fit yields one error scale; the optional background floor \(\hat\sigma_\mathrm{res}^2 \ge \sigma_\mathrm{bg}^2\) is applied at the same point, once, rather than on individual consumers. Evaluating a truncated model to rescale a wider fit would charge genuine fitted structure to the noise, and would leave two parts of the same isophote reporting errors on different scales. Second, when the fit is exactly determined — as many samples as parameters, which is precisely where ISOFIT switches on — the model passes through every point and the data carry no information about the noise level. The residual variance is then reported as zero, meaning "not measurable", which is a different statement from "not supplied".

The WLS normal equations replace \(\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}\) with their weighted analogues, using the diagonal weight matrix \(\mathbf{W} = \mathrm{diag}(1 / \sigma_i^2)\) where \(\sigma_i^2\) is the per-pixel variance at the \(i\)-th sample point along the ellipse:

\[ \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{y}, \]

with parameter covariance

\[ \mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{x}})_\mathrm{WLS} = (\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{A})^{-1}. \]

The WLS covariance requires no residual-variance rescaling. The inverse-variance weights have units of \(1/\mathrm{intensity}^2\), so the dimensional argument that forced the OLS rescaling does not apply here: \((\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{A})^{-1}\) already has units of \(\mathrm{intensity}^2\) on the parameter axes that are themselves in intensity units.

Calling it exact would overstate the case, and the conditions under which it is a calibrated uncertainty are worth naming, since both are routinely violated by survey data. The first is that the variance map correctly describes the per-pixel noise; correlated noise from coaddition, underestimated sky variance, or a zeropoint calibration error all propagate straight through into over-confident error bars, and §1.4.2.4 returns to this. The second is subtler and is a property of ISOSTER's own sampling rather than of the input: the samples along a ring are produced by bilinear interpolation from the underlying pixel grid, so neighbouring samples share source pixels and are not statistically independent, while \(\mathbf{W}\) is diagonal and the covariance expression assumes they are. At the default sampling density of roughly one sample per pixel of perimeter the correlation is modest, but it grows as the sampling density rises relative to the pixel scale, and it biases the reported uncertainties low. The WLS covariance is therefore best described as free of the OLS estimator's structural bias, and calibrated to the extent that the variance map is calibrated and the ring samples can be treated as independent.

The two practical consequences of switching from OLS to WLS are worth naming explicitly. Outlier down-weighting: a single hot-pixel sample with \(\sigma_i^2 = 10^{6}\) relative to the \(\sigma^2 \sim 1\) of the neighbouring sky-noise pixels carries a weight \(10^{-6}\) times smaller than its neighbours in the harmonic fit. The classical OLS path would weight that pixel equally and let a single outlier swing the dominant harmonic amplitude; WLS effectively masks it without the caller having to identify the pixel ahead of time. Error-bar decoupling: the two estimators answer different questions, and it is worth being careful about what does and does not follow from that.

Under the textbook model the residual-scatter estimator is not deficient at all. If the samples are independent with a common variance, then \(\hat\sigma_\mathrm{res}^2\) is an unbiased estimate of that variance and the OLS covariance is a correct — indeed optimal — description of the photon noise. In that case OLS and WLS have the same expected covariance, and neither is systematically larger. Any claim that the scatter estimator is "bounded below by the photon noise it fails to capture" is simply false in this regime, and an earlier version of this section made it.

What separates the two in practice is the failure of the textbook model's two assumptions. When the variance is not common across the ring, the weighted estimator uses information the unweighted one discards, and the two diverge in a direction that depends on where the low-variance samples sit relative to the structure being fitted — it is not one-signed. When the residual contains real azimuthal structure the five-parameter model does not absorb — spiral arms, dust lanes, orders \(n \ge 3\) — the scatter estimator counts that structure as noise and is inflated relative to pure photon noise; this is the regime where OLS error bars are larger, not smaller. And \(\hat\sigma_\mathrm{res}^2\) carries its own sampling error of order \(\sqrt{2/(N-P)}\), so on a single ring it can land either side of the truth.

How far apart the two estimators fall on real survey data, and in which direction, is what the demonstration of §1.4.2.5 is for. That galaxy has not yet been selected and the comparison has not been run, so no ratio is quoted here; an earlier version of this section gave one, but it described an experiment that had not been performed. The durable argument for WLS does not depend on the answer: it is that WLS returns error bars traceable to a stated noise model, which can be checked against the survey's own variance map, rather than to a residual scatter that mixes photon noise with whatever the model failed to fit.

docs.title: §1.4.2.2 Per-pixel gradient error propagation
docs.text:
The error bar on the mean intensity \(I_0\) propagates straightforwardly from the variance map. In the free fit, \(I_0\) is the intercept of the harmonic fit, so its variance is the intercept element of the WLS parameter covariance,

\[ \mathrm{Var}(I_0)_\mathrm{WLS} = \left[(\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{A})^{-1}\right]_{0,0}, \]

and ISOSTER reports \(\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(I_0)}\) as intens_err in the WLS path. Two qualifications. When the fit covariance is unavailable, the fallback is the variance of an inverse-variance- weighted mean, \(\left(\sum_i \sigma_i^{-2}\right)^{-1}\) — the right form there, because template-based forced photometry reports a plain weighted mean rather than a fitted intercept. And under the 'median' integrator the reported intensity is not the fitted intercept at all, so intens_err comes from the median's own variance instead; see the paragraph on the deliberate mean/median asymmetry below. The OLS analogue is \(\mathrm{rms} / \sqrt{N}\) (with the \(\sqrt{\pi/2}\) median penalty where applicable), which inherits the photon-noise-vs-azimuthal-scatter conflation discussed above.

The more interesting propagation is the radial gradient error, because that is the quantity that drives the convergence criterion and the gradient-SNR damping (§1.1, §1.3) and because its OLS estimate is structurally biased in a way the intensity-error estimate is not. The radial gradient \(dI / da\) is computed in ISOSTER from two samples at offset SMAs: a central sample at the current \(a\) and an offset sample at \(a + \Delta a\) (or \(a (1 + \Delta a)\) for multiplicative SMA stepping). The two samples produce two mean intensities \(\bar I_c\) and \(\bar I_g\) (plain unweighted means, or medians under the 'median' integrator), and the gradient is

\[ \widehat{dI/da} = \frac{\bar I_g - \bar I_c}{\Delta r}, \]

with \(\Delta r\) equal to the radial separation between the two samples (either \(\Delta a\) in linear-stepping mode or \(a \cdot \Delta a\) in multiplicative-stepping mode). Assuming the two samples are statistically independent — they sample different elliptical paths through the image and the per-pixel photon noise is uncorrelated between distinct pixels — the variance of the gradient is

\[ \mathrm{Var}\!\left(\widehat{dI/da}\right) = \frac{\mathrm{Var}(\bar I_c) + \mathrm{Var}(\bar I_g)}{(\Delta r)^2}, \]

and the WLS gradient error is

\[ \sigma_{dI/da}^\mathrm{WLS} = \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\bar I_c) + \mathrm{Var}(\bar I_g)}}{\Delta r}. \]

The per-ring variance on the right-hand side must be the variance of the estimator that was actually used to locate the ring, and this is the point at which a plausible-looking shortcut goes wrong. The two ring locations are an unweighted mean or an unweighted median; the variance of an inverse-variance-weighted mean, \(\left(\sum_i \sigma_i^{-2}\right)^{-1}\), belongs to a different estimator and understates the uncertainty of an unweighted mean whenever the variances differ around the ring. ISOSTER therefore computes location and variance together in one helper (_ring_statistic_and_variance in isoster/_shared.py), so the reported gradient and its error can never come from two different estimators on two different sample sets. For a ring of \(N\) surviving samples with per-sample variances \(\sigma_i^2\) the two forms are

\[ \mathrm{Var}(\bar I)_\mathrm{mean} = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sigma_i^2, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\bar I)_\mathrm{median} = \frac{\pi N}{2 \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sigma_i^{-1}\right)^{2}}. \]

The first is the ordinary variance of a mean of independent, non-identically-distributed measurements. The second is a normal-theory asymptotic result which, for uniform variance \(\sigma_i^2 = \sigma^2\), reduces to \(\pi\sigma^2 / (2N)\) — the mean's \(\sigma^2/N\) inflated by the familiar factor \(\pi/2 \approx 1.571\) that makes the median the less efficient estimator under Gaussian noise. The median form is an approximation rather than an exact result: its derivation assumes independent, identically distributed Gaussian samples, whereas a real ring carries genuine azimuthal structure and neighbouring samples are correlated through the bilinear interpolation that produced them. Monte Carlo tests agree with the closed forms to about \(0.08\%\) for uniform per-sample variance and \(1.4\%\) for spatially varying variance — accurate enough to trust as an error estimate, but not exact in the way a first-principles derivation on independent samples would be.

Either way the expression is pure photon noise: the only quantities on the right-hand side are the per-pixel variances at the two sampled ellipses and the geometric separation \(\Delta r\). Galaxy-structure scatter does not appear, because the harmonic-fit residuals are not used.

A deliberate asymmetry between the reported intensity and the gradient. Under WLS with the default mean integrator, the ring intensity ISOSTER reports is not the unweighted mean that enters the gradient: it is the inverse-variance-weighted intercept of the harmonic fit, whose error is the exact covariance element of equation §1.4.2.2 above. The gradient, by contrast, always uses the unweighted ring statistic on both rings. The two quantities are computed for different purposes and the difference is intentional. The intensity is a per-isophote photometric measurement, where down-weighting noisier pixels is exactly what one wants; the gradient is a comparison between two rings, where using the same simple estimator on both sides is what keeps the comparison honest. Under the median integrator the reported intensity is an unweighted median even when a variance map is supplied, so intens_err comes from the median's own variance above rather than from the weighted intercept. Rescaling the weighted intercept's error by \(\sqrt{\pi/2}\) to manufacture a median error is correct only for uniform variance: once the noise varies with angle, the intercept of a five-parameter fit becomes correlated with the sine and cosine terms and its variance is no longer the median's by any constant factor. Measured across several spatial variance patterns, the rescaled value ranged from \(0.75\times\) to \(3.21\times\) the correct median error, so the shortcut can understate as well as overstate the uncertainty.

The OLS analogue, by contrast, replaces both \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar I_c)\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\bar I_g)\) with scatter-based estimates of the form \(s_c^2 / N_c\) and \(s_g^2 / N_g\), where \(s_c^2\) and \(s_g^2\) are the plain sample variances of the intensities around the two ellipses (with the same \(\pi/2\) penalty applied under the median integrator). This substitution looks innocent — both quantities have units of \(\mathrm{intensity}^2\) — but it conflates two different sources of variance. The scatter \(s_c^2\) at a single ellipse contains both the per-pixel photon noise and the intrinsic azimuthal variation of the galaxy structure at that radius. The latter is precisely what the harmonic decomposition is trying to measure. Subtracting the fitted harmonic contribution would help, and would be the natural refinement, but even the residual after the five-parameter fit still carries azimuthal structure from orders \(n \ge 3\) that the geometry fit does not absorb. The scatter-based gradient error should therefore be read as an upper bound on the photon noise rather than an estimate of it, and the size of the excess depends on the morphological complexity of the galaxy in a way that is difficult to characterize a priori.

The bias matters because \(\sigma_{dI/da}\) does not merely decorate the output: it feeds the convergence criterion through the gradient-SNR damping (§1.3.2), where a gradient SNR below 3 reduces the geometry-update damping factor to prevent overfitting the noise floor, and it feeds the maxgerr gate that decides when the outward sweep has run out of usable gradient. It also decides, through the relative error \(|\sigma_{dI/da} / (dI/da)|\), whether ISOSTER pays for a second, wider-baseline gradient sample at \(a + 2\Delta a\) before accepting the value. Overestimating \(\sigma_{dI/da}\) — the typical scatter-estimator failure mode on a galaxy with prominent spiral structure — therefore damps the geometry update more aggressively than the data warrants, spends sampling effort on a second baseline that was not needed, and can stop the outward sweep early on a gradient that was in fact well measured. WLS removes the bias by replacing the scatter estimate with the variance-map propagation, and the gradient-SNR criterion then reflects the actual photon noise. When either ring's variance is not finite, ISOSTER reports the gradient error as unavailable rather than as an enormous number, so a degenerate ring cannot masquerade as a merely uncertain one.

A practical observation. The WLS gradient error formula above is algebraically equivalent to the standard photon-noise propagation for the difference of two means; nothing in it is novel. What is novel is that the classical isophote-fit literature predates the routine availability of per-pixel inverse-variance maps, and implementations written in that era reasonably estimated gradient errors from residual scatter because that was the only available estimate. The WLS path in ISOSTER simply uses the better estimate when the user supplies the data for it.

docs.title: §1.4.2.3 Input handling and safeguards
docs.text:
The variance_map argument is an array of the same shape as the science image (a ValueError is raised at the top of fit_image otherwise) carrying the per-pixel variance \(\sigma_i^2\). The following sanitization rules are applied in order:

  • Shape and dtype check. The variance map is coerced to a float-64 NumPy array; integer or float-32 inputs are converted with a copy. The caller's array is never mutated.

  • Invalid entries are marked, then dropped. A per-pixel variance carries usable information only if it is finite and strictly positive. Every entry that is not — NaN, \(\pm\infty\), zero, or negative — is marked NaN internally, and the sampler then excludes the affected samples outright, exactly the way it already excludes masked pixels. One RuntimeWarning is emitted per category (non-finite, non-positive) reporting how many entries were affected. The marking is performed on a copy; the caller's variance_map remains as supplied.

  • Copy-on-write. The internal sanitized array is held in a buffer separate from the caller's variance_map. A caller can pass the same variance_map to multiple fit_image calls (typical of survey pipelines that fit the same galaxy at multiple bands or with multiple IsosterConfig variants) without worrying about cumulative side effects.

The governing principle is that a ring statistic and its uncertainty must always describe the identical set of samples. Dropping is the only policy that satisfies it. Two earlier mechanisms, both now retired, substituted a placeholder value instead: non-finite entries became a large sentinel (\(10^{30}\)), intended to give the pixel a negligible weight, and non-positive entries were clamped to a small positive value (\(10^{-30}\)), intended to bound the weight instead of dividing by zero. Both kept the flagged pixel inside the ring while distorting how much it counted. The sentinel is finite and strictly positive, so the validity rule kept it despite the intent; the clamp was worse, giving a single unusable pixel a near-infinite weight that could collapse an inverse-variance-weighted error by fourteen orders of magnitude. Neither failure announced itself in the output, which is the reason to state the policy explicitly rather than leave it to a docstring.

Checking the sampled value alone is not sufficient. Variances are read with bilinear interpolation, which blends each sample from the four surrounding image pixels. A NaN or an infinity propagates through that blend on its own and always reaches the validity check. Zero and negative entries do not: an isolated zero-variance pixel averaged with three positive neighbours yields a positive interpolated variance that the check accepts, leaving an unusable sample in the ring with an understated variance. Measured on a flat test map with a true variance of \(4.0\), one zero-variance source pixel produced an interpolated variance of \(1.95\), and one negative pixel produced \(1.44\). ISOSTER therefore also validates the four source pixels feeding each sample. Because fit_image has already marked every unusable entry before any sampling happens, the source check is redundant on that path and is skipped there; it costs at most about \(0.11\,\mathrm{ms}\) per ring on a direct call to the lower-level fitting functions, which are public and may legitimately be handed a raw, unvalidated map. Instrumenting a 62-isophote fit of a \(1133 \times 1133\) image confirms the check runs zero times inside fit_image, so the normal pipeline carries no extra cost.

The canonical inverse-variance-to-variance conversion is therefore:

variance_map = np.where(invvar > 0, 1.0 / invvar, np.nan)

This states the invvar = 0 masked-out convention explicitly at the call site, which is clearer than relying on ISOSTER's internal marking, though the two give the same result. Callers who prefer to be explicit about exclusion may equivalently fold those pixels into the mask argument; ISOSTER treats the two routes identically.

The multi-band path (§1.4.5) applies the same rule to each band's map. It differs in one structural detail: every multi-band entry point that accepts a raw variance map routes through a single resolver, so the arrays handed to the sampler are always pre-marked and the source-pixel check has nothing left to catch. There is consequently no multi-band equivalent of the "already prepared" flag, because there is no unprepared path.

docs.title: §1.4.2.4 Caveats and composability
docs.text:
Three caveats apply to the WLS path:

Variance maps do not replace masking. The drop policy of §1.4.2.3 applies only to variances that are invalid — non-finite or non-positive. A pixel that is merely very noisy is valid data: with \(\sigma_i^2 = 10^{6}\) it still contributes a weight of \(10^{-6}\) to the harmonic fit, not zero. For a single bad pixel on an isophote with \(N \sim 1000\) samples this is negligible; for pathological cases where a large fraction of the ellipse is covered by high-variance pixels (a defect that spans an arc of the ellipse, a bright companion's diffraction spike crossing the isophote) the residual weight can still bias the fit. The recommended practice is to combine variance_map with a binary mask array that excludes pixels the caller knows to be unusable; WLS then operates on the remaining pixels with weights derived from their physical photon noise.

Variance maps inherit upstream systematics. If the survey inverse-variance map underestimates the true noise — typically the case for coadded imaging where pixel-to-pixel noise is correlated and the naive per-pixel variance does not reflect the effective noise per resolution element — WLS produces over-confident error bars on the harmonic-fit parameters and on the gradient. ISOSTER cannot diagnose this from the variance map alone; the caller is responsible for correcting the variance map upstream, typically through a noise-rescaling factor estimated from blank-sky regions or from a covariance-matrix model of the coaddition.

Uniform-variance equivalence. What makes WLS and OLS coincide on the fitted values is the variance being nearly uniform around the ellipse — not the signal-to-noise being high. The two are easily confused because they often occur together, but they are independent conditions, and it is the first that matters: WLS differs from OLS only through the relative weights it assigns to samples, so a ring whose per-pixel variances are all equal produces the same normal equations either way, at any signal level. Where the variances do vary around the ring — a coadd depth gradient, a dither-pattern seam, a masked region's soft edge — the weights are non-uniform, and the fitted geometry, harmonic coefficients and curve-of-growth differ between the two paths regardless of how bright the galaxy is. In the uniform case the fitted values agree to within LAPACK floating-point determinism and only the error bars differ, WLS using the variance-map propagation and OLS the residual scatter. Users who do not have a variance map should not invent one to enable WLS "just in case"; the OLS path produces correct geometry estimates on its own, and a fabricated variance map only contaminates the error bars.

The WLS path composes cleanly with every other ISOSTER feature. All sampling modes (φ-uniform and ψ-uniform), all harmonic-fit modes (post-hoc, 'in_loop' ISOFIT, 'original' ISOFIT), all constraint flags (fix_center, fix_pa, fix_eps), the LSB outskirt features (§1.4.3), the batch-robustness primitives (§1.4.4), and the multi-band joint free fit (§1.4.5) all carry the WLS weights through unchanged. (The multi-band case adds a wrinkle worth naming here rather than leaving entirely to §1.4.5.2: the joint solve composes the per-pixel inverse-variance weights with a per-band factor derived from that band's radial gradient, so the effective weight on the shared geometry is not \(1/\sigma_i^2\) alone. The per-pixel weights enter unchanged; what changes is what they are multiplied by.) The composability is a property of the implementation: the weight matrix enters as a single row-wise prescaling of \(\mathbf{A}\) before the normal equations are formed, \(\mathbf{A}_W = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{A}\), after which \(\mathbf{A}_W^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{A}_W^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}\) are solved directly. (The OLS branch instead calls NumPy's least-squares driver on the unweighted \(\mathbf{A}\); the two branches are deliberately separate so that the OLS path is untouched by the existence of the WLS one, which is what makes the byte-identity claim of §1.4.2.1 checkable rather than merely asserted.) Every harmonic fit in the package — the five-parameter geometry solve, the wider ISOFIT solves, the higher-order post-hoc fits — goes through this same pair of branches. Adding a new feature that affects the harmonic fit does not require a parallel WLS implementation; it inherits the weighted solve automatically.

docs.title: §1.4.2.5 Demonstration: LegacySurvey galaxy with inverse-variance map
docs.text:
To make the OLS / WLS difference visible we use a LegacySurvey (DECaLS) galaxy from the SGA-2020 sample, drawn from the curated demonstration subset in sga_isoster/data/demo/ (an external companion repository, not part of the ISOSTER source tree). The galaxy is a moderately bright disk-dominated late-type system at intermediate inclination, large enough that the outward fit pushes well into the LSB regime where the OLS / WLS distinction becomes quantitatively significant. The science image is the \(r\)-band coadded frame in nanomaggies, and the variance map is constructed from the LegacySurvey per-pixel inverse-variance (\(\mathtt{invvar}\)) extension by

\[ \sigma^2(x, y) = \begin{cases} 1 / \mathtt{invvar}(x, y) & \mathtt{invvar} > 0,\\ \mathrm{NaN} & \mathtt{invvar} = 0, \end{cases} \]

following the canonical recipe of §1.4.2.3, so that pixels the survey excluded from its own inverse-variance calculation are excluded from the isophote fit as well rather than being assigned a weight.

[FIG X.4.2 — to be generated. Two-panel figure. Panel A: the LegacySurvey \(r\)-band image with the WLS-fitted isophotes overlaid in cyan. Panel B: the surface-brightness profiles \(\mu(a)\) in \(\mathrm{mag\,arcsec^{-2}}\) from the two separate fits of the recipe below — OLS (red) and WLS (blue) — each drawn with its own central curve and its own error envelope. The two fits share a configuration and an image but not a result: the weights enter the solve, so the fitted geometry and intensities can differ as well as the error bars, and drawing one shared central curve would hide that. Whether the two central curves in fact lie close together is a property of the galaxy's variance map that the figure should report, not assume: it holds to the extent that the LegacySurvey inverse-variance map is uniform across each ring, which we have not verified for any particular object. Two ways to make this honest are open — select the galaxy on a stated ring-uniformity criterion and say so, or select on other grounds and show the ring-variance profile alongside — and the figure should adopt one of them explicitly. Whether the error envelopes converge in the inner \(\mu \lesssim 25\,\mathrm{mag\,arcsec^{-2}}\) region is governed by the same unverified condition, so it too is something the panel would show rather than something we can state in advance. How they compare in the LSB outskirts (\(\mu \gtrsim 26.5\,\mathrm{mag\,arcsec^{-2}}\)) — by how much, and in which direction — is the question the panel exists to answer; §1.4.2.1 explains why it cannot be predicted in advance. Data source: sga_isoster/data/demo/ (external companion repository); the specific galaxy has not yet been selected, so no envelope ratio is quoted here — the figure and its numbers are pending.]

The comparison this figure is meant to draw is between two error models, not between a right answer and a wrong one. In the LSB outskirts — the regime where the photometric science cases are most demanding: disk-truncation edges, intracluster light, stellar-halo profiles — the two estimators are answering different questions, and the figure's job is to show how far apart their answers fall on real survey data and in which direction. As §1.4.2.1 sets out, that direction is not determined a priori: the scatter estimator is inflated where the model leaves real azimuthal structure in the residual and can fall either side of the truth on any single ring. Whichever way the envelopes separate, the argument for WLS is that its envelope is traceable to a stated noise model that can be checked independently.

The inner region is the intended control, and it is a control only if a condition holds that we have not yet checked. The two solves coincide when the weights are near-constant around a ring — a variance-uniformity condition, not a signal-to-noise one. Whether the LegacySurvey inverse-variance map satisfies it for the galaxy eventually chosen is exactly the thing the figure should report, either by stating the ring-uniformity criterion the object was selected on or by showing the ring-variance profile alongside. If it does not hold, the inner envelopes will separate too, and that would be a finding rather than a failure of the figure.

The reproducibility recipe is:

import numpy as np
from astropy.io import fits
from isoster import fit_image
from isoster.config import IsosterConfig

image = fits.getdata("galaxy-r.fits.fz")
invvar = fits.getdata("galaxy-invvar-r.fits.fz")
variance_map = np.where(invvar > 0, 1.0 / invvar, np.nan)

config = IsosterConfig(sma0=10.0, maxsma=200.0,
                       full_photometry=True)

# OLS baseline (no variance map)
results_ols = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config)

# WLS fit (same config, variance map supplied)
results_wls = fit_image(image, mask=mask, config=config,
                        variance_map=variance_map)

The two results dictionaries are two independent fits, and how far they differ outside the *_err fields depends on the variance map. Where the weights are nearly constant along each ellipse — the uniform-variance condition of §1.4.2.4, not a high-\(S/N\) condition — the fitted geometry, the harmonic coefficients and the curve-of-growth fields agree to within LAPACK floating-point determinism. Where the map varies on the scale of a ring, the weights change the solve itself and the fitted values move too. The plotting recipe accordingly reads both dictionaries and draws each fit's own \(\mu(a)\) curve with its own envelope. Collapsing them onto one shared central curve would silently assert the uniform-variance case rather than displaying it.

A final practical point. The structural cost of WLS is small: the weighted solve is the same size as the unweighted one, the weights enter as a single elementwise row scaling, and the wider design matrix that makes the ISOFIT path of §1.4.1 expensive has no counterpart here. The one genuine addition is sampling the variance map alongside the image on every ring, which is a second map_coordinates call per sampling pass. We have not isolated the resulting overhead in a controlled benchmark, so we quote no number for it; the expectation from the operation count is that it is small relative to a fit's total cost, and confirming that belongs with the other timing measurements in the benchmark chapters. For survey pipelines processing thousands of galaxies with already-computed inverse-variance maps, turning on WLS is the obvious default.

docs.title: §1.4.3 Low-surface-brightness outskirt strategy
docs.text:
The fitting of galaxy isophotes in the low-surface-brightness (LSB) regime — at radii where the galaxy intensity has dropped to within a factor of a few of the sky noise — is a different problem from the fitting of inner isophotes, even though the algorithm is nominally unchanged. Three things go wrong simultaneously. The radial intensity gradient \(dI/da\) shrinks toward the photon-noise floor, so the geometry-update step (which divides each harmonic amplitude by \(dI/da\)) becomes unstable: small numerator noise produces large denominator-amplified geometry corrections. The harmonic-fit residual RMS drops below the sky noise per sample, so the convergence criterion \(|a_\max| < c \cdot S(a) \cdot \sigma_\mathrm{eff}\) (with the SMA-dependent scale factor \(S(a)\) of §1.1) would let the solver chase noise-induced asymmetries indefinitely if not for the \(\sigma_\mathrm{bg}/\sqrt{N}\) floor of §1.1. And contaminants — faint companions, scattered light, diffuse intracluster light, a bright source's extended PSF wings — that were negligible in the inner high-\(S/N\) region now contribute fractional intensity perturbations of order unity to the isophote, biasing the geometry-update direction.

The textbook solution is to fix the geometry — center, ellipticity, position angle — at some user-chosen SMA and let the outer isophotes be evaluated as forced photometry on that fixed geometry. This works but is harsh in two ways. The transition SMA is set by hand, which is a per-galaxy parameter that scales poorly to survey samples; and the transition is binary, with no graceful degradation between the fully-free inner fit and the fully-fixed outer extraction. ISOSTER introduces two complementary features that together replace the hand-tuned transition with an adaptive one. Outer-region center regularization is a soft mechanism: a logistic Tikhonov ramp that damps geometry updates in the outer SMA range toward an inner reference centroid, with strength that grows continuously from negligible (at \(a = a_0\)) to substantial (at \(a \gg a_0\)). It runs in every outward iteration. The automatic LSB geometry lock is a hard mechanism: a one-way state-machine triggered by per-isophote gradient diagnostics that, once committed, freezes the geometry to the last clean isophote and runs the remaining outward growth as forced extraction with a robust integrator. The two features are independent — either can be used alone — but they are designed to compose: the soft regularization runs in the pre-lock phase and is silently absorbed into the locked clone when the hard lock fires.

This section explains both features and their composition. We focus on the algorithmic and implementation details; the empirical performance of the strategy across many galaxies belongs to the benchmark chapters.

docs.title: Motivation and design
docs.text:
The classical algorithm has no information about where the real galaxy center is, beyond what the harmonic fit at each isophote tells it. In the inner high-\(S/N\) region this is sufficient: every isophote converges to nearly the same \((x_0, y_0)\), and the geometry is well-constrained. In the outer LSB region the same harmonic fit on a much noisier signal produces a much larger parameter covariance, and the per-isophote center estimate begins to wander. The wandering is not random — contaminants pull the center systematically toward themselves; PSF wings of a nearby bright source bias the centroid along a fixed direction; an incompletely-masked companion shifts the fitted center toward the companion's position. The outward geometry trajectory can drift by several pixels over the LSB tail and produce isophotes that no longer share a center with the inner ones.

The soft regularization assumes that the inner isophotes, where the center is well-determined, carry the correct center information, and that the outer fit should be encouraged to remain consistent with it. The encouragement is implemented as a Tikhonov-style penalty on the geometry-update step: each step in a geometry coordinate is multiplied by a shrinkage factor that grows with SMA and with the local uncertainty of that coordinate, measured through the harmonic-to-geometry Jacobian (which scales as \(1 / (dI/da)\)). Where the radial gradient is steep and the data constrain the geometry well (the inner high-\(S/N\) region), the shrinkage is negligible; where the gradient shallows toward the photon-noise floor (the LSB regime), the shrinkage engages strongly. The mechanism has no effect on the inner isophotes and its largest effect exactly where the user is most concerned — the noise-dominated LSB tail, where unconstrained geometry corrections are denominator-amplified noise.

docs.title: The logistic ramp and the inner reference
docs.text:
Two ingredients enter the soft regularization. The first is a scalar strength \(\lambda(a)\) that grows continuously with SMA:

\[ \lambda(a) = \frac{\lambda_0}{1 + \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{a - a_\mathrm{onset}}{\Delta a_\mathrm{ramp}}\right)}, \]

where \(\lambda_0\) is the asymptotic strength (config field outer_reg_strength, default \(2.0\), suggested LSB range 1 to 3), \(a_\mathrm{onset}\) is the SMA at which the ramp reaches half its asymptotic value (config outer_reg_sma_onset), and \(\Delta a_\mathrm{ramp}\) controls the width of the transition (config outer_reg_sma_width). The logistic shape was chosen over a step function and a linear ramp for two reasons: it is smooth (no derivative discontinuities at the transition), and it has explicit "on" and "off" tails (the ramp asymptotes to \(0\) for \(a \ll a_\mathrm{onset}\) and to \(\lambda_0\) for \(a \gg a_\mathrm{onset}\)), which makes the strength interpretable at the endpoints. The width \(\Delta a_\mathrm{ramp}\) defaults to None, in which case it is auto-computed as \(0.4 \cdot a_\mathrm{onset}\); this keeps the ramp gentle on a typical SMA grid.

The second ingredient is the inner reference geometry. ISOSTER constructs this once, between the inward loop and the outward loop. Let \(\mathcal{I}_\mathrm{inner}\) be the set of inward isophotes plus the anchor isophote at \(a_0\) that satisfy two conditions: stop code \(\in \{0, 1, 2\}\) (acceptable for propagation) and \(a \le a_0 \cdot f_\mathrm{ref}\) where \(f_\mathrm{ref}\) is the config field outer_reg_ref_sma_factor (default \(2.0\)). The reference is the flux-weighted mean of their geometries:

\[ g_\mathrm{ref} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_\mathrm{inner}} w_i \, g_i} {\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_\mathrm{inner}} w_i}, \qquad w_i = I_{0, i}, \]

where \(g\) stands separately for each of the center and ellipticity coordinates \((x_0, y_0, \varepsilon)\) and \(I_{0,i}\) is the inner-isophote intensity. The flux weighting concentrates the reference on the high-\(S/N\) isophotes nearest the galaxy center, where the geometry is best determined. The position angle is an axis-like quantity defined mod \(\pi\), so an arithmetic mean would map PAs near \(0\) and near \(\pi\) to the spurious value \(\pi/2\); ISOSTER instead averages PA as a flux-weighted circular mean on the doubled angle \(2\,\mathrm{PA}\), falling back to the anchor PA when the resultant length is too small for the mean to be well-defined (highly scattered inner PAs).

If no inward isophotes qualify — typically because the inward loop never converged or because no inner isophotes met the stop-code cut — the reference silently falls back to the anchor isophote geometry at \(a_0\) alone.

docs.title: Per-axis weights and the per-coordinate shrinkage factor
docs.text:
Once \(\lambda(a)\) and \(g_\mathrm{ref}\) are in hand, the regularization acts on each geometry coordinate independently. Let \(J_g\) be the harmonic-to-geometry Jacobian coefficient that converts the dominant harmonic amplitude into the update of coordinate \(g\) — for example \(J = (1 - \varepsilon)/(dI/da)\) for the minor-axis center term and \(J = 2(1-\varepsilon)/(a \cdot dI/da)\) for the ellipticity term; every \(J_g\) scales as \(1/(dI/da)\). The shrinkage factor is

\[ \alpha(g, a) = \frac{\lambda(a) \, w_g \, J_g^2}{1 + \lambda(a) \, w_g \, J_g^2}, \]

with \(w_g\) the per-axis weight from outer_reg_weights (three keys — "center", covering both center axes, "eps", and "pa" — default \(\{1, 1, 1\}\); a weight of zero disables the regularization on that axis entirely). Note what drives \(\alpha\): not the size of the proposed step, which does not enter the formula at all, but the shallowness of the local radial gradient. On a steep inner profile \(|J_g|\) is small and \(\alpha \to 0\); in the LSB regime \(dI/da\) approaches the noise floor, \(|J_g|\) grows, and \(\alpha \to 1\). The damping therefore engages exactly in the regime it was built for. The shrunk update under outer_reg_mode = 'damping' (default) is

\[ \Delta g_\mathrm{damped} = (1 - \alpha) \, \Delta g, \]

which leaves the direction of the update unchanged but reduces its magnitude. The closed form has the convenient property that \(\alpha \in [0, 1)\) identically, so the damped update never overshoots the original step direction.

The per-axis weights are a binary switch, not a dial — and this is worth stating because the formula invites the opposite reading. \(\alpha\) is a saturating function of \(\lambda w_g J_g^2\), and in the LSB regime that product is enormous. On a real BCG test case (PGC006669), the per-axis Jacobian \(J = (1 - \varepsilon)/(dI/da)\) reaches \(\sim\!700\) in the outer LSB, because the denominator is heading toward zero; \(J^2 \approx 5 \times 10^5\), so \(\lambda w_g J_g^2 \gg 1\) for any weight above roughly \(10^{-4}\). A strength × weights sweep confirmed the consequence directly: reducing the eps and pa weights from \(1.0\) to \(0.25\) produced essentially identical outer-region pinning, with \(\alpha\) saturating above \(99.99\%\) across the whole user-intuition range. Intermediate values such as \(\{1, 0.5, 0.5\}\) are not a middle ground; they behave like \(\{1, 1, 1\}\). An honest "partial damping" regime would require \(w \sim 10^{-4}\), far below any value a user would think to type. The practical rule is therefore that each axis is either pinned (\(w_g > 0\)) or free (\(w_g = 0\)), and the choice should be made on whether that axis's outer geometry is expected to evolve.

This is also why the single-band default \(\{1, 1, 1\}\) and the multi-band default \(\{1, 0, 0\}\) differ. Pinning ellipticity and position angle is right for a confirmed-static outer envelope — a cD galaxy, an isolated massive elliptical — and wrong for anything whose outer disc geometry might genuinely change with radius: barred and spiral systems, and the BCG-to-ICL transition. The multi-band path carries the more conservative default because the joint solver already supplies cross-band stability on ellipticity and position angle through the shared harmonic constraint, making that damping largely redundant there.

Under outer_reg_mode = 'solver', the regularization additionally pulls the geometry toward the reference. The effective update becomes

\[ \Delta g_\mathrm{solver} = (1 - \alpha) \, \Delta g + \alpha \, (g_\mathrm{ref} - g), \]

i.e. a convex combination of the proposed step and a step toward the inner reference, weighted by the same shrinkage factor. The 'solver' mode is more aggressive in the sense that it actively moves the geometry back toward the inner reference even when the proposed update happens to be zero; the 'damping' mode is purely a shrinkage and leaves the equilibrium where the iteration would otherwise have placed it. For most science cases the 'damping' mode suffices; the 'solver' mode is reserved for the most demanding contamination scenarios where the LSB tail is being actively pulled away from the inner geometry.

docs.title: Selector-level penalty
docs.text:
A complementary mechanism operates one level higher. ISOSTER's fit loop tracks not only the per-iteration converged geometry but also a best-iteration candidate via the effective amplitude \(a_\mathrm{eff} = |a_\max| + \mathcal{R}(g)\) (§1.1). The regularization contributes to \(\mathcal{R}\) a penalty term

\[ \mathcal{R}_\mathrm{outer}(g, a) = \lambda(a) \sum_{g\text{-axes}} w_g \, (g - g_\mathrm{ref})^2, \]

so that, when multiple iterations have produced candidate geometries with similar \(|a_\max|\), the iteration whose geometry is closest to the inner reference is preferred. This is a soft-tie-breaking effect; the iteration that minimizes the bare harmonic amplitude usually also minimizes the effective amplitude, because the harmonic-amplitude term dominates in the high-\(S/N\) regime. In the LSB regime the two terms become comparable, and the regularization penalty bounds the cumulative drift through the best-iteration selector even when the per-iteration shrinkage factor would by itself permit larger excursions.

docs.title: §1.4.3.2 Hard automatic LSB geometry lock
docs.text: The soft regularization is a gentle mechanism that scales with SMA and step size; it does not enforce a hard upper bound on how far the geometry can drift. For deep enough LSB tails the soft regularization is insufficient on its own, and the algorithm needs a hard mechanism that freezes the geometry once the per-isophote diagnostics indicate that the fit has crossed into a regime where free fitting is no longer scientifically meaningful.

docs.title: Trigger detector and debouncing
docs.text:
The detector runs after each outward isophote has converged (or failed to converge) and inspects three per-isophote quantities: the radial gradient \(\widehat{dI/da}\), the gradient uncertainty \(\sigma_{dI/da}\), and the stop code. The relative gradient error

\[ \rho = \frac{\sigma_{dI/da}}{\left|\widehat{dI/da}\right|} \]

is the primary trigger. The detector flags the isophote as triggered when \(\rho\) exceeds a user-configurable threshold \(\rho_\mathrm{trig}\) (config field lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr, default \(0.30\)), when the gradient is non-negative (\(\widehat{dI/da} \ge 0\) — an unphysical flat or rising profile at this point in the fit), or when the isophote ended with stop code \(-1\) (a gradient-related failure). The threshold \(\rho_\mathrm{trig} = 0.30\) is deliberately tighter than the per-isophote gradient acceptability threshold \(\rho_\mathrm{accept} = 0.50\) (config maxgerr) that produces stop code \(-1\) on its own. This is the key design choice: the lock detector fires before the gradient checks would have terminated the outward growth, so the lock commits while there are still clean isophotes upstream to anchor to.

Single isolated triggers are not sufficient to commit the lock. A faint companion intersected by a single isophote, an interpolation artefact along one ellipse, or a transient noise spike can produce a one-off elevated \(\rho\) without indicating that the LSB transition has actually been reached. The detector therefore debounces the trigger: \(N_\mathrm{deb}\) consecutive outward isophotes (config field lsb_auto_lock_debounce, default \(2\)) must all be triggered for the lock to commit. A clean isophote appearing in the streak resets the counter to zero. The debounce default of \(2\) means that two consecutive bad isophotes are required, which empirically distinguishes a genuine LSB transition (where the gradient diagnostics break down monotonically as \(a\) grows) from isolated isophote failures.

docs.title: Anchor selection and the locked clone
docs.text:
When the debounce streak reaches \(N_\mathrm{deb}\), the lock commits. The locked-anchor isophote is not the most recent triggered isophote (whose geometry may already have drifted); it is the last clean isophote before the streak began. Concretely, if the streak occupies indices \(k, k+1, \ldots, k + N_\mathrm{deb} - 1\) in the outward growth list, the anchor is isophote \(k - 1\). Its geometry \((x_0^\star, y_0^\star, \varepsilon^\star, \mathrm{PA}^\star)\) is the geometry that will be enforced on every subsequent outward isophote.

The lock is implemented as a cloned configuration. ISOSTER calls

locked_config = config.model_copy(update=dict(
    fix_center=True, fix_pa=True, fix_eps=True,
    integrator=config.lsb_auto_lock_integrator,
))

and the subsequent outward isophotes are fit with the locked clone. Three concrete effects follow. First, the geometry-update machinery (§1.1) sees fix_center=True, fix_pa=True, fix_eps=True and zeros all four geometry coordinates' updates by zeroing the corresponding harmonic amplitudes before the dominant-amplitude selector runs. The fitted geometry is held at the anchor exactly; no iterative drift is possible. Second, the integrator switches from the default 'mean' to whatever the user-configured lsb_auto_lock_integrator is — by default 'median', which is more robust to the asymmetric residual distributions typical of LSB-regime contamination. Third, the lock is one-way: once committed, the locked clone is used for the remainder of outward growth and the original config is never restored within the same fit_image call. The inward loop and the central pixel are unaffected because both have already completed before the outward loop begins.

The locked isophotes carry two additional output fields. The boolean lsb_locked is set on every locked isophote so the caller can filter the output by lock state. The boolean lsb_auto_lock_anchor is set on the committing trigger isophote — the last isophote of the debounce streak, which was itself still fit free — serving as a marker in QA overlays for the exact SMA at which the lock committed. (The geometry that is enforced from the next isophote onward is that of the clean anchor isophote just before the streak, not that of the marked trigger isophote.) The top-level results dict gains four companion fields: lsb_auto_lock (echo that the feature was on), lsb_auto_lock_sma (the SMA at which the lock committed, or None if the detector never triggered), lsb_auto_lock_anchor_sma (the SMA of the true geometry anchor — the last clean isophote before the streak, whose geometry the lock enforces — or None), and lsb_auto_lock_count (the number of outward isophotes fit under the locked clone).

docs.title: Implementation prerequisites and conflict checks
docs.text:
The detector reads grad, grad_error, and grad_r_error from each outward isophote's output dictionary. These fields are only present when debug=True is set in the config. ISOSTER's config validator does not require the caller to set debug=True explicitly; instead, when lsb_auto_lock=True is set with debug=False, ISOSTER emits a UserWarning and internally clones the config with debug=True for the duration of the fit. The caller's original config remains unchanged. This trade is deliberate: forcing the caller to enable a debug flag for a production feature would be confusing, and the storage overhead of the five extra fields per isophote (grad, grad_error, grad_r_error, plus the ndata / nflag sample counts) is negligible.

The Pydantic validator enforces three hard rejection rules at config-construction time. lsb_auto_lock=True cannot coexist with fix_center=True, fix_pa=True, or fix_eps=True; the combination is rejected with ValidationError because the auto-lock is itself a mechanism for fixing the geometry, and pairing it with manual fixed-geometry flags would be either redundant or self-contradictory depending on which fix is meant to take precedence. The auto-lock is also silently inactive when combined with template-based forced photometry (template=…); a UserWarning is emitted at the top of fit_image and the feature is bypassed entirely. The reason is that template-based forced extraction already enforces fixed geometry per SMA from the template, leaving nothing for the lock to do.

docs.title: §1.4.3.3 Composition of the two mechanisms
docs.text:
Both features are independent in the sense that either can be enabled without the other. They are also designed to compose: when both are on, the soft regularization runs from \(a_0\) outward and gradually damps the geometry trajectory; if the LSB tail is deep enough that the gradient diagnostics begin to break down, the hard lock then commits and freezes the geometry for the remainder.

The composition is mechanically clean. The locked-clone config that the auto-lock installs has fix_center=True, fix_pa=True, fix_eps=True, which zeroes the geometry-update directions before the soft regularization shrinkage would have a chance to multiply them. The shrinkage factor \(\alpha\) is multiplying a zero step, so the regularization is a silent no-op for the locked tail. There is no need to disable the regularization explicitly when the lock fires; the math takes care of it.

docs.title: One composition that does not work
docs.text:
The outer-region regularization and ISOFIT (§1.4.1) do not fully compose, and the limitation is worth stating rather than leaving to a runtime warning. The Tikhonov term is applied at the point where a five-parameter harmonic solve is converted into a geometry step; it was never wired into the wider ISOFIT joint solver. Setting use_outer_center_regularization=True together with simultaneous_harmonics=True therefore silently loses the solver-level shrinkage: only the selector-level penalty of the previous section still applies, so the best-iteration tie-break survives but the per-iteration step damping does not. ISOSTER emits a UserWarning naming exactly this at configuration time rather than proceeding quietly, but the combination is a genuine gap, not a design choice, and closing it is on the roadmap (§1.6).

This is the one exception to the composability claim made elsewhere in §1.4: with that single pair, enabling both features does not give the union of their effects.

The intended division of labor between the two mechanisms can be read off this composition. The soft regularization is a prophylactic measure that operates while the gradient diagnostics are still within tolerance: it bounds the cumulative drift in the pre-LSB regime, where the fit is technically still valid but where small contamination can pull the centroid off its inner-isophote consensus. The hard lock is a terminal measure that activates when the gradient diagnostics indicate the fit can no longer be trusted to follow the galaxy. The two failure modes the strategy is designed to address are therefore different in character: contamination-driven drift in the pre-lock regime, and noise-driven divergence in the post-lock regime. Each mechanism is targeted at one of them, and the composition produces a single ISOSTER fit that spans both regimes without a hand-tuned transition.

A practical observation. The auto-lock's debounce default of \(2\) and the trigger threshold of \(0.30\) are calibrated so that the lock typically commits a few isophotes before the unconstrained fit would have produced stop code \(-1\). The soft regularization therefore operates over a non-zero range of SMAs before the lock fires, and that range can be substantial — tens of SMAs on a deeply-fit galaxy. The soft regularization is not a vestigial warm-up step; it is doing real work in that range.

docs.title: §1.4.3.4 Caveats
docs.text:
The two features carry a small number of caveats that bear on when to enable them.

Both features are disabled by default. The user has to opt in explicitly. ISOSTER's default fit is the classical Jedrzejewski / photutils behaviour with no LSB-regime intervention. This is the right default for fits that do not push into LSB territory; the features should be enabled when the user is fitting deep imaging where they expect contamination or noise-driven drift.

The soft regularization is still being calibrated across surveys. The default parameter values (outer_reg_sma_onset, outer_reg_sma_width, outer_reg_strength) are heuristic recommendations; the values that work well on HSC edge cases may be sub-optimal on DECaLS, which has different seeing, sky brightness, and noise characteristics. The recommended-range values in docs/02-configuration-reference.md are starting points, not survey-blind defaults.

The hard lock detector reads gradient diagnostics, not the image directly. It is therefore agnostic to the image content beyond what the per-isophote fit reports. A galaxy with structurally unusual outskirts (truncated disks, tidal streams) may produce gradient diagnostics that look like LSB-regime divergence even when the image data are still informative. The lock will commit in that case, and the user will need to inspect the locked tail to decide whether the freeze was appropriate. The output fields lsb_auto_lock_sma and lsb_locked make this inspection straightforward.

The lock is one-way per fit. There is no "unlock and re-fit free" mode. If the lock commits early on a galaxy where the user believed the inner region warranted a longer free fit, the recommended workflow is to raise the trigger threshold lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr (or the debounce count lsb_auto_lock_debounce) and re-run, rather than to post-process the locked isophotes back into free isophotes. The locked isophotes are output with their fixed-geometry origin clearly marked; they should be interpreted as forced photometry, not as free-fit results.

Forced photometry through template=… disables both features silently. This is a property of the template-based forced extraction path, which is structurally distinct from the regular iterative driver. A UserWarning is emitted at the top of fit_image to make the bypass visible. Users who need the LSB strategy on a multi-band workflow should prefer the joint multi-band free fit of §1.4.5, which does pass the LSB features through to each band's converged geometry.

docs.title: §1.4.3.5 Proposed demonstration: deep mock with bright contaminant
docs.text:
To make the composition of the two features visible in isolation we use a synthetic galaxy generated through the MockGal renderer.
