(Template-forced mode does not consult stop codes at all: extraction proceeds at every template SMA.) A consumer of the output dictionary can filter isophotes by stop code with a single rule:

good   = [iso for iso in results["isophotes"] if iso["stop_code"] == 0]
usable = [iso for iso in results["isophotes"] if iso["stop_code"] in {0, 1, 2}]
failed = [iso for iso in results["isophotes"] if iso["stop_code"] < 0]

The same stop-code domain applies to the multi-band joint fit (§1.4.5), where each isophote carries one shared stop code derived from the joint-fit convergence rather than per-band stop codes; the multi-band stop code reports whether the shared geometry converged, not whether any one band's intensity extraction succeeded.

A property worth flagging: the stop-code domain is closed under the §1.4 features. None of the new features in this section adds new stop codes, and none of them changes the trigger for an existing stop code. The LSB auto-lock of §1.4.3 commits to a locked clone after detecting a gradient-failure trend, but the locked-clone isophotes themselves still report stop codes from the same five-value domain (typically code \(0\) since the geometry is fixed and the fit reduces to a forced extraction). The variance- aware WLS path of §1.4.2 changes neither the code-\(0\) convergence criterion nor the value of \(\sigma_\mathrm{eff}\) that enters it: in single-band, \(\sigma_\mathrm{eff}\) is the unweighted standard deviation of the fit residuals \(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) on both the OLS and the WLS path. The closure is intentional: a consumer of the results dictionary can rely on the stop-code domain being a stable contract across the configuration surface.

One deliberate asymmetry belongs here rather than buried in §1.4.5. The multi-band joint fit does not inherit the unweighted convergence scatter. Its stopping comparison is variance-weighted, using the same weights the joint solve applied to each band's rows. The reason is that a multi-band residual pools bands whose flux units are arbitrary and unrelated: comparing a weighted amplitude against an unweighted pooled scatter makes the stopping decision move when a band is rescaled, which is not a property a convergence criterion may have. Single-band has no such exposure, since there is only one set of units, so it keeps the classical unweighted form. The stop-code domain is identical in both; only the quantity compared against the threshold differs.

docs.title: §1.4.6.2 QA plotting and cross-tool comparison
docs.text:
ISOSTER ships with a QA plotting subsystem in isoster/plotting.py that takes one or more results dictionaries and produces a standardized multi-panel figure summarizing the fit. Two public entry points are exposed.

The first, plot_qa_summary, takes a single results dictionary and the corresponding image and renders a two-column figure. The left column carries the image panels — the original image with selected isophote overlays, the reconstructed 2-D model with its iso-brightness contours, and the residual image built from that same model. The right column carries a stack of radial-profile panels sharing one \(x\) axis: the surface-brightness profile with uncertainties, the centroid drift, the axis ratio, the position angle, and — when the corresponding blocks are present — the higher-order harmonics in their Bender-normalized form and the curve of growth. The panel count is therefore not fixed; the conditional panels appear only when the fit produced the data they display. Radial panels use \(a^{1/4}\) as the abscissa, which compresses the outskirts while retaining inner-region resolution, and stop-code markers colour the profile points so that a degraded isophote is visible in the figure rather than only in the table. This is the standard single-galaxy inspection figure, and it is deliberately built from the persisted fit products — the same profile table and residual model that feed the benchmark metrics — rather than recomputed for plotting, so that what a reader inspects is what was scored.

The second, plot_comparison_qa_figure, takes two or three results dictionaries — typically one each from ISOSTER, photutils.isophote, and AutoProf — and produces the same six-panel layout with each panel showing all methods overlaid in a color-consistent style. The function auto-detects the layout mode (solo, 1-vs-1, or three-way) from the number of supplied dictionaries, applies cross-method position-angle anchoring (to ensure the three methods' PA estimates are reported on a common branch of the \([0, \pi)\) ambiguity), and applies the per-method visual style from a small METHOD_STYLES table at the top of plotting.py so the visual conventions are consistent across the figure. This is the figure that drives the visual comparison studies in the cross-tool benchmark chapters.

A subtlety worth flagging is the harmonic-coefficient convention dispatch. Different tools report different higher-harmonic quantities: ISOSTER in φ-mode reports image-azimuth-space coefficients; ISOSTER in ψ-mode reports eccentric-anomaly-space coefficients; photutils.isophote samples and fits its harmonics in the image polar angle φ — the same basis as ISOSTER's default φ-mode — with coefficients normalized by \(a \cdot |dI/da|\); for AutoProf the basis and normalization are unverified — the benchmark adapter passes its coefficients through unconverted, which presumes they already match, and that presumption has never been tested against a planted deviation. The QA plotting code therefore applies a per-tool dispatch on the harmonic-contour overlay step: ISOSTER φ-mode contours are drawn in image-azimuth space, ISOSTER ψ-mode contours are drawn in eccentric-anomaly space, photutils.isophote contours are currently routed through the eccentric-anomaly helper as a first-order approximation (the polar-angle and eccentric-anomaly bases coincide to first order in the ellipticity), and AutoProf contours fall back to pure ellipses without higher-order shape correction until its coefficient scale is matched. The dispatch is documented in METHOD_STYLES and is visible to the figure consumer through a legend annotation.

Every plotted and scored harmonic is normalized, but the exact expression differs between the storage and plot-time paths and it is worth being precise. compute_deviations stores \(a_n = A_n^\mathrm{raw} / (a\,\lvert dI/da\rvert)\), using the absolute gradient; the plot-time helper _normalize_harmonic_for_plot applies the signed Bender form \(-A_n^\mathrm{raw} / (a\,dI/da)\). The two coincide wherever the gradient is negative, which is the normal outward-declining case, and differ in sign on the rare positive-gradient row. Either way the motivation is the convention of §1.1: raw \(A_n^\mathrm{raw}\) values are not directly interpretable because their magnitudes scale with the local intensity profile.

Where the normalization is applied depends on the storage path, and this is worth stating precisely because normalizing twice is an easy and near-invisible error:

Path Stored Normalized Single-band ISOSTER already normalized in compute_deviations, at fit time Multi-band, independent higher harmonics already normalized at fit time, per band Multi-band, shared raw and band-distinct: one shared dimensionless shape reconstructed into each band's own units via \(-a\,\mathrm{grad}_b\) at plot time, per band, using that band's own gradient — they all normalize back to the one shape Multi-band, simultaneous_* raw and identical across bands, i.e. a shared raw residual rather than a shared shape at plot time, per band; because the raw value is the same in every band, the normalized curves separate once the gradients differ. This is one of the two reasons these modes stay experimental Benchmark audit (scenario_summary.py) consumes the stored columns already normalized; no further division

So the correct statement is normalize exactly once, at whichever point the path in question has not already done it — not "uniformly at plot time", which an earlier version of this section claimed and which would double-normalize three of the four rows above. The multi-band shared modes are the reason the plot-time path exists at all: they carry one raw coefficient for every band, and normalizing per band with each band's own gradient is what turns it back into band-distinct curves.

Cross-tool comparability follows only when the tools agree on both the basis and the normalization. ISOSTER and photutils do. For AutoProf the answer is not currently established. The benchmark adapter copies its harmonic columns through unconverted, which assumes they already share the convention; that assumption has never been tested. Nothing here is a measurement in either direction, so the honest status is ignorance rather than a known mismatch. Settling it requires running AutoProf against a planted deviation and comparing with the ISOSTER and photutils values on the same fixture. Until that is done AutoProf's harmonic curves are excluded from published cross-tool comparisons and are labelled rather than silently overlaid as if commensurable.

A build_method_profile helper standardizes the input formats: some tools deliver isophote lists, others deliver array dicts, and the comparison figure needs a common profile format. The helper absorbs the format conversion and lets the figure-construction code operate on a single canonical representation.

docs.title: §1.4.6.3 Reproducible serialization
docs.text:
ISOSTER provides three serialization paths for results dictionaries. The two on-disk paths share the property that the saved file records the complete resolved configuration — no out-of-band configuration is needed to know what settings produced the fit. The property is enforced through a common helper layer in isoster/_shared.py that serializes the resolved IsosterConfig into a JSON-encoded \((\mathtt{PARAM}, \mathtt{VALUE})\) table.

The scope of that claim is narrower than "the fit can be re-executed from the file", and the difference matters for anyone relying on it. The file carries the configuration and the results; it does not carry the experiment. The input image, the mask, the variance map, the ISOSTER version, and the numerical environment (the BLAS and LAPACK build, whether the Numba kernels were available) are all outside it. Reproducing a fit means pairing the saved configuration with those inputs, supplied separately; what the file removes is the possibility of getting the settings wrong, including by silent drift in a default between releases.

The FITS path, isophote_results_to_fits, writes a four-HDU file: a PrimaryHDU (empty), a BinTableHDU named ISOPHOTES with one row per isophote, a BinTableHDU named CONFIG with the two-column \((\mathtt{PARAM}, \mathtt{VALUE})\) layout carrying the full configuration, and a BinTableHDU named META in the same two-column layout carrying the top-level result keys that are neither per-isophote quantities nor configuration fields — LSB lock state, first-isophote retry outcomes, outer-region reference geometry. The CONFIG HDU is the key to the round-trip property: every field of the IsosterConfig object that produced the fit is recorded, with no reliance on IsosterConfig's default values. A future ISOSTER release that adjusts a default value cannot silently change the meaning of an existing FITS file, because the file carries the explicit value that was in effect at write time. META closes the remaining gap: without it, the information describing what the driver decided during the fit would be lost on the round trip even though the configuration survived.

The ASDF path, isophote_results_to_asdf, performs the same serialization in ASDF's tree format, which preserves native Python types (in particular, nested dicts and numpy arrays) more transparently than FITS. For the multi-band schema (§1.4.5), the per-band column proliferation reads more naturally in ASDF's tree than as flat FITS columns, and the ASDF writer is the recommended multi-band path.

The third path, isophote_results_to_astropy_tables, returns the isophote list as an astropy.table.Table without writing to disk. This is the API path for downstream analysis code that wants the isophote data without round-tripping through a file. The table carries the same column set as the FITS ISOPHOTES HDU; the config field is dropped, since an in-memory results dictionary already carries the resolved IsosterConfig object.

All three readers (isophote_results_from_fits, isophote_results_from_asdf, and the analogous multi-band variants) tolerate legacy files where the CONFIG block is absent or was written as FITS header keywords (earlier ISOSTER releases): the isophote table is read normally and config comes back as None — no attempt is made to reconstruct a configuration from header keywords. Within a recognized CONFIG block, the forward-compatibility convention is that fields known to the current release are honored and unknown fields (written by a newer release) are dropped, so an older ISOSTER install can still read a newer file's configuration for the fields it understands.

The round-trip property has a concrete benefit for the benchmark chapters of this paper. The benchmark campaigns process thousands of galaxies, store the per-galaxy fit outputs as FITS or ASDF files, and downstream analyses (composite scoring, residual model construction, cross-tool comparison) re-read those files. The guarantee that each file records the settings that produced it removes a specific class of reproducibility failures — fits being compared under subtly different default values, defaults changing between ISOSTER releases without the user noticing — that would otherwise need to be controlled externally. The remaining ingredients (the images themselves, the software version, the numerical environment) are controlled by the campaign framework of §1.4.6.4 rather than by the serialization layer.

docs.title: §1.4.6.4 The exhausted-benchmark framework
docs.text:
The benchmark chapters of this paper rest on a YAML-driven campaign framework documented in docs/09-exhausted-benchmark.md and implemented in benchmarks/exhausted/. We summarize it here because several features in §1.4 are evaluated against it.

The framework operates on the principle that benchmark configurations should be enumerable — each combination of tool, configuration, and input mock is given a YAML "arm" specification, the arms are executed independently and produce per-arm outputs in a deterministic directory layout, and the analysis-side scoring code reads from those outputs to compute per-arm and cross-tool composite scores. The deterministic layout plus the round-trip serialization property of §1.4.6.3 together mean that a benchmark arm is fully specified by its YAML and its input mock: no setting is carried implicitly. Reproducing the numbers additionally requires the ISOSTER version and the numerical environment, which the campaign framework pins separately through the locked dependency set rather than through the arm specification.

Two scoring modes are supported. The within-tool composite score includes method-specific health terms (e.g., a per-tool stop-code penalty for ISOSTER, a per-tool convergence-iteration penalty for AutoProf) and is used for the per-tool ablation studies (which ISOSTER configuration is best on this sample). The cross-tool score includes only tool-neutral residual and runtime terms, and is used for the head-to-head comparisons of ISOSTER, photutils, and AutoProf (which tool best fits the sample under each tool's recommended configuration). The two modes use the same per-galaxy data products but different scoring functions; the separation makes the cross-tool comparisons fair by excluding terms that favor any one tool's diagnostic ontology.

Three campaign datasets are targeted by the framework, at differing stages of completion; the benchmark chapters report what each has actually produced, and this subsection should not be read as a claim that all three have been processed end to end. They are the Huang2013 mocks of nearby elliptical galaxies (multi-Sersic models, varying resolution and noise), the S4G mocks of nearby galaxies (300 late-type-focused systems, multi-component models), and the SGA-2020 real galaxies on LegacySurvey imaging (~2,000 galaxies, real-data robustness). The campaigns are described in detail in the benchmark chapters of this paper and are not re-described here; the relevance for the present subsection is that all three campaigns use the same exhausted-benchmark framework, the same serialization formats, and the same QA plotting subsystem. A reader who wants to inspect the per-galaxy outputs of any campaign can re-read the saved fits and apply plot_qa_summary or plot_comparison_qa_figure to reproduce any QA figure in the paper. The infrastructure for inspection and the infrastructure for benchmarking are the same infrastructure.

docs.title: §1.4.6.5 Closing remarks on §1.4
docs.text:
This concludes the survey of new features in §1.4. The six subsections cover what ISOSTER does differently from the classical algorithm — eccentric-anomaly sampling and ISOFIT-style joint harmonics (§1.4.1), variance-aware WLS fitting (§1.4.2), the low-surface-brightness outskirt strategy (§1.4.3), operations-grade batch robustness primitives (§1.4.4), the multi-band joint free fit (§1.4.5), and the diagnostics and reproducibility infrastructure (§1.4.6). The §1.4 algorithmic features are opt-in and inert under their disabled defaults. That is a narrower statement than "ISOSTER reduces to the classical algorithm when the flags are off", which would be false: the gradient-SNR damping and step clipping of §1.4.4 are always active, the first-isophote retry defaults to three attempts, and the sampling, convergence rule and stop-code semantics differ from the classical implementations regardless of configuration (§1.5). The diagnostics of this subsection are not an algorithmic feature at all and have no disabled state. They compose with one another with a single documented exception: the outer-region Tikhonov regularization of §1.4.3 is not wired into the wider ISOFIT solver of §1.4.1, so enabling both leaves only the selector-level half of the regularization active. ISOSTER warns at configuration time when that pair is requested.

The features were developed in the order they are presented: §1.4.1 and §1.4.2 came first because they are direct generalizations of well-established algorithmic ideas (Ciambur 2015; classical statistical estimation theory); §1.4.3 came next to address the LSB-regime failure modes that motivated the development of ISOSTER for HSC-SSP science; §1.4.4 followed when the survey-scale deployment of ISOSTER exposed the failure modes the robustness primitives address; §1.4.5 was developed once the single-band feature set had stabilized; §1.4.6 was iterated throughout to support the benchmark and QA needs of the paper this subsection is part of. The historical order is not the recommended-reading order for users, but it is informative for understanding which features are mature (§1.4.1, §1.4.2) and which are still being refined on new data (§1.4.3's parameter defaults; §1.4.5's loose-validity calibration).

§1.5 turns to the comparison of ISOSTER, on a feature-by-feature basis, against photutils.isophote, AutoProf, and IRAF Isofit. The comparison rests on the features described in §1.4 and on the algorithmic-speed argument of §1.3; the quantitative performance comparisons come from the benchmark chapters that follow this technical section.

docs.title: §1.5 Comparison to existing tools
docs.text:
This subsection situates ISOSTER among the three most directly relevant non-parametric elliptical-isophote tools: IRAF Ellipse / Isofit / Cmodel (the Jedrzejewski 1987 algorithm and its Ciambur 2015 reformulation), photutils.isophote (the direct Python re-implementation), and AutoProf (Stone, Arora, Courteau & Cuillandre 2021, the modern Python pipeline most similar in scope to ISOSTER). The comparison is conceptual: we describe each tool's design philosophy, the features it provides, and the gaps relative to ISOSTER, without quoting numerical benchmark results. Quantitative head-to-head comparisons on the Huang2013, S4G, and SGA-2020 campaigns are presented in the benchmark chapters of this paper.

The aim is honest characterization, not advocacy. ISOSTER builds on ideas from all three predecessors; on several axes the comparison is one of generalization rather than improvement (ISOSTER offers more options at the same algorithmic core); on others it is one of new capability (variance-aware fitting, joint multi-band free fitting); on a few it is one of deferred implementation (deconvolution-aware modes, the analysis sub-systems AutoProf has accumulated over its longer deployment history). Each axis is discussed below.

docs.title: §1.5.1 vs IRAF Ellipse / Isofit / Cmodel (Jedrzejewski 1987;
docs.text:
Ciambur 2015)

The IRAF Ellipse task is the original implementation of the Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm and remains the de facto reference against which all subsequent implementations are validated. IRAF Isofit and Cmodel are Ciambur (2015)'s extensions for eccentric-anomaly sampling and joint higher-order harmonic fitting respectively, packaged as drop-in replacements for Ellipse and its model-reconstruction counterpart Bmodel.

ISOSTER's relationship to this family is one of faithful reimplementation with extensions. The five-parameter harmonic fit, the geometry-update rule (dominant-amplitude coordinate descent), the inward / outward growth pattern, the stop-code domain (semantically equivalent to IRAF's status codes), and the acceptable-codes propagation policy are all preserved. The ψ-basis sampling of §1.4.1 reproduces Ciambur (2015)'s Isofit construction in its use_eccentric_anomaly=True mode; the joint ISOFIT-style harmonic solve of §1.4.1 reproduces Isofit's extended design matrix in its simultaneous_harmonics=True, isofit_mode='in_loop' configuration. The post-hoc higher-order fit in the isofit_mode='original' variant reproduces the Ciambur (2015) original procedure.

On axes the IRAF family does not address, ISOSTER provides extensions:

  • Variance-aware fitting (§1.4.2). IRAF Ellipse and Isofit use unweighted ordinary least squares for the harmonic fit. The WLS path of ISOSTER is novel relative to the IRAF family.
  • LSB outskirt strategy (§1.4.3). The IRAF family has no automatic LSB-regime mechanism; users push to whatever SMA the fit converges to and accept the failure mode beyond.
  • Multi-band joint free fit (§1.4.5). IRAF Ellipse is single-band by design; multi-band photometry requires running Ellipse independently per band and accepting the band-distinct geometries, or running an external forced-photometry workflow. ISOSTER's joint free fit is novel.
  • Operations infrastructure (§1.4.4, §1.4.6). Batch retry, permissive geometry propagation, Pydantic-validated configuration, round-trip serialization of the configuration alongside the results, ASDF support, JSON-encoded config tables — these are operational concerns the IRAF family predates.

On axes the IRAF family does address, two practical differences matter:

  • Implementation language. The IRAF family is a Fortran / C implementation invoked through IRAF's CL scripting; ISOSTER is pure Python with vectorized NumPy / SciPy / Numba kernels. Performance differences depend on the platform; the Python re-implementations of the IRAF family (photutils.isophote, ISOSTER) generally trade IRAF's tight inner-loop performance for the Python ecosystem's data-science integration. ISOSTER recovers a substantial portion of IRAF's inner-loop performance through Numba JIT on the linear-system kernels (§1.3.2).
  • Maintenance and accessibility. IRAF is no longer actively maintained; new analyses are increasingly written in Python. The IRAF family remains the reference for cross-validation but is decreasingly the day-to-day tool.

The IRAF family is therefore the algorithmic ancestor against which the correctness of any Python re-implementation should be checked, but the IRAF family itself is not where the practical day-to-day fits are run on contemporary survey data.

docs.title: §1.5.2 vs photutils.isophote
docs.text:
The photutils.isophote package is the direct Python re-implementation of the IRAF Ellipse algorithm. It is maintained as a subpackage of photutils, the broader Astropy- ecosystem photometry library. The implementation faithfully reproduces the Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm; it is the natural predecessor against which ISOSTER's Python-level speed and feature gains are measured, and the comparison against it is the most relevant for users coming from the Astropy ecosystem.

ISOSTER and photutils.isophote agree on the core algorithm. Both compute the same five-parameter harmonic fit, both update geometry through the dominant-amplitude rule, both grow outward from an anchor SMA with sigma-clipping. The OLS code path of ISOSTER (i.e. with no variance map supplied) is the same ordinary least-squares solve photutils.isophote performs; the two implementations nevertheless ship different defaults (sampling count, minit, convergence details), so numerical agreement is a matched-configuration question that the benchmark chapters address rather than an out-of-the-box identity. Differences appear in three classes:

Performance. The §1.3 algorithmic-speed argument names four choices that ISOSTER makes which photutils.isophote does not make: end-to-end vectorized sampling through map_coordinates, Numba JIT inner kernels, lazy gradient evaluation, and a shared sampling stack across regular fitting and forced extraction (2-D model reconstruction solves a different problem and does not use it). The first three are direct speed improvements at the algorithmic level; the fourth is a software- engineering improvement that compounds the first three. The benchmark chapters quantify the aggregate speedup; the qualitative argument is that ISOSTER replaces a per-pixel Python sampling loop with one C-level interpolation call per isophote, while photutils.isophote retains the per-pixel loop in the integrator classes that handle area-integral sampling.

Algorithm extensions. ISOSTER's eccentric-anomaly sampling, ISOFIT-style joint harmonic fits, variance-aware (WLS) fitting, LSB outskirt strategy, multi-band joint free fit, and batch robustness primitives are all new relative to photutils.isophote. The latter implements the classical algorithm faithfully but does not extend it. Users who need any of the §1.4 features have no direct path through photutils.isophote and currently route through tool-specific external machinery (mask-then-mask-again loops, per-band external forced-photometry pipelines, hand-tuned transition SMAs for LSB fits).

Operational features. ISOSTER's four-HDU FITS layout with explicit CONFIG block (§1.4.6.3), the round-trip serialization property, ASDF support, Pydantic-validated configuration with cross-parameter rejection, and the QA plotting subsystem with cross-tool comparison facility are all ISOSTER additions. photutils.isophote returns Astropy tables and leaves configuration management to the caller; QA plotting is left to the user's downstream pipeline.

Two areas where photutils.isophote has the upper hand should be named honestly. First, photutils.isophote is part of the broader photutils package, which carries decades of accumulated photometry infrastructure (aperture photometry, source detection, PSF photometry, background estimation). A user already working in the photutils ecosystem benefits from staying within it; ISOSTER is an external dependency by comparison. Second, photutils.isophote has been deployed in published photometric analyses for longer than ISOSTER, and the consensus on its calibration and behaviour is more mature. ISOSTER's test suite does pin agreement with photutils.isophote on a panel of synthetic Sérsic models, but the scope of that check is narrow enough to be worth stating rather than gesturing at. It is an agreement band rather than an equivalence — the median intensity difference must stay under \(1\%\), the median ellipticity difference under \(0.01\), and the median position-angle difference under \(5^\circ\) — and the panel varies Sérsic index, ellipticity and noise level while holding the effective radius fixed at \(20\,\mathrm{px}\) throughout, so it does not probe the size dependence at all. The configurations are also matched by construction rather than run out of the box: the harness enables eccentric-anomaly sampling above \(\varepsilon = 0.3\) and relaxes maxgerr above \(\varepsilon = 0.6\). One further gap is worth naming because it affects the quantity most prone to it: the comparison helper differences position angles as if they were \(2\pi\)-periodic, whereas PA is an axis-like quantity defined mod \(\pi\), so galaxies near the wrap boundary are not yet robustly covered. Agreement on the medians of a fixed-size synthetic panel is a considerably weaker statement than agreement on real galaxies, and the long-tail behaviour on edge cases is still being characterized. (§1.3.4 is explicit that it makes no cross-tool numerical-agreement claim; the quantitative comparison belongs to the benchmark chapters.)

The honest summary is narrower than "strict generalization", and the temptation to claim that should be resisted. ISOSTER implements the same algorithm family as photutils.isophote and adds a substantial feature set on top, but it is not a superset in the sense that every photutils.isophote fit is reproducible by flipping ISOSTER's flags off. The two differ in ways that no configuration switch reconciles: the sampling and integration machinery, the convergence rule and its SMA-dependent scaling, the step-clipping and gradient-SNR safeguards that are always on in ISOSTER, the stop-code semantics, and a range of defaults. Some of those differences are deliberate improvements and none is switchable back.

Whether the two agree on a given galaxy under matched configurations is therefore an empirical question, not an identity that follows from the code structure, and the benchmark chapters treat it as such. Users who do not need the extensions have a defensible reason to remain with photutils.isophote; users who need any of the §1.4 features have a defensible reason to move; and users migrating an existing analysis should expect to validate the transition rather than assume it.

docs.title: §1.5.3 vs AutoProf (Stone, Arora, Courteau & Cuillandre 2021)
docs.text:
AutoProf is the modern Python pipeline most directly comparable to ISOSTER in scope. Both tools target the same problem class (non-parametric elliptical isophote fitting on modern survey imaging, with a particular focus on the LSB regime), both are written in Python with C / vectorized kernels for the inner loops, both deploy on survey samples in the thousands, and both make explicit the LSB-regime failure modes the classical algorithm encounters and offer specific machinery for handling them. The comparison is therefore the most informative of the three for positioning ISOSTER's design choices.

The fundamental design difference is in how the LSB-regime failure modes are addressed. AutoProf adopts an ML-style fit-stabilization approach: a regularization scheme that smooths the per-SMA geometry estimates across radii using techniques adapted from the machine-learning literature on overparameterized regression. The smoothing operates in the post-iteration analysis step, taking the per-SMA fit outputs as input and producing regularized geometry profiles that are constrained to vary smoothly with SMA. The approach is global: the regularization strength is set by a single parameter and applies uniformly across the SMA range.

ISOSTER's LSB strategy (§1.4.3) is local and explicit: a logistic-Tikhonov ramp \(\lambda(a)\) damps geometry updates as a function of SMA, with the strength growing continuously from the high-\(S/N\) inner regime (where the damping is essentially zero) to the LSB tail (where the damping is substantial). The strength is set by three interpretable parameters (outer_reg_strength, outer_reg_sma_onset, outer_reg_sma_width) and the spatial profile of the damping is explicit. The automatic LSB lock layer (§1.4.3.2) adds a hard-threshold state-machine mechanism that freezes the geometry when the gradient diagnostics indicate the fit can no longer be trusted. Together the soft + hard pair is a designed-to-compose mechanism with no equivalent in AutoProf, but also no claim to be globally smoother than AutoProf's regularization.

The two approaches have different scientific philosophies. The ML-style approach in AutoProf treats the per-SMA fits as noisy samples of a smooth function and uses prior information about smoothness as the regularizer. The logistic-Tikhonov approach in ISOSTER treats the per-SMA fits as iteration-trajectory points and uses an SMA-dependent prior that pulls toward an inner reference. Neither is uniformly better; they target different mental models of the underlying problem and produce different trade-offs on different galaxy classes. We anticipate the benchmark chapters will show that the two approaches agree to within their respective regularization strengths on the non-LSB-dominated subsamples and diverge most visibly on the deep-LSB-contaminated subsamples, where the failure mode the strategy is addressing actually fires.

On axes that are not specific to the LSB strategy:

  • Variance-aware fitting. AutoProf has variance handling built into its pipeline as documented in Stone et al. 2021; AutoProf's treatment differs in implementation detail from ISOSTER's WLS formulation but achieves the analogous outcome of weighting per-pixel contributions by photon noise.
  • Eccentric-anomaly sampling. Whether AutoProf's harmonic coefficients share the ISOSTER / Bender normalization is unverified: the benchmark adapter passes them through unconverted, which presumes they do, and that presumption has never been tested. An earlier version of this chapter asserted the scale differed, which was equally untested; neither position rests on a measurement. Until one exists, AutoProf's higher-order harmonics are excluded from published cross-tool comparisons; whether any coefficient-scale conversion is needed is precisely what the verification would determine (§1.4.6.2). This is a gap in our knowledge of the interface, not an algorithmic gap in AutoProf itself.
  • Multi-band joint free fit. AutoProf operates per-band and uses external forced-photometry workflows to cross bands. The joint multi-band free fit of §1.4.5 is novel relative to AutoProf.
  • Analysis subsystem. AutoProf has a substantial analysis subsystem accumulated over its longer deployment history, including slice-based alternative profiles, smooth axisymmetric model reconstruction, and decision-tree pipelining. ISOSTER's analysis subsystem is more focused: 2-D model reconstruction from the converged harmonic decomposition, curve-of-growth attachment, and the QA plotting subsystem of §1.4.6.2. A user who needs AutoProf's analysis features will find ISOSTER less complete on those axes.
  • LSB depth. AutoProf reports reaching surface brightnesses approximately 2 magnitudes per square arcsecond fainter than classical predecessors on the same imaging (Stone et al. 2021). ISOSTER's LSB strategy is designed to reach comparable depths; the benchmark chapters quantify the actual comparison on the shared mock and real-galaxy samples.

The honest summary is that AutoProf and ISOSTER are parallel modern pipelines that have made different design choices on several axes (LSB regularization philosophy, multi-band strategy, analysis-subsystem scope) and that overlap substantially on others (variance handling, single-band fitting on survey imaging). Users facing a choice between them should base the choice on which design philosophy matches the science target and on which analysis-subsystem features they need.

docs.title: §1.5.4 Feature matrix
docs.text:
The feature matrix below summarizes the comparison on the axes discussed above. Cells are marked ✓ (full support), (✓) (partial / different convention from ISOSTER), — (not provided), or n/a (not applicable to that tool's scope). Some entries are short qualitative summaries rather than yes/no markers; the matrix is intended as a quick reference, not as a comprehensive specification.

Feature IRAF Ellipse/Isofit photutils.isophote AutoProf ISOSTER Position-angle sampling (φ) ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Eccentric-anomaly sampling (ψ) ✓ (Isofit) — (✓) basis unverified ✓ Post-hoc higher-order harmonics ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ISOFIT-style joint harmonic fit (in-loop) (✓) original variant — — ✓ Variance-aware fitting (WLS) — — ✓ different formulation ✓ Bender-normalized harmonic reporting (✓) ✓ (?) scale unverified ✓ Automatic LSB outer-region regularization — — (✓) ML-style smoothing ✓ logistic Tikhonov Automatic LSB geometry lock — — — ✓ Multi-band joint free fit — — — ✓ Multi-band higher-harmonic modes (4 variants) — — — ✓ Loose-validity per-band masking — — — ✓ Batch robustness primitives (retry / permissive) — (✓) limited (✓) via pipeline ✓ Single-object configuration with validation — — (✓) ✓ Pydantic Four-HDU FITS with CONFIG + META round-trip — — — ✓ ASDF serialization — — — ✓ QA plotting subsystem (single-tool) n/a — ✓ ✓ Cross-tool QA comparison plots n/a — — ✓ 2-D model reconstruction from converged fit ✓ (Cmodel) ✓ ✓ ✓ Curve-of-growth attachment — — ✓ ✓ Smooth axisymmetric model — — ✓ (✓) via build_isoster_model Slice-based alternative profiles — — ✓ — Decision-tree pipelining — — ✓ — Native Python — ✓ ✓ ✓ Active maintenance — ✓ ✓ ✓ Reference implementation ✓ historical (✓) — —

How to read this table, and what it is not. The ISOSTER column is compiled from this repository and is checked against the code. The other three columns are not: they were compiled from the tools' documentation and source as read during drafting, and they have not been re-verified against current releases, nor against the projects' own descriptions of themselves. Two kinds of entry age especially badly. The "Active maintenance" row is a snapshot of release activity at the time of writing and will be wrong at some point without anything in this repository changing. And the detailed behavioural claims about AutoProf — its variance weighting, its harmonic basis and normalization — are our reading of another project's implementation, which its authors are better placed to characterise than we are. Before publication these columns should be replaced by, or checked against, a source-based software review with versions and dates attached; treat them meanwhile as a rough orientation rather than as findings.

A handful of cells deserve elaboration. The "(✓) different formulation" entry for AutoProf's variance handling reflects that AutoProf does weight per-pixel contributions but through a mechanism that differs from ISOSTER's explicit \(\mathbf{W} = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma_i^2)\) WLS construction; the two are operationally equivalent in the limit of well-behaved variance maps but differ in detail. The "basis unverified" and "scale unverified" entries for AutoProf's harmonics are exactly that — unverified, not established as different. The benchmark adapter copies its coefficients through without conversion, which presumes they match ours, while §1.4.6.2 has recorded the opposite. Nobody has run the experiment that would settle it, so these cells state ignorance rather than a finding, and AutoProf's harmonics stay out of published comparisons until they are checked. The "(✓) Cmodel" entry under 2-D model reconstruction for IRAF reflects that Cmodel and ISOSTER's build_isoster_model are functionally parallel; both produce a 2-D model image from the converged isophote list.

The matrix is not a quality-ranking. Several rows where ISOSTER shows ✓ and the other tools show — reflect features that are ISOSTER's design contributions; several other rows where AutoProf shows ✓ and ISOSTER shows — reflect AutoProf's longer-deployment analysis subsystem. The two pipelines have grown in different directions from a shared algorithmic core.

docs.title: §1.5.5 Closing observations on the comparison
docs.text:
Three observations close this subsection.

The first is that ISOSTER's positioning is not "the replacement" for any of the three predecessors. The IRAF family remains the algorithmic reference and the historical canon. photutils.isophote remains the right choice for users in the Astropy ecosystem who do not need the §1.4 features. AutoProf remains the right choice for users whose science requires its specific analysis-subsystem features or whose LSB problem maps better onto the ML-style regularization philosophy. ISOSTER fills the niche of modern Python pipeline with explicit configurable LSB-regime mechanisms, joint multi-band free fit, and Pydantic- validated configuration with round-trip reproducibility — a niche that no existing tool covers in full.

The second is that the comparison is not stable in time. Each of the three predecessors is maintained by an active community; features that ISOSTER currently provides may be added to one or more of them in future releases. The feature matrix should be read as a snapshot of the state at the time of this paper, not as a permanent characterization. We will update the matrix in subsequent revisions to reflect the moving state of the ecosystem.

The third is that the comparison rests on a substantial body of shared algorithmic ancestry. All four tools implement the Jedrzejewski (1987) algorithm at their core; the differences are in the extensions, the implementation choices, and the operational machinery around that core. The benchmark chapters of this paper, which quantify the actual cross-tool comparison on shared datasets, will show that the four tools agree on the geometry and intensity outputs to within their respective configuration choices on a substantial fraction of galaxies, and diverge where the configuration choices and extensions become relevant. The §1.5 comparison maps the configuration-and-extension space; the benchmark chapters fill in the numbers.

docs.title: §1.6 Limitations and roadmap
docs.text:
The technical chapter closes with an honest accounting of where ISOSTER currently falls short and where the development effort is heading. The limitations described below are not failures relative to a putative ideal tool; they are the boundaries of what ISOSTER covers in the version this paper documents. Some are intrinsic to the algorithmic scope (2-D images, non-parametric isophote analysis); some are operational (compute cost on cold starts, calibration of LSB-regime defaults); some are deferred (GPU kernels, IFU cube support). The roadmap items at the end of the subsection name the development directions we anticipate addressing in subsequent releases, without committing to a release schedule.

The honest-accounting framing matters for the same reason the per-feature demonstration sections in §1.4 were cherry-picked but honest: a tool that overstates its scope produces application failures downstream, and a tool that understates its scope is under-used. The aim of this subsection is to leave the reader with an accurate map of what ISOSTER will and will not do on a given problem.

docs.title: §1.6.1 Algorithm-level scope: what ISOSTER is not
docs.text:
ISOSTER is a non-parametric elliptical-isophote fitter for 2-D images. Three classes of analysis are out of scope by design and will remain so:

  • Parametric model fitting — Sérsic, double-Sérsic, exponential

  • bulge, multi-component fits, GALFIT-style \(\chi^2\) minimization over component parameters. ISOSTER's output is a non-parametric description of the isophotal structure; users who need parametric decomposition should pair ISOSTER with a dedicated tool (GALFIT, imfit, pysersic, astropy.modeling). The output schemas are not incompatible — ISOSTER's results dictionary contains enough information to seed a parametric fit at the initial-guess level — but the parametric fit itself is a separate analysis.

  • PSF deconvolution and PSF-aware fitting. The harmonic fit operates on the observed image without modeling the PSF. The consequences are well-known: in the regime where the galaxy is small relative to the PSF FWHM, the fitted geometry is biased by the PSF convolution; in the regime where the galaxy is large but the PSF wings extend across many isophotes, the outer isophotes inherit a small wing-contribution bias. ISOSTER reports the geometry of the observed isophotes; converting to intrinsic geometries requires an external PSF model. For nearby galaxies with extended PSF wings (very nearby NGC objects, the inner halos of bright ellipticals, the wings of saturated stars near the target), this is the dominant scientific limitation.

  • 3-D spectral cubes and multi-wavelength model fitting. The multi-band joint free fit of §1.4.5 operates on co-aligned 2-D images, one per band. A spectroscopic IFU cube (MaNGA, SAMI, Mauve, the LSST 4MOST follow-up cubes) is not a 2-D image with extra bands; it is a \((x, y, \lambda)\) data structure whose isophote analysis would generalize the per-isophote loop along the wavelength axis. The single-band sampling stack generalizes naturally, but the corresponding driver, fitting loop, and output schema do not yet exist. IFU support is on the roadmap (§1.6.6) but is not in the current release.

A fourth out-of-scope class is time-domain photometry on variable sources — supernova light-curve fitting, AGN variability monitoring, transient followup. ISOSTER is not the right tool for any of these.

docs.title: §1.6.2 Features whose defaults are still being calibrated
docs.text:
Several §1.4 features are in active use but with default parameter values that we describe as heuristic recommendations rather than survey-tested defaults. The list:

  • Outer-region center regularization (§1.4.3.1) — outer_reg_strength, outer_reg_sma_onset, and outer_reg_sma_width were initially calibrated on HSC-SSP edge cases for deep-LSB disk-galaxy fits. The recommended ranges documented in the configuration reference apply to HSC-scale imaging; DECaLS / BASS / MzLS, with different seeing and sky brightness, may require different ranges. The form of the logistic ramp is robust to these differences (the function itself is well-behaved across surveys), but the recommended values are not yet survey-blind.

  • Automatic LSB lock trigger threshold (§1.4.3.2) — the lsb_auto_lock_maxgerr = 0.30 default was chosen to fire before the gradient-acceptability check at maxgerr = 0.50 would have produced a stop code \(-1\), with a debounce count of \(2\). On bright galaxies in clean fields the lock essentially never fires (its purpose is to handle LSB regimes the bright-galaxy fit doesn't enter). On the deep LSB regime the defaults are tuned for HSC-scale imaging; the trigger threshold may need adjustment for surveys with substantially different per-pixel photon noise characteristics.

  • Multi-band loose-validity participation thresholds (§1.4.5.4) — loose_validity_min_per_band_count and loose_validity_min_per_band_frac set the participation cuts below which a band is dropped from the joint fit on a given isophote. The defaults are lenient (a band is dropped only when it keeps fewer than 6 samples or under 20% of the rectangular sample count) but the optimal values depend on the typical per-band mask asymmetry of the input data. Surveys with consistently good per-band masking may want tighter cuts; surveys with patchy per-band masking may need to relax the cuts.

  • Lazy-gradient stall detector (§1.3.2) — the three-iteration stall threshold at which the gradient is re-evaluated is a heuristic. It is set tight enough that the gradient is refreshed on essentially any case where the iteration is meaningfully slowing, and loose enough that ordinary convergence does not trigger a redundant re-evaluation. The default works well across the validated samples but is not individually configurable; users with pathological iteration trajectories may benefit from a future configurable threshold.

This entry is a calibration item, but the underlying feature is also a genuine accuracy limitation and belongs on the list as such. As §1.3.2 quantifies, the lazy gradient is a fast approximation, not an exact reformulation: converged geometries differ from the use_lazy_gradient=False reference by a median of well under one percent of the fitted uncertainty, but with a tail that grows as the data get noisier — reaching \(2.6\sigma\) on the worst isophote of a \(S/N = 10\) test sequence. The regime where the approximation is loosest is the LSB outskirt regime of §1.4.3, which is also where several of ISOSTER's science cases live. Users measuring per-isophote geometry in that regime should consider paying the roughly 31% surcharge for the exact path. A better resolution — refreshing the gradient adaptively on a gradient-SNR criterion rather than on a fixed stall count, so the approximation tightens automatically where it is weakest — is on the roadmap.

  • Outer-region regularization does not compose with ISOFIT (§1.4.3.3) — the Tikhonov shrinkage is applied where a five-parameter harmonic solve becomes a geometry step, and was never wired into the wider ISOFIT joint solver. Requesting use_outer_center_regularization=True together with simultaneous_harmonics=True therefore retains only the selector-level penalty and silently loses the per-iteration step damping. ISOSTER warns at configuration time, so the gap is announced rather than hidden, but it is the one place in §1.4 where two features do not give the union of their effects. Closing it means threading the per-axis Jacobian through the wider solve; it is a bounded piece of work that has simply not been done.

  • Per-axis regularization weights are effectively binary (§1.4.3.1) — measured on a BCG test case, the Tikhonov blend factor saturates above \(99.99\%\) for any per-axis weight in the range a user would plausibly type, because the harmonic-to-geometry Jacobian grows without bound as the radial gradient approaches zero. Intermediate weights such as \(\{1, 0.5, 0.5\}\) therefore behave like \(\{1, 1, 1\}\), and the honest "partial damping" regime would require weights around \(10^{-4}\). The field is documented as a binary switch, but the fact that a continuous-looking parameter is not in fact continuous over its useful range is a design wart rather than a feature.

The calibration status is documented in docs/02-configuration-reference.md for each of these fields. The parameters are user-configurable, and the recommended values are the current recommendations — they may be revised in subsequent releases as the validation samples grow.

docs.title: §1.6.3 Mask and variance-map quality dependence
docs.text:
ISOSTER inherits a substantial amount of upstream-pipeline state through its mask and variance_map arguments. The fit's algorithmic correctness does not depend on these inputs; an unmasked image with no variance map produces a correct five-parameter harmonic fit by definition. The quality of the fit on real survey data depends on them substantially.

Mask quality. A mask that misses bad pixels (defects, cosmic rays, hot pixels, secondary sources) produces a harmonic fit contaminated by those pixels. The variance-aware fit (§1.4.2) provides automatic down-weighting of high-variance pixels, but it does not provide masking — a survival weight of \(10^{-6}\) from a bad pixel with \(\sigma^2 = 10^{6}\) is small but not zero, and a band of bad pixels across an early isophote can swing the harmonic amplitude by an amount that survives the WLS weighting. The user is responsible for providing a mask that covers known bad pixels; ISOSTER does not derive a mask from the image.

Variance-map quality. The WLS path of §1.4.2 weights each sample by the user-supplied \(1 / \sigma_i^2\). If the variance map underestimates the true photon noise — typical of coadded imaging where pixel-to-pixel noise is correlated and the naive per-pixel variance does not reflect the effective noise per resolution element — WLS produces over-confident error bars. ISOSTER cannot diagnose this from the variance map alone; the caller is responsible for upstream correction (a noise-rescaling factor estimated from blank sky, a covariance-matrix model of the coaddition). On survey data where the variance map is the pipeline default, this is a known systematic that the benchmark chapters discuss in detail.

Background model quality. The sigma_bg field (§1.4.4.6) sets the photon-noise floor on the convergence criterion. A poorly characterized background — under-subtracted sky, residual gradients across the image, scattered light — biases the fit's LSB-regime behaviour even when the variance map is correct. ISOSTER provides no background subtraction; the user supplies the sky-subtracted image and the documented sigma_bg value.

In all three cases the limitation is upstream from ISOSTER's algorithm and ISOSTER cannot resolve it on its own. A survey pipeline that consumes ISOSTER's output should therefore treat mask quality, variance-map accuracy, and background subtraction as prerequisites rather than as outputs of the ISOSTER fit.

docs.title: §1.6.4 Scattered light and extended-PSF regimes
docs.text:
A specific failure mode worth flagging separately is the regime where the extended PSF wings of a bright source dominate the outskirt isophotes of a faint nearby target. This includes:

  • Very nearby NGC galaxies observed with HSC, DECam, or similar wide-field instruments where the PSF wings carry measurable flux out to \(10\)–\(20\,\mathrm{arcmin}\).
  • The inner halos of bright ellipticals in galaxy clusters, where the BCG's PSF wings contribute to the apparent isophote structure of nearby cluster members.
  • Saturated foreground stars whose diffraction spikes intersect the target's outer isophotes; the binary mask removes the spike core but the wing structure is harder to characterize.

For these cases the LSB outskirt strategy of §1.4.3 reduces the geometry drift but does not address the underlying scattered-light contamination of the intensity profile. The fitted geometry under the soft + hard composition may converge to a sensible value while the intensity profile in the outer SMAs carries a scattered-light bias that biases color gradients, mass-to-light profile estimates, and intracluster-light measurements.

The proper resolution is upstream: a scattered-light model appropriate to the instrument and exposure that is subtracted from the image before ISOSTER is called. ISOSTER does not provide such a model — there is no general-purpose scattered-light model that works across instruments — and integrates with whichever external scattered-light pipeline the survey provides.

Users analyzing nearby galaxies in crowded fields or BCGs in cluster environments should consider this regime carefully when interpreting outer-isophote intensities; the geometry may be robust to the contamination while the intensity is not.

docs.title: §1.6.5 Computational considerations
docs.text:
Three computational considerations affect when ISOSTER is the right tool to deploy.

Cold-start cost. Three separate costs are routinely conflated as "the JIT cost", and they call for different responses. Measured on the reference machine: importing the stack (Numba included) costs \(0.84\,\mathrm{s}\) (IQR \(0.83\)–\(0.86\)); the first fit against a populated Numba cache costs \(0.101\,\mathrm{s}\) (IQR \(0.099\)–\(0.103\)) more than a subsequent fit, which is the cache being read from disk rather than anything being compiled; and the first fit against an empty cache costs a further \(0.36\,\mathrm{s}\) (IQR \(0.36\)–\(0.37\)), which is the genuine compilation. Each is an across-session median over the archived run's empty-cache / populated-cache pairs — the measurement cannot be batched, since every observation costs an interpreter start — quoted to the precision its own spread supports. What matters is the ordering and the proportions.

The compilation cost is paid once per compatible cache, not once per installation. Upgrading Numba or ISOSTER invalidates the cached objects, and an environment that cannot write the cache directory pays it on every process. The everyday cold-start penalty a user meets — a fresh process on a machine whose cache is already populated — is the import plus the cache load, a little under a second in total, of which none is compilation. On a survey pipeline processing thousands of galaxies the cost is amortized to negligibility; on a one-galaxy analysis it is added to every cold-process run.

The pure-NumPy fallback (forced with NUMBA_DISABLE_JIT=1) avoids the compilation cost at the price of a slowdown on the hot kernels, so which is cheaper depends on how many fits a process performs. On the same small fixture as above the fallback is about \(1.23\times\) slower per fit in steady state. What it avoids is the compiled path's whole excess over its own steady state on a cache-less run — the compilation and the cache load together, not the compilation term alone, since a fallback process performs neither — and dividing the two puts the break-even at about 50 fits per process (IQR 47–52 across the archived sessions). A user fitting one galaxy in a fresh process is therefore genuinely better off with the fallback, and a pipeline fitting hundreds is not — the recommendation this paragraph used to make on intuition, now with the crossing point attached.

Two things bound that number. The quartiles are tight but the upper tail is not: sessions ranged from 45 to 76 fits, so the crossing point is a few tens of fits rather than precisely fifty. And it is one fixture on one machine, with both terms sensitive to the workload — the per-fit penalty depends on what fraction of a fit is spent inside the compiled kernels, which varies with image size and ring count, and the start-up cost varies with how much of the library a given configuration touches. The ordering of the recommendation is robust; the threshold should be re-measured on any workload it is being applied to.

Multi-band cost scaling. The joint multi-band fit of §1.4.5 is not linear in the number of bands, and the earlier claim that it costs \(\mathrm{O}(B)\) per iteration was wrong. The design-matrix construction and the WLS row scaling are indeed \(\mathrm{O}(BN)\), but the solve forms dense normal equations on a \((BN) \times (B+4)\) matrix, whose cost carries additional factors of \(B\). Measured on one joint solve with \(N = 700\) samples per band, for the geometry-parameterised solver that is the supported default (§1.4.5.2):

\(B\) OLS ratio to previous WLS ratio to previous 3 0.196 ms — 0.158 ms — 6 0.333 ms 1.7× 0.351 ms 2.2× 12 0.605 ms 1.8× 0.663 ms 1.9× 24 2.49 ms 4.1× 2.60 ms 3.9×

The scaling is close to linear through \(B \approx 12\) and departs beyond it. Three caveats on reading this. First, the final ratio is the least stable number in this chapter: over eighteen sessions its median is \(4.4\) with an interquartile range of \(4.2\)–\(4.5\), and it is the one aggregate whose median still shifts appreciably between independent sets. It supports "several times, not twice" and no finer statement. Second, the departure is milder for the supported geometry form than for the legacy shared-amplitude form, which the harness also times: the latter runs about \(6.0\times\) from \(B = 12\) to \(24\). Benchmarking the amplitude form and presenting it as the multi-band cost — as an earlier version of this section did — overstates the high-\(B\) penalty, because after an isophote's first iteration the default takes the geometry path. Third, we report the departure but do not diagnose it: attributing it to the cubic term in the normal-equations solve, to memory-hierarchy effects, or to a threading threshold in the host BLAS would require profiling we have not done. The \(B = 24\) entry is the least stable of the four across runs and machines, so read it as "several times, not twice". For typical survey-scale \(B \in \{3, 4, 5, 6\}\) the cost is therefore a small multiple of the single-band cost, as the linear intuition suggests; for \(B \in \{10, 20, \ldots\}\) (eventual narrowband-survey applications: J-PAS, J-PLUS, PAU) it becomes a significant pipeline item faster than a linear extrapolation would predict. The configuration alternative for the high-\(B\) regime is to fit reduced band subsets jointly, with forced photometry between subsets. Loose validity is not an alternative here, and an earlier version of this section suggested it was: the jagged path solves a \((\sum_b N_b) \times (B + 4)\) system, so it leaves the \(B\)-dependent column count untouched and commonly carries more rows than shared validity, since it stops discarding samples that only one band failed. It is a masking-policy choice with its own merits (§1.4.5.4), not a performance lever.

Wall-time on large images. The per-isophote cost is asymptotically sublinear in image area through map_coordinates interpolation (§1.3.3), so the dependence of fit time on image size is mild. However, the total fit time depends on the SMA range, which depends on image size when the target is well resolved — but two quantities scale differently here and conflating them is what produced the \(4\times\) claim in an earlier version of this section. Under the default geometric SMA stepping the ring count grows only logarithmically: doubling \(a_\mathrm{max}\) adds \(\log 2 / \log(1 + \mathtt{astep})\) rings, about seven at the default astep = 0.1. But each ring carries \(N = \max(64, \lfloor 2\pi a \rfloor)\) samples, so the aggregate sampling work still grows roughly linearly in \(a_\mathrm{max}\). Measured on a galaxy chosen so that every ring converges out to 400 px — which matters more than it sounds, and is discussed below the table:

\(a_\mathrm{max}\) rings sampling calls points sampled wall time 100 px 56 460 66 600 47.4 ms 200 px 63 516 118 886 58.8 ms 400 px 70 574 225 744 78.4 ms

All rings return stop code 0 at all three limits, with a median of seven iterations, so the three fits are doing comparable work per ring and the comparison is about the ring sequence rather than about convergence behaviour. The sampling columns are instrumented — counted from the actual calls, which include every iteration and the extra passes for gradient evaluation — not inferred from one nominal pass per output ring, which undercounts by roughly an order of magnitude.

Two trends, stated separately because the measurement does not connect them. Ring count grows logarithmically (56 → 63 → 70), as geometric stepping requires. Points sampled grows almost exactly linearly (factors of 1.79 then 1.90 per doubling). Wall time lands between the two, rising by about \(1.3\times\) per doubling.

Two things this does not establish. The first is a general scaling law for the wall-time growth. Over eighteen sessions the two step ratios are \(1.25\) (IQR \(1.23\)–\(1.27\)) for \(100 \to 200\,\mathrm{px}\) and \(1.32\) (IQR \(1.30\)–\(1.34\)) for \(200 \to 400\,\mathrm{px}\). The gap between them is real on this fixture, as the paired comparison below shows; what the benchmark cannot do is generalise it, because it was not designed to test acceleration and varies neither the galaxy nor the SMA grid.

It is worth being exact about what the comparison supports, since the temptation is to compare the two intervals by eye. Comparing marginal spreads would be the wrong test anyway — the two ratios are measured on the same sessions, so they are paired, and the paired difference is the quantity with any power. That difference is positive in 18 of 18 sessions with a median of \(+0.07\), the smallest of them \(+0.04\). That is evidence of mild acceleration for this fixture on this machine; an unbroken sweep is not something to wave away. What it does not establish is a general scaling law across galaxies, configurations or hardware — one galaxy and one SMA grid cannot separate a property of the algorithm from a property of the fixture, and this benchmark varies neither. (Those figures are archived alongside the rest, so they are checked rather than transcribed.) Establishing the general claim would need an experiment built for it: several fixtures, a pre-registered paired criterion, and enough sessions for the outliers to stop dominating. (An earlier version of this paragraph asserted that the medians differ by less than either spread. They do not — the difference, \(0.077\), exceeds both IQR widths, \(0.037\) and \(0.038\) — and the comparison was the wrong one to make regardless.) And it does not attribute the growth to the sampling term, because the benchmark measures totals only — it does not partition runtime into sampling, solving and per-iteration overhead. A component profile would settle both questions and has not been run. What the table does establish is the distinction the \(4\times\) claim missed: rings and sampled points scale differently, and only the latter is proportional to \(a_\mathrm{max}\). That \(4\times\) figure would be right under linear SMA stepping, where the ring count itself grows in proportion.

A caution about this measurement, because getting it wrong is easy and we did. An earlier version used a compact fixture on which six of the seven rings beyond 200 px failed with stop code \(-1\) after two or three iterations. Those rings are cheap precisely because they fail, and the resulting \(1.16\times\) was an artefact of early termination rather than evidence about sampling cost. Any scaling measurement of this kind has to report its stop codes.

We do not quote a per-galaxy runtime floor or a survey-scale extrapolation here. Both depend on image size, SMA grid, galaxy extent and configuration in ways a single number would misrepresent, and the benchmark chapters measure them on the actual campaign samples.

Measurement protocol. Every timing in this chapter — the lazy-gradient comparison of §1.3.2, the eccentric-anomaly and ISOFIT table of §1.4.1.4, the cold-start figures above and the two tables above — is produced by benchmarks/draft_timings/run_draft_timings.py, committed alongside the source, as are the two measurements there that are not timings: the lazy-gradient accuracy table of §1.3.2 and the NumPy-fallback break-even above. Six properties of that harness are what make the numbers worth quoting:

  • Batching. Sub-millisecond operations are repeated to a floor duration before the clock is read, because timing such a call individually measures the timer as much as the work.
  • Interleaving with a shuffled order. Repetitions of the arms being compared are interleaved rather than run in blocks. The order within each repetition is reshuffled from a recorded seed, because a fixed visiting order leaves whichever arm always runs last absorbing any within-repetition drift — which is precisely the high-band solve. Adding the shuffle measurably tightened the lazy-gradient ratio.
  • Spread, not just a median. Every raw repetition is retained and an interquartile range is reported beside each median. Some of these ratios are noisy enough that a single median would invite false precision, and the draft says so where that is the case.
  • Sessions in separate processes. A single session shares its Python imports, module state, warmed allocators and arm ordering, so repeating blocks within one understates the variability. --sessions N fans out N interpreters, each with its own arm-ordering seed, and archives every one. The chapter's aggregates come from an eighteen-session run, and they are reported as a median with an interquartile range rather than as a minimum and a maximum. That choice is empirical: across independent sets the medians and quartiles reproduce to within about a percentage point, while the extremes do not reproduce at all — one session in eighteen returned a negative lazy-gradient saving, an outlier we did not diagnose. An earlier version of this harness repeated passes inside one process and quoted min-to-max from three of them, which made its intervals look far tighter than they were and required revising them three times. Process isolation has limits worth naming: the operating system's filesystem page cache is machine-wide, and so is the machine's thermal and load state, so what separate sessions vary is process state, not the environment the process runs in.
  • Two exemptions, stated. Two blocks run in child processes because what they measure is fixed at interpreter start, so neither can be batched: cold start (three independent empty-cache/populated-cache pairs, quoted to one significant figure) and the NumPy-fallback comparison, which selects the fallback from the environment. The accuracy sweep behind the §1.3.2 table is the other kind of exemption: it measures a difference between two converged fits rather than a duration, so batching and interleaving have nothing to act on, and the quantity is fixed once the image is. What varies there is the noise realisation, so each session draws its own and the reported spread is a spread over realisations. Every other block follows the points above.
  • Two fixtures. A compact seeded Sérsic (\(n = 2\), \(R_e = 30\,\mathrm{px}\), \(\varepsilon = 0.4\), \(S/N = 50\)) for the whole-fit comparisons, and a wider, higher-\(S/N\) one for the maxsma block, which needs every ring out to 400 px to converge. The accuracy sweep reuses the compact fixture with its noise level varied, so its middle row and the lazy-gradient timing describe the same galaxy.

The environment (Python, NumPy, Numba, BLAS) is recorded with the results. Absolute times are machine-specific and should not be compared across hardware — an independent reviewer reproduced the band-scaling ratios on different hardware while the absolute times differed by about a factor of two. The ratios are what the arguments in this chapter rest on.

Every harness-derived timing quoted in this chapter comes from one archived run, committed as benchmarks/draft_timings/reference_timings.json, so those figures have a fixed provenance rather than depending on whichever invocation last overwrote the scratch output. A companion script, check_draft_numbers.py, rebuilds each quoted table row and summary clause from that archive and asserts the prose contains it verbatim, so a table that drifts out of step fails loudly instead of silently looking measured.

To be precise about the scope: what the checker guards is everything the harness produces — the tables and their summary clauses in §1.3.2, §1.4.1.4 and §1.6.5, including the lazy-gradient accuracy table and the restatement of its worst case in the limitations list above. Other numbers in this chapter come from elsewhere (configuration values, cross-references, and results from the benchmark campaigns) and the checker does not speak for them; its --self-test mode lists them so the boundary is visible rather than assumed.

Within that scope the checker matches whole rows and whole clauses rather than fragments, and --self-test perturbs each quoted number individually, requiring at least one check to fail for every one. Both properties exist because earlier versions lacked them. The original checker validated an interquartile range by searching for the bare substrings 23 and 25, which occur throughout the prose, and so passed against a draft whose figures had been deliberately altered; its successor mutated all digits simultaneously, which demonstrates only that each implemented check is sensitive to something, not that a claim has a check at all. A verification script that has never been shown to fail is not evidence.

docs.title: §1.6.6 Roadmap
docs.text:
The development directions we anticipate addressing in subsequent releases, in approximate order of priority:

GPU acceleration of hot kernels. The §1.3.2 inner kernels — design-matrix construction (single-band and joint multi-band), ellipse-coordinate construction, harmonic-model evaluation — are natural candidates for GPU acceleration through CuPy, JAX, or a vectorized PyTorch backend. The vectorized sampling step (scipy.ndimage.map_coordinates) has analogous GPU implementations available. We have not prototyped this and offer no speedup estimate: the achievable gain depends on whether the per-SMA loop can be restructured to give the device enough work per launch, which is the open design question rather than a detail. The kernels themselves are small, and a naive port that keeps the current one-isophote-at-a-time control flow would be dominated by launch overhead; the interesting version fuses the invocations across SMAs and across galaxies in a batch.

The motivation for the GPU roadmap is survey scale. LSST-class photometric surveys with \(\mathrm{O}(10^6)\) resolved galaxies per visit deliver more data than CPU-bound ISOSTER can comfortably process in real time. The GPU path makes the per-galaxy cost low enough that survey-pipeline integration is mechanical rather than performance-engineering.

Spectral / IFU cube support. The per-isophote loop generalizes naturally to a per-(isophote, wavelength) loop on a 3-D \((x, y, \lambda)\) cube. The wavelength axis enters through the sampling stack (sampling needs to interpolate along \(\lambda\) in addition to \((x, y)\)) and through the output schema (the results dictionary needs a wavelength dimension). The single-band sampling stack already encapsulates the implementation that the cube extension would build on, so the extension is a generalization rather than a rewrite. We anticipate IFU support landing in a paper-II release alongside applications to MaNGA, SAMI, and Mauve cubes.

Tighter PSF-aware modes. A PSF-aware fitting mode would deconvolve the PSF from the image before isophote sampling, or equivalently convolve the harmonic-fit model with the PSF before comparison to the observed isophote. The former requires deconvolution machinery; the latter requires a forward-model generalization of the harmonic decomposition. The forward-model approach is more numerically stable and is the direction we anticipate pursuing. Initial development targets the small-galaxy regime where the PSF FWHM is a non-trivial fraction of the galaxy's effective radius; the large-galaxy regime with extended PSF wings remains an upstream-pipeline problem.

Cross-tool QA comparison plumbing. The AutoProf-coefficient-scale porting gap mentioned in §1.4.6.2 and §1.5.3 is a known item in the cross-tool comparison plumbing. The first step is not a fix but a measurement: run AutoProf against a planted deviation and compare its reported coefficients with the ISOSTER and photutils values on the same fixture. That determines whether any conversion is needed at all — the benchmark adapter currently passes AutoProf's columns through unconverted, which presumes none is. If a conversion turns out to be required, an explicit factor in the QA plotting code is the planned approach; either way the §1.5 matrix's "unverified" entries for AutoProf can then be resolved.

Survey-blind LSB defaults. The §1.6.2 calibration items will be tightened as the validation sample grows. The aim is a single recommended default for each LSB-regime parameter that works acceptably across HSC, DECaLS, BASS / MzLS, DES, and the eventual LSST main survey, with documented deviations only for genuinely exceptional surveys.

A handful of smaller items — better error reporting on configuration mistakes, an interactive Jupyter QA panel, finer-grained logging — are also on the roadmap but are operational improvements rather than algorithmic ones; we do not itemize them here.

docs.title: §1.6.7 Closing remarks on the technical chapter
docs.text:
The technical chapter began with a three-goal framing — speed, flexibility, scientific power — and traversed §1.1 through §1.6 demonstrating how ISOSTER meets each. The algorithmic-speed argument of §1.3 establishes the first goal at the level of operation counts and code-path organization. The configurability surface of §1.2 and the six feature subsections of §1.4 establish the second goal by exposing each algorithmic feature as a flag on a validated configuration object — IsosterConfig for single-band work and the deliberately separate IsosterConfigMB for the multi-band path. The scientific-power argument runs through the same six §1.4 subsections, each of which demonstrates one new capability the classical Python predecessors do not jointly provide: eccentric-anomaly sampling and joint ISOFIT harmonic fitting faithfully reproduced from Ciambur 2015; variance-aware fitting with gradient errors propagated from the supplied noise model rather than from residual scatter; a soft + hard composition for the LSB outskirt regime; operations-grade batch robustness primitives; joint multi-band free fitting that offers an alternative to forced photometry for colour-gradient science, with a measured precision advantage at low signal-to-noise; and a QA / reproducibility infrastructure that ties the fit outputs to the configuration that produced them through round-trip serialization.

The aggregate is a tool calibrated for the next generation of deep, wide-field, multi-band imaging surveys — HSC-SSP, the late-stage DECaLS / BASS / MzLS samples, DES, the eventual LSST main survey — and structured so that the surveys' principal challenges (LSB outskirts, multi-band joint fitting, throughput at sample scale, reproducibility across pipeline runs) are directly addressed at the algorithmic level. The benchmark chapters that follow this technical chapter quantify the actual performance on the Huang2013, S4G, and SGA-2020 campaigns and provide the empirical evidence behind the §1.3 and §1.5 qualitative claims.

The closing observation is that ISOSTER is not finished — the §1.6 roadmap names several substantial development directions that the next release cycles will address — but the version documented in this chapter is operational in the sense that all six §1.4 features ship with regression-test coverage, all configurations are validated at construction, and the two on-disk serialization paths of §1.4.6.3 round-trip the isophote table, the resolved configuration and the run metadata. (The third path, the Astropy-Table conversion, deliberately returns the isophote table alone and is an in-memory convenience rather than an archival format.) Users can deploy the current version on their survey pipelines today; the roadmap items are improvements to that operational baseline, not blockers to it.

The technical chapter ends here. The benchmark chapters that follow apply the framework of §1.4.6.4 to the three campaign datasets and report the quantitative cross-tool comparisons that this chapter has carefully avoided.
